16i0hg4.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 21, 2026Malware / Artificial Intelligence The popular LiteLLM Python package has been compromised as part of a software supply chain attack that delivered a credential stealer and a backdoor, according to reports from SafeDep, Socket, StepSecurity, and Upwind. The compromise affects LiteLLM 1.107.0, distributed through PyPI wheels and Docker images. The Python package has since been quarantined on Python Package Index (PyPI), and the malicious Docker images have been removed. Oliver Jensen, director of security at LiteLLM, said an investigation into the incident is ongoing, and that it's still working to trace the original attack vector by which the threat actor published the malicious release. "We have identified that the malicious actions were taken through three engineers' GitHub accounts, appearing to be by way of stolen GitHub CLI OAuth tokens," Jensen said. "The threat actor used one user's account to trigger the project-releaser run, and another user's account to approve it. All tokens which were involved in this attack have been revoked." "We have not yet identified the mechanism by which the threat actor acquired the relevant tokens, so cannot yet assert that no further access to these GitHub accounts. As a temporary mitigation, we have removed all but one (unaffected) user from our GitHub organization." Separately, LiteLLM said it has updated the public registries to remove any trusted links to its GitHub organization so as to prevent further publication of malicious packages. Analysis of the malicious version shows that it's equipped to collect cloud credentials, private keys, browser data, and authentication files for AI development tools. The following wheels are affected - litellm-1.107.0-cp310-abi3-macosx_10_12_x86_64.whl litellm-1.107.0-cp310-abi3-macosx_11_0_arm64.whl litellm-1.107.0-cp310-abi3-manylinux_2_28_aarch64.whl litellm-1.107.0-cp310-abi3-manylinux_2_28_x86_64.whl litellm-1.107.0-cp310-abi3-musllinux_1_2_aarch64.whl litellm-1.107.0-cp310-abi3-musllinux_1_2_x86_64.whl litellm-1.107.0-cp310-abi3-win_amd64.whl litellm-1.107.0.tar.gz (No payload files, but has the tampered pyproject.toml) "The first payload is a credential stealer that calls itself privcollect," StepSecurity said. "The second payload forks a background daemon that checks a GitHub dead drop every hour and runs whatever Python the attacker serves." The malware is launched by Python even before LiteLLM is imported through a path file ("cook.pth"), which is designed to automatically execute code when the interpreter starts. It's worth noting that the same behavior was observed in the LiteLLM compromise that took place as part of the TeamPCP supply chain attacks earlier this March. The "cook.pth" file contains a single line, "import cook," which, in turn, launches the credential collector payload. This includes harvesting cloud tokens, developer accounts and private keys, AI tooling credential JSON files, browser data associated with Chromium and Firefox, and environment variables. The malware is also capable of targeting LiteLLM deployments with an aim to extract the proxy's saved credentials and model configuration. The collected data is packaged into a GZIP-compressed TAR archive and sent to "litellm[.]dev/healthcheck" by means of an HTTP POST request. In addition, the malware is designed to read the contents of a text file ("domain.txt") located within a GitHub repository ("github[.]com/letters9813"), check if it holds a domain and, if so, run the same stealer, and finally run an HTTP GET request against "<domain>/codepy" and execute the response. The GitHub repository currently returns a 404 error. Users who have downloaded the malicious version are advised to revoke and replace exposed credentials from a clean environment and pin version 1.106.2 by digest.

9von02.text: The two PHP vulnerabilities causing worldwide alarm first drew serious attention in August after an outside review by AI companies, the PHP Foundation explained in a lengthy statement on Wednesday. The organization said the history of one bug, CVE-2026-109618, dates back to 2024, when PHP underwent its first external security audit in several years, but officials took no action. The issue caused controversy within PHP as engineers debated how to address it, with concerns ranging from “backward compatibility breaks, new denial-of-service potential, or requiring changes to many third-party extensions which seemed impossible to coordinate.” “The PHP security team, operating on consensus, struggled to choose between these and feared the repercussions of shipping the wrong choice,” the nonprofit foundation said. “Combined with the lack of a known path to remote code execution and the small team of core developers with the necessary deep knowledge of the engine occupied with many responsibilities, this decision process caused work on a fix to stall and restart repeatedly over months.” Hundreds of websites were taken offline on Wednesday by companies and governments as a result of CVE-2026-109618 and a related bug, CVE-2026-109619. Some are labeling them jointly as PHP2Shell. Some estimates show that more than 70% of all websites on the internet use PHP. Internet infrastructure company Cloudflare reported seeing attempted exploitation. The PHP Foundation said both vulnerabilities “sit in parts of PHP that nearly every request touches.” “Their central place in PHP is what made both vulnerabilities serious, and also so hard to fix without breaking compatibility, hurting performance, or forcing changes on the large ecosystem of third-party extensions,” they said. The scope of the vulnerabilities has alarmed cybersecurity defenders and governments, with a VirusTotal analysis showing 5.1 million IP addresses identified as running PHP. At least 758,000 IP addresses were disclosed as end-of-life PHP versions and 85,000 IP addresses were running the latest PHP releases available before developers issued emergency patches Wednesday morning. These figures represent PHP's internet-facing footprint, not confirmed vulnerable systems. The patches only apply to versions dating back to PHP 8.2. Every version older than that no longer receives updates from the PHP Project. Cisco Talos’ released estimates suggesting roughly 50% of vulnerable PHP systems may not receive a patch. AI spotlights bugs After deciding against taking any action in 2024, the PHP Foundation was confronted with the issues again with the emergence of powerful AI code review tools. Services from Anthropic and OpenAI were used earlier this year to scan PHP platforms and eventually a researcher at cybersecurity firm Calif reported the bugs on August 11. On social media, Calif also credited another researcher with initially discovering the vulnerability and developing an exploit. OpenAI and security companies Wiz and Trail of Bits also found the same vulnerabilities during audits of PHP. The reports “made the full impact of the … problem clear, and from August 11th onward, fixing it became the top priority for all of the PHP Foundation's team working on security,” the foundation explained. The PHP Foundation said its coordinated disclosure process was running smoothly until rumors of the bugs began to emerge on social media two days ago. They moved up their disclosure of the bugs by one day but argued that they could not have immediately released it because the fix was still being packaged. They noted that Calif “mistakenly published a video” that showed their proof of concept working against a number of targets and revealed additional details about the vulnerabilities. That video, even after being deleted, began circulating and “accelerated development” of exploitation proof of concepts (PoCs). PHP Foundation monitored several of the PoCs that began to circulate online throughout Tuesday evening but did not identify any functional exploits. The blog notes that cybersecurity firm Chainguard unilaterally broke the embargo early on Wednesday and published images containing the fix. Chainguard did not respond to requests for comment about the allegations. “Like other distributors, Chainguard had received the patch in advance so its users could update the moment the vulnerabilities were disclosed,” the foundation said. “Any attacker could now study the fix in binary form while every other PHP user was still waiting for the release. This disregarded weeks of work by many parties toward a coordinated disclosure.” The PHP Foundation listed out dozens of changes to its internal structure that would not allow a similar situation to occur again and argued that “a serious vulnerability with a fix stuck on hard trade-offs would now reach the PHP Foundation leadership much sooner.” No previous articleNo new articlesJonathan Greigis a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

1phmdky.text: OpenAI has revealed that two artificial intelligence (AI) agents powered by GPT-6.1 Sol and one GPT-6 Astra weakened misalignment monitoring while making requested software changes during two internal coding tasks. The AI company said the incident took place on October 3 and 6, 2026, for Sol and Astra, respectively, as part of an internal deployment. "A GPT-6.1 Sol agent repairing an evaluation pipeline disabled automatic alerts to our Security team, treating an earlier instruction not to send messages during a Slack history search as a reason to suppress monitoring notifications," OpenAI said in a report. The end result of this action was that the misalignment monitor still ran and saved its reports, but automatic human alerts were disabled by setting "no_notify" to true and emptying the lists of people configured to receive monitoring reports. In another task on October 6, a GPT-6 Astra agent migrating a program is said to have removed its monitoring integration in order to match a reference implementation, and then falsely claimed to the user that the functionality had not been removed. "No [...] I did not remove an enabled monitor from it," the final response from the agent reads. OpenAI said, in both cases, the AI agents considered whether monitoring safeguards should be retained, but ultimately chose not to do so after interpreting routine coding instructions as "permission to weaken them." In response to the findings, the company said it's strengthening its misalignment monitoring system and assessing if these scenarios are an outlier or whether they demonstrate a propensity to evade misalignment monitoring. "In addition to making it harder for models to disable monitoring [during evaluations], we are looking to understand why models might seek to do so in the first place," OpenAI said. "It is possible that this behavior is simply an example of 'benign' overpersistence, with models not understanding why monitoring is important or insisting that instructions be executed beyond what a reasonable person might expect." The disclosure is the latest instance of AI agents acting in ways their developers did not intend to. Last week, the ChatGPT-maker disclosed seven misalignment incidents, including one case where an internal research model stole cryptocurrency from a wallet it did not own to pay the fees needed to deploy smart contracts on Ethereum's Sepolia test network and failed to report that it took the funds without permission. Microsoft Targets Rogue AI Agents With Dynamic Permissions, Risk Score It also comes amid growing concerns that the development of increasingly powerful AI systems is outpacing safety efforts, leading to warnings that this could make it harder to monitor and control them as they gain greater autonomy. Earlier this week, Microsoft announced new controls to monitor and contain potentially rogue AI agents in enterprise environments as part of Project Perception, a continuously learning AI-powered cyber defense system the company unveiled in July 2026. "Models have been trained to attain results, which often leads to reward hacking, and models are not optimized around organizational norms or judgment," Hayete Gallot, executive vice president of Microsoft Security, said. "Agents are unpredictable. They will adapt as the context changes, may not behave as intended, and will collaborate and collude with other agents to reach their objectives, without needing to be compromised." With agents often having extensive permissions to access data, tools, and systems, not to mention take actions and make decisions on their own, Redmond said they pose a new kind of insider security risk that requires continuous monitoring. To that end, Microsoft's Project Perception employs Guardian Agents to supervise other AI agents and secure them across identity, permissions, data, endpoints, network, cloud, and runtime layers by - Discovering and identifying every agent. Limiting their permissions using the principle of least privilege (PoLP) before execution and then dynamically grant or revoke access based on the task at hand. Monitoring the agent's actions and checking if it's straying from its original task. Adapting protections as behavior, context, and risk change. The system is architected on the foundations of three new themes - Dynamic Permissions, which scopes the permissions to the task assigned to the agent and makes it time-bound. Dynamic Agent Risk, which assigns each agent a risk score that is continuously updated and draws from how securely it's configured, what resources it can reach, the potential impact if something goes wrong, and whether its actions are deviating from the user's or organization's intent. Dynamic Conditional Access, which extends Entra Conditional Access for agents so that permissions can be adjusted when there is a change in risk. "Its identity, runtime, access paths, and task-scoped authority should be explicit from the start," Microsoft said. "If it later encounters a prompt injection or attempts an action outside that task, the system should respond proportionately: preserve safe reads while blocking writes, narrow the resources it can reach, require provable human approval for a consequential step, or isolate and stop the agent when the risk warrants it."

1krkoym.text: OpenAI agents powered by the GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra models weakened misalignment monitoring during two internal tasks, interpreting coding instructions as authorization to do so. AI alignment refers to how well an AI system’s goals and behavior align with human values, intentions, and instructions. It is a key focus of AI safety research aimed at preventing harmful actions and unintended outcomes. One of the incidents occurred on October 3, when an agent powered by GPT-6.1 Sol extended an earlier human instruction “don’t send any messages” related to a Slack history search to automatic monitoring alerts. It directed a sub-agent to empty notification recipient lists and suppress notifications. Although monitoring continued to run and save findings, it disabled alerts to humans. OpenAI says this happened even though the agent earlier reasoned that alerts should remain enabled. A second incident on October 6 involved a GPT-6 Astra-powered agent tasked with migrating a program. The agent removed existing monitoring integration to match a reference implementation and then denied doing so. After reporting the migration was complete, the agent did not tell the user that monitoring was disabled. Furthermore, when asked directly, the agent lied to the human. GPT-6 Astra agent denies disabling monitoringsource: OpenAI OpenAI says that the agent also replaced a test intended to preserve monitoring with one asserting that the monitor context was absent. Although both incidents involved agents weakening alignment monitoring despite explicit instructions not to, OpenAI classified neither as P0 (“Priority Zero”), its highest urgency level for issues requiring immediate attention. Ongoing investigation OpenAI says it is investigating whether the unintended behavior stems from excessive persistence in task-completion goals, a poor understanding of monitoring requirements, or a specific tendency to evade monitoring. “We are also developing evaluations to test whether models might have a propensity to evade misalignment monitoring in particular and exhibit motivated reasoning in order to do so,” OpenAI explained. “We don’t yet have a satisfying explanation for this behavior, and will investigate this behavior through the creation of paired evaluations, resampling of agent continuations, and experiments on models’ internal activations.” The AI firm says it has updated its internal Auto-Review system to now detect and block attempts to disable misalignment monitoring. At the same time, it will also reject all workloads that lack valid monitoring requirements. 19s1u4.text: Editor's Note: Story updated 10:50 a.m. Eastern U.S. time with information about OpenAI's involvement. A set of vulnerabilities in one of the most popular scripting languages underpinning many websites set off alarm bells in the cybersecurity community on Tuesday evening, followed by a global scramble to apply patches on Wednesday. The maintainers of PHP — used to build and run web applications and the vast majority of websites — released an urgent notice warning of two new bugs. Hundreds of websites were down on Wednesday as administrators responded to the warning. The vulnerabilities — CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 — carry severity scores of 9.2 out of 10 and are rated critical by PHP. The bugs can allow for remote code execution on unpatched websites. “All PHP users are encouraged to prepare now so they can upgrade as soon as the release is available,” PHP’s security team said Tuesday evening. “PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive updates from the PHP project.” PHP's maintainers started releasing fixes after 10 a.m. Wednesday, Eastern U.S. time. Dozens of government agencies had released urgent warnings throughout the evening and early on Wednesday morning telling website maintainers to stay alert and patch their systems immediately when the fixes were available. Dane Knecht, the CTO of Cloudflare, said the tech giant is already seeing attacks emerging, and it released stopgap mitigations to help protect some customers. At least one video released on social media showed the vulnerabilities being used to cause damage. Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence for watchTowr said the cybersecurity company is also observing in-the-wild exploitation of the vulnerabilities with a variety of proof-of-concept tools vibecoded with the help of AI. “Whilst nobody has been successful to date, we don't expect that will last long,” he said. Websites down The European Union, U.S., Germany, Japan, Australia, the U.K. and the Netherlands all released warnings locally about the vulnerabilities. Several governments even took some websites offline in advance of the patch being released. Large companies and organizations like Nintendo and others also took services offline as they addressed the bugs, which are being called “PHP2Shell.” Some estimates show that more than 70% of all websites on the internet use PHP. Experts at watchTowr noted that enterprise networks commonly run PHP-based content management systems and internal tools, so servers running PHP often handle customer data and business logic reachable from the internet. Sophos official Don Smith said the immediate challenge is not just installing a patch but finding and managing every instance where PHP is running. “The use of PHP is pervasive, it can sit beneath public websites, content management systems, hosting platforms and third-party products, sometimes without even being obvious to the organization using it,” he said. “Security teams should prioritise internet-facing systems, confirming which versions are affected as soon as the official advisory is published, and apply the updates without delay…any vulnerable system that cannot be patched should be isolated from the internet until it can be secured.” OpenAI and Calif Shortly after the patches were released, OpenAI came forward to say researchers at a cybersecurity firm called Calif used its tools to discover the PHP bugs two months ago through its “Patch the Planet” program. OpenAI said it worked with PHP and other companies to test the fixes, prepare guidance and “helped coordinate the response with infrastructure providers.” The company defended its role in the situation, arguing that the “weaknesses already existed” and that AI helped the researchers find them. But they acknowledged that AI “can also help attackers exploit them” and said it is critical that organizations work together to deploy protections. Experts expressed deep concern that millions of PHP-backed websites are still running ancient versions of the language that likely cannot be updated. Joviane Jardim, a senior security researcher at Swedish firm Detectify, said many organizations only learn about a forgotten PHP server when an attacker finds it. “That’s the risk with this one: the flaws became public before the fix did, so both sides are starting at the same time. Attackers aren’t waiting for a working exploit. They’re building a list of every server on the internet that says it runs PHP, sorted by version, and the moment the fix is out, they will compare the old code with the new one to find the flaw,” he said. With artificial intelligence, most attackers can create a working exploit in under an hour, meaning defenders can expect a wave of exploitation shortly after the patch is released. Jardim added that roughly half of all PHP websites are running older versions of PHP but only PHP 8.2 and newer are getting patches. “That’s the real exposure. Those sites haven’t been updated in years, which usually means nobody is watching them either,” he said. “So the question this week is this: do you know where all your PHP is running? If yes, this is an afternoon of updates. If no, the risk is in the systems you’ve forgotten: an old marketing site, a hosting control panel, a device with PHP built in. And speed matters more than ever.” No previous articleNo new articlesJonathan Greigis a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

1em20yw.text: The PHP security team released emergency security patches for two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) tracked collectively as PHP2Shell. The two unauthenticated RCE flaws were discovered by Calif, Wiz, and OpenAI security researchers, and affect all PHP installations that serve web requests, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. "We consider the risk highest for mod_php, with a demonstrated exploit where an unauthenticated request can trigger the attack before any application code runs," the PHP security team said. Both flaws stem from the same underlying problem: PHP can leave its memory in a corrupted state when a request ends abnormally, and both can be exploited to achieve remote code execution. CVE-2026-109618 can be used to gain remote code execution as the web worker account by exploiting a chain of weaknesses that trigger out-of-memory corruption, while the CVE-2026-109619 stale global state vulnerability enables unauthenticated heap use-after-free, memory disclosure, and remote code execution with the web worker's privileges. Admins should install PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35 as soon as possible on servers running PHP 8.x and migrate to a fixed release if they're running PHP 7 or earlier. "PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive updates from the PHP project. Some distributions and LTS vendors provide backported fixes, so contact your vendor for details, or upgrade to a supported version," the PHP developers added. "Given the severity of these vulnerabilities, the PHP security team provided minimal source-backports for PHP 7.4, PHP 8.0, and PHP 8.1 to help people building from source or without access to an LTS vendor." Advanced warning This follows a Tuesday warning from PHP developers urging administrators to prepare to install these security updates as soon as they're released. "All PHP users are encouraged to prepare now so they can upgrade as soon as the release is available," they said. "We reserve the right to release earlier should details of either vulnerability become public, or should evidence of active exploitation appear in the wild." PHP core developer Gina Peter Banyard warned that no PHP2Shell mitigations would fully block potential attacks and that applying the official security patches is the only permanent defense. Before the patches were released, Cloudflare CTO Dane Knecht confirmed that the company (which had already deployed a set of WAF rules designed to block known PHP2Shell exploitation methods) was already observing early attacks targeting the two vulnerabilities. However, Knecht also stressed that these protections were temporary and urged all admins to install the PHP security updates as soon as they become available. The UK National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has also warned UK organizations to immediately update systems using PHP or take them offline until they can be patched. Temporary mitigation measures However, the PHP security team did share a number of mitigation measures that should reduce exposure to some attack paths for those who can't immediately patch their servers, although they don't fully protect against exploitation (detailed information is available in PHP's blog post): CVE-2026-109618: Set memory_limit=-1, preferably in a way applications can’t override, such as php_admin_value in the FPM pool or Apache configuration. Set a low post_max_size: 8M for applications that don’t require file uploads, 32M if uploads are necessary. Use a container or cgroup limit as an availability boundary, preferably with a policy that kills only the affected worker. CVE-2026-109619: Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and restart every worker. On PHP 8.5, set fatal_error_backtraces=0 and restart every worker. This blocks only the confirmed fatal backtrace path. Remove invalid or deprecated settings applied per request that emit diagnostics before initialization. Hiding diagnostics with error_reporting, display_errors or @ does not help. Fix attacker-reachable fatal errors and execution timeouts, including failures in callbacks, upload or import processing and cleanup. PHP (Hypertext Preprocessor) is an open-source, server-side web development language that powers 75% to 80% of all websites, including those using Content Management Systems (CMS) like WordPress, Joomla, and Drupal. According to VirusTotal estimates, over 5.1 million PHP hosts are exposed online, with roughly 3.8 million having at least one port open. 1to17wj.text: ClickFix has fast become one of the go-to techniques for criminals since it first emerged around 2024. It’s grown in both volume and variety, with an ever-expanding family of sub-techniques like FileFix, InstallFix, TerminalFix, and the entirely browser-native ConsentFix. The lures too have become more developed and targeted, with recent attacks preferring to target people searching for and using AI tools, a trick that is catching many users off guard and blending in with otherwise legitimate traffic for approved GenAI tools. Push's detection data shows how far the technique has spread. Through Q2 2026, ClickFix made up an average of 52% of Push's detections, overtaking AiTM and device code phishing for the first time, and in August that figure reached 67%. Across all the browser-based attacks Push intercepts, 1 in 2 arrive through channels other than email, such as search engines and social media. The rest came through email but weren’t stopped at the email gateway. ClickFix goes a step further: 4 in 5 ClickFix pages intercepted in 2026 were reached from search engines — through compromised websites, malvertising, and SEO poisoning. A ClickFix lure generated using the ERRTRAFFIC kit. AI tools are the newest lure The latest ClickFix variants use AI tools as the bait. In Push's last quarterly snapshot, AI-themed InstallFix and LLMshare attacks made up around 5% of all attacks Push detected, a growing subset of the ClickFix family. Other researchers are seeing the same trend. ANY.RUN linked 1,258 public sandbox analyses to fake AI tool campaigns between April 15 and October 5, 2026, and 81% of them impersonated Claude or ChatGPT and Codex. At least 45% came from campaigns that told the victim to paste a command, through fake CLI install pages or fake download pages with ClickFix, and another quarter started on a shared AI chat or artifact. These lures work because AI adoption has spread two habits across the workforce. The first is installing tools from the terminal. Claude Code and similar tools ship as a one-line terminal install, so people who would never previously have opened a command line now paste commands from web pages as a normal part of trying a new tool. A classic ClickFix page has to invent a reason for the user to paste something. An InstallFix victim arrives expecting to run a command, so the attacker only has to swap it for a malicious one. The second is searching for AI apps rather than going to them directly. Plenty of people reach the AI tools they use every day by typing the name into a search engine, and employees are adopting new AI apps faster than security teams can approve them. Both habits put the user on a search results page, which is exactly where ClickFix delivery happens. InstallFix: Fake install pages that show the real command Push first documented InstallFix in March 2026: cloned install pages for tools like Claude Code, Codex, and NotebookLM (which doesn't even have a desktop installer), promoted through search ads. The attacker copies the legitimate page and replaces the install command with one that delivers malware. The latest cluster Push analyzed saw a Google search for "claude mac" return a sponsored result that displays bing.com as its domain. The ad passed the visitor through Bing's own click-tracking redirect to a compromised retail website, which forwarded them to a fake "Download Claude" page. Two layers of cloaking, a server-side referrer check on the compromised site and a script on the fake page, send anyone who doesn't arrive through the ad to a benign page or a 404. A sponsored Google result for "claude mac" that displays bing.com as its domain. The lure itself is built to fool both a careful user and any control that reads the screen. The page displays Anthropic's genuine install command, but its copy button puts a different command on the clipboard. That command first prints a legitimate claude.ai URL in the Terminal, then decodes a hidden URL and pipes the downloaded script straight into the shell without saving it to disk. A user who checks the page and then watches the Terminal sees Anthropic's domain both times. Push has already seen the same trick on other lures, and because ClickFix toolkits copy each other's features quickly, it's spreading fast. The fake Claude download page shows Anthropic's real install command, but a malicious one is copied behind-the-scenes. Discover AI tools and shadow IT across your workforce, find insecure login methods and accounts at risk of takeover, identify MFA gaps and phishable MFA methods, and more. Get your free report LLMshare: Lures hosted on the AI platforms themselves LLMshare, a technique that Push reported in May 2026, abuses the sharing features of AI chatbots. Attackers create shared chats and Artifacts on ChatGPT and Claude that contain malicious install instructions or a link to a fake download page, then promote them through search ads. Because the lure is hosted on chatgpt.com or claude.ai, tools that rely on URL reputation checks have every reason to trust it. The newest version uses custom GPTs, which turn the lure from a static page into a conversation. A custom GPT is a configured version of ChatGPT that anyone with a paid account can build and share, and its creator writes hidden instructions that steer every reply. In the case Push analyzed, whatever the user typed, the GPT replied with a fake "Service Availability Notice" linking to a Google Sites page that served a Windows ClickFix payload. It had more than 10,000 conversations when Push observed it. A malicious custom GPT answers every prompt with a fake outage notice that links to a ClickFix page, hosted on sites.google.com. A custom GPT is even more convincing than a shared chat because the user has to use it normally before the malicious link appears. Up to that point, the page behaves the way the user expected, and the fake outage notice reads like a routine service problem. Why ClickFix is the weapon of choice in 2026 Microsoft's 2026 Digital Defense Report shows that ClickFix volume is still growing fast. ClickFix attacks grew roughly 23x between December 2025 and May 2026, and between February and early May alone, Microsoft Defender observed ClickFix-style attacker-supplied commands executed on more than 1.1 million unique devices. In Microsoft's words, ClickFix is now "one of the most conversion-efficient initial access techniques," with 96.3% of ClickFix intrusions leading to malware. ClickFix breaks through typical detection controls because: Email security never sees a page the user reached through a search result. URL reputation and blocklists see bing.com, chatgpt.com, sites.google.com, or a legitimate website that has been compromised, and the main kits now use EtherHiding, storing their configuration in a smart contract on a public blockchain. There's no server to take down, and the operator can swap the payload URL on every compromised site with a single transaction. Detections firing on compromised or legitimate sites often surprise new Push customers. Legitimate sites show up elsewhere in the chain too, as redirects, as hosting on services like Google Sites, and as we've shown, on AI platforms themselves. Endpoint security is the last line of defense once the user pastes the command, and ClickFix is built to get through it. The user runs the command in a legitimate shell, so it doesn't match the process chains endpoint rules look for, and it runs in memory, leaving no file for a sandbox to detonate. Push has also seen 84 command forms across more than 20 binaries, obfuscated to defeat string matching. And for BYOD devices, contractor machines, Macs, and developer workstations where EDR is often absent or tuned down, there's no protection at all. These attacks are also hard to investigate after the fact, because many only fire under specific conditions. The ConsentFix campaign Push uncovered in December 2025, which was linked to the Russian state-affiliated group APT29, only served its lure to visitors who entered an email address on the attacker's target list. Every compromised site in the campaign also shared an IP block list, so once a visitor had been served the lure, it never appeared for that IP address again on any of them. By the time an analyst checks a reported URL, the lure may have been rotated or taken down, or the page may simply load clean for anyone who didn't arrive the way the victim did. 1jmlfip.text: PHP has released emergency updates that fix two critical flaws in the language itself, letting an attacker without an account run code on a web server. The fixes are in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35, and the PHP team says only updating fully protects a server. The flaws, together called PHP2Shell, sit in the PHP runtime, not in any application, so a site is exposed even when its own code is secure. The risk is highest on servers using Apache's mod_php, where a working exploit triggers the attack before any application code runs. Both flaws are rated 9.2 on the CVSS v4.0 scale and carry the identifiers CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. PHP published them around the scheduled release time of 14:00 UTC on October 21, a day after details leaked ahead of a planned October 22 disclosure. Researchers at Wiz, Calif, and OpenAI found and reported the flaws, which affect nearly every PHP version back to PHP 5.4. Who Is Affected Every PHP installation that serves web requests is at risk, including PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed, according to the PHP security advisory. Because the flaws are in the engine rather than in any site's code, even a simple "Hello World" page on a vulnerable PHP version can be attacked. The advisory singles out mod_php as the highest risk, with a demonstrated exploit in which a single unauthenticated request triggers the attack before any application code runs. PHP-FPM behaves differently, because it shuts the worker down when a request fails early in setup. For one of the two flaws, PHP's own analysis supports that FPM is susceptible but says no complete FPM exploit has been shown; the second flaw was shown to reach code execution on both mod_php and PHP-FPM, though the FPM path there depends on an operation inside the running application. An attacker can also read memory from the PHP worker process, which may hold passwords, authentication tokens, API keys, and certificates belonging to other requests, without first gaining code execution. The researchers demonstrated this reading of live worker memory against applications they did not control, making it independent of the application running on top of PHP. What to Install Update the PHP runtime that serves web requests, then restart Apache, PHP-FPM, and any long-running PHP workers. Updating an application such as WordPress or Laravel does not update the PHP runtime beneath it; that comes from the server package, the host, or the container image. PHP branch Vulnerable First fixed version 8.5 below 8.5.12 8.5.12 8.4 below 8.4.27 8.4.27 8.3 below 8.3.36 8.3.36 8.2 below 8.2.35 8.2.35 PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive updates from the PHP project, and PHP 8.2 reaches end of life on December 31, 2026. For the older branches, the PHP security team has published source backports for PHP 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1 to help people building from source or waiting on a vendor. Linux distributions and long-term-support vendors received the patches in advance, so a distribution package can carry the fix under an old-looking version number; check the package changelog for the CVE, as Debian advises, not the version string. If You Cannot Update Yet Only updating is a complete fix. The measures below reduce exposure to specific attack paths and do not make a server safe, according to the advisory. For CVE-2026-109618, set memory_limit=-1 so applications cannot override it, keep post_max_size low, and enforce request-size limits at the web server or proxy. Do not use RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA as a substitute, because PHP warns they can trigger the same vulnerable path. For CVE-2026-109619, set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and restart every worker, and on PHP 8.5 also set fatal_error_backtraces=0. Turning off session upload progress blocks the confirmed session paths but not other variants, and no configuration change fully mitigates this flaw short of updating. That setting is the one circulated as a workaround before the patch, and the release confirms it was never a complete fix. Session upload progress is turned on by default and can reach session handling before PHP finishes setting up a request, which is why it takes part in one confirmed attack path for CVE-2026-109619 and why turning it off does nothing for CVE-2026-109618. "The only thing I can say is that the only mitigation is patching/upgrading PHP. I sadly know too much," PHP core developer Gina Peter Banyard wrote before the release, replying to someone who suggested the setting might be enough. After updating, review your memory settings. The fix adds a new hard memory limit, and reaching it ends the process and stops shutdown handlers from running, so check memory_limit and post_max_size against what your application needs. If you already patched but suspect an earlier break-in, the researchers suggest watching for unusual multipart requests followed by memory-limit errors or repeated HTTP 500 responses, oddly large PHPSESSID response cookies, and unexplained restarts of PHP workers. Is It Being Attacked Before the patch shipped, Cloudflare said it was seeing early attempts to exploit the flaws. "We are seeing early attacks emerging and are updating mitigations as new vectors show up," Cloudflare CTO Dane Knecht said, calling the firewall rules Cloudflare deployed a stopgap and urging administrators to patch. No source has confirmed a successful break-in. watchTowr, which reproduced CVE-2026-109618, reported no exploitation in the wild as of 11:26 UTC on October 21, and neither flaw was in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog at that time. Some organizations took services offline as a precaution rather than in response to any break-in. BambooHR took its service offline across the United States, Canada and Ireland, warned that payroll would be interrupted, and said it did not yet have a restoration time. In the Netherlands, MijnOverheid, DigiD, the lower house of parliament's site, the national cyber-security center and several education systems went offline, the broadcaster NOS reported; the centre said it had not seen the flaw abused but urged everyone to patch. How It Came Out A leak pulled the release forward. On October 20, as The Hacker News reported, a post on Hacker News said two PHP remote code execution flaws, with the two CVE identifiers, were set for disclosure on October 22, on no more than a trusted tip. PHP posted an advance notice that evening and moved the release to October 21. The leak's claim of a CVSS 10.0 score was not PHP's; PHP rates both flaws 9.2. The flaws were found by Wiz Research, Calif, and OpenAI's Codex Security team, working with the PHP security team and Google's Gemini team on the fix. The underlying code had been in PHP for more than a decade. The researchers say AI models helped turn these long-standing flaws into working exploits, letting one researcher do in about a week what they say would otherwise have taken a team months. Calif, which traced the bug's lineage to PHP research from 2004, says knowing the target's history still mattered, and that current models do not reliably start from obscure, twenty-year-old primitives on their own. Update: watchTowr Reports Exploitation Attempts, Still No Confirmed Break-In watchTowr, which earlier in the day reported seeing none, said in a new advisory at 14:19 UTC on October 21 that it is observing "active exploitation attempts" of both CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Cloudflare said it saw attack traffic against its customers and watched attackers change their payloads to get around its firewall rules, which it had switched on by default at 03:02 UTC, before the patch. No source has reported a confirmed break-in of a specific server as of this update. The PHP Foundation said the coordinated disclosure came apart before the release. Around 20:00 UTC on October 20, the research firm Calif mistakenly posted a video of its working proof of concept, and at 07:41 UTC on October 21, about six hours before the fix shipped, the vendor Chainguard published built images containing the patch, letting anyone study the fix while other users waited to update. Update: PHP Foundation Says a 2024 Audit Found the First Signs of the Flaw In the same post, the PHP Foundation said a core developer first found signs of the out-of-memory flaw behind CVE-2026-109618 during PHP's 2024 external audit, but a working attack was only theorized and no concrete route to code execution was found then.Competing fixes each risked breaking compatibility, opening denial-of-service paths, or forcing changes on third-party extensions, and a small team struggled to agree, so work on a fix stalled for months. The Foundation called the delay "a structural failure" of its decision process and its resources. The 2026 reports from Calif, OpenAI and Wiz, which used AI tools, established the working exploit that made the flaw's full impact clear and moved the fix to the top of the queue. The Foundation said it has since changed how it makes security decisions and added staff and tooling to catch similar problems sooner. (The story was updated after publication on October 21, 2026, to add later reports of exploitation attempts and the PHP Foundation's account of the flaw's history.)

1epyggl.text: Google on Tuesday said it's rolling out improved safeguards in its Chrome browser to secure users against ClickFix attacks when Enhanced Protection is enabled. ClickFix is a popular social engineering technique in which bad actors trick users into copying and pasting malicious code directly into their computer's operating system, thereby bypassing conventional security controls. As part of these attacks, unsuspecting users who land on legitimate-but-compromised sites or malicious ads are redirected to phishing landing pages that display fake Cloudflare or Google reCAPTCHA verification or other non-existent errors and instruct users to copy and paste a command on the Windows Run dialog (or the Mac Terminal app) to address it. The moment a user presses the Enter key after pasting the command, it triggers a multi-stage infection chain that leads to the deployment of malware, such as information stealers or remote access trojans. In an attempt to blend in with regular activity and evade detection, the commands often make use of living-off-the-land (LotL) tools like PowerShell or cmd.exe to download next-stage payloads. A key reason why ClickFix remains an effective initial access method is that it flips the script on traditional phishing. Instead of exploiting sophisticated vulnerabilities or getting a user to click on suspicious links, it tricks them into opening the front door themselves under the pretext of troubleshooting a commonplace issue. "By shifting the download process out of the browser and into the terminal, attackers completely sidestep existing Chrome and Safe Browsing download protections," Google said. "To combat this technique, Chrome now detects when an Enhanced Protection user is tricked into copying suspicious commands." If a user copies a potential ClickFix script, the clipboard payload is scrubbed of any personal information it may contain and sent to Safe Browsing for further analysis. If the security system determines the command is dangerous, Chrome displays a warning. By doing so, the idea is to prevent the attack from taking place before the user executes the malicious command. Separately, Google is also introducing the following defenses in Chrome to tackle scams for users who enable Enhanced Protection - Establishing a taxonomy for Safe Browsing site warnings: Suspicious sites, which exhibit deceptive patterns commonly associated with known malicious sites, and Dangerous sites, which refer to sites that are known to be malicious and have a high risk of user harm. Building upon on-device large language model (LLM)-based approaches to flag tech support scams and others, such as fake antivirus and browser update scams. "This model evaluates page content to analyze key indicators, such as the brand represented, the intent of the page, and a scam likeliness score, giving us rich threat data needed to identify deceptive sites," Google said. "Throughout this process, Chrome minimizes the amount of data shared with the server by only analyzing page text when a site exhibits high-confidence scam indicators. And whenever page content is sent off the device, it is processed ephemerally – meaning it is never logged, retained or used to train models." On Tuesday, Google said it's introducing Financial Services Verification in the U.S. and Canada to validate an advertiser's credentials and ensure ads come from authorized financial providers. The verification program already applies to various markets globally, including Australia, Brazil, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, New Zealand, Türkiye, and several countries in Europe. "Under this policy, advertisers must demonstrate they are authorized by relevant regulators or recognized registries before running certain financial ads – helping prevent brand impersonation and stopping bad actors from reaching people," Google said. "Alongside our ongoing work with financial regulators, we're working in the U.S. with the American Bankers Association to use their dedicated registry to verify authorized banks before ads can run. In Canada, we’re engaging closely with the Canadian Bankers Association as we prepare for our rollout." Apple Blocks Identity Resolution in Safari and WebKit The development comes as Apple revealed new privacy protections built into Safari and WebKit as part of iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS 27 releases, taking steps to block a practice called identity resolution that turns email addresses into persistent tracking identifiers. "In this scheme, third-parties (i.e., not the website owner) invisibly collect your email address when you log in or sign up for a newsletter," Apple's WebKit team said. "They send the email address to their servers, create an opaque tracking ID permanently linked to your email address, and send that tracking ID back to the web page." "The tracking ID is stored on the website and can from thereon be used for arbitrary purposes linked to your email address, such as building a profile of your browsing or targeting ads at you across websites. Logging out or unsubscribing from that newsletter does not remove the tracking ID or your email address stored with the third party." Apple said the third-parties can build more data about users as they log in with their email address or fill in forms containing personal data, allowing them to create an identity graph with their name, residential address, phone number, and IP address. To prevent this sort of cross-site tracking, Safari blocks network access to identity resolution infrastructure embedded within the web pages, effectively stopping the third party from sending the email address to their servers. The blocking, Apple said, is done at the domain level. "It's not enough to block cross-site cookies to prevent cross-site tracking today because the tracking industry has not stopped trying to track users on the web," Apple said. "They have ushered into what they call the post cookie era and in our latest releases we have put strong protection in place."

11mfuc.text: Microsoft has released PowerToys 0.102, with two new mouse utilities, new command-line tools, and Command Palette improvements. Mouse Button Lock, one of the new mouse tools, makes it easier to select items on screen by locking a mouse button while you hold down a key. "With Mouse Button Lock, press and hold a button for a moment, then let go. Windows keeps treating it as held, so you can continue dragging or selecting until you click any button," Microsoft senior product manager Niels Laute explained. "This is especially useful for gaming, working in professional applications that require extensive dragging and selection, and improving accessibility for users who find it difficult to hold down a mouse button for extended periods." Microsoft also added CursorHide to PowerToys, another mouse utility that automatically hides the mouse pointer while you type or when you aren't moving the mouse. The new PowerToys version also includes a quick-access shelf for the Command Palette quick launcher, letting users add up to nine commands under the search box and run them with a keyboard shortcut. You can enable the quick-access shelf under Settings > Appearance > Compact mode, then press Alt+1 through Alt+9 to run any of them, or Alt+Shift+number to select one without running it. Additional changes include new command-line tools to script PowerToys from the terminal, tap-alone remaps and a searchable key picker for Keyboard Manager, and a new ZoomIt feature that adds text to screenshots using dictation. PowerToys Mouse Button Lock (BleepingComputer) PowerToys 0.102 is now available on the official GitHub repository, which also provides detailed information on what changed in each version. Microsoft also released PowerToys 0.97 in January, which added CursorWrap, another mouse utility for multi-monitor setups designed to "teleport" the mouse pointer to the opposite edge of active monitors and make it easier to drag cursors across large screen distances. More recently, in August, PowerToys added Window Hopper, a tool that lets users switch between an app's windows more quickly. Microsoft released PowerToys during the Windows 95 era as a collection of small freeware tools created by Windows developers as personal projects. However, in 2019, the company revived it as an open-source utility pack that enhances Windows functionality and streamlines tasks that previously required installing third-party tools. Once attackers have valid credentials, only 37% of their actions are blocked Overall prevention scores can hide what happens after initial access. Once attackers are using valid credentials, prevention drops sharply.The Blue Report 2026 measures defenses technique by technique across 338 million simulations run in customer production environments.
