5lp12c.text: Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a previously undocumented China-aligned threat cluster known as Bronze Sandcastle that has been observed targeting organizations in Asia and Africa since mid-2025. "The most distinctive technical marker for Bronze Sandcastle is its consistent use of Sandboxie DLL sideloading," Sophos security researcher Gabor Szappanos said in a post published Tuesday. Between August 2025 and August 2026, attacks mounted by the threat actor have resulted in victims in the Philippines, Taiwan, Afghanistan, Namibia, and likely South Korea. Evidence indicates that Bronze Sandcastle is most active in the UTC+8 time zone. DLL sideloading is a popular adversarial technique that exploits the way Windows loads DLL files, allowing an attacker to trick a legitimate program into loading a malicious DLL. When an application is launched, it needs to load various DLLs in order to function correctly. If the application does not provide the full path to a required DLL, the operating system looks for it in a predetermined sequence of directories. An attacker can take advantage of this behavior by planting a malicious DLL with the same name as a legitimate one in a location that Windows searches before the folder that contains the actual DLL. Thus, when the legitimate application starts, it proceeds to load and run the malicious DLL, giving the attacker a way in to the system. "Because the malicious code is executed by a trusted and often digitally signed application, it is less likely to be flagged by antivirus software and other security solutions," Zscaler noted in an analysis last week. "If the legitimate application runs with elevated privileges, the malicious DLL will inherit those same permissions, allowing the attacker to perform more sensitive actions on the system." What's more, the technique enables persistence if the compromised application is configured to automatically run every time a system is rebooted, thereby allowing the attacker's code to execute on the infected host. Sophos said it observed legitimate Sandboxie executables placed in multiple victim environments, along with a malicious "sbiedll.dll" file, which, in turn, causes the trusted application ("SandboxieWUAU.exe") to load attacker-controlled code during runtime. Besides Sandboxie, Bronze Sandcastle has been leveraged in seven other DLL sideloading combinations - javaw.exe (Java application) - jli.dll Krita.exe (Krita digital painting) - Krita.dll NvdaHelper.exe (NVDA NonVisual Desktop Access) - NvdaHelperRemote.dll Jcef_helper.exe (Java Chromium Embedded Framework Helper) - Libcef.dll Vmmap.exe (Sysinternals process memory analyzer) - version.dll LineAppMgr.exe (LINE messaging application) - msvcp140.dll bginfo64.exe (Sysinternals utility that displays system information) - snmpapi.dll "The sideloaded DLLs typically read and execute payloads stored in encrypted config.ini files," Sophos said. "This design minimizes static detection and allows operators to adjust behavior without replacing DLL binaries. Renamed legitimate executables are frequently used to blend into victims' environments, with execution resulting in in-memory shellcode activity rather than additional disk artifacts." The DLL is designed to load and execute an encrypted payload ("config.ini"), which functions as a backdoor designed to enumerate local network and user accounts, as well as collect system metadata, running processes, keystrokes, and screenshots. Two different versions of the payload have been identified to date: 1.1.5 and 1.1.7. The payload has also been found to communicate with external sites (e.g., file[.]io, gofile[.]io, ably[.]net, and ably[.]io), likely in an attempt to receive additional tasking from its operators. In addition, version 1.1.5 has been observed using dc.cathaypacifice[.]com and net.dpworldto[.]com for command-and-control (C2). Version 1.1.7 payloads, on the other hand, have been observed communicating with GitHub repositories ("github[.]com/LatonyCharnleyaW") via the API to download encrypted config files. The GitHub account is no longer accessible. This is not the first time Chinese hacking groups have relied on DLL sideloading, nor is it the first time Sandboxie has been employed in such attacks. In July 2024, the APT41 threat actor leveraged a different executable signed by Sandboxie ("taskhost.exe") to sideload a malicious version of "sbiedll.dll" to deploy a backdoor called MoonWalk ultimately. "The threat group predominantly uses encrypted payload and configuration files that are decoded at runtime, meaning that static file-based detections may be ineffective," Sophos said. "Organizations should instead focus on behavioral indicators such as DLLs reading local files followed by immediate in-memory execution, which may indicate decoding and staging activity."

1np46pa.text: Generative AI has changed what a malicious email looks like. Messages that once gave themselves away through clumsy wording, generic pretexts, and reused templates now arrive fluent, personalized, and unique to each recipient, and the behavioral signals email filters have relied on for years are fading as a result. Proofpoint shared several examples of the shift at its Protect 2026 conference. In one, a single threat actor contacted more than 30 real estate agents at the same company, each from a different account, about a different property, and in different words, before closing every thread with the same request: join a video meeting. Federal data points the same way. The FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center counted more than 22,000 complaints involving AI in 2025, with nearly $900 million in associated losses, and logged 24,768 business email compromise (BEC) complaints with about $3.05 billion in reported losses, according to its 2025 Internet Crime Report. What AI Changed Email filters were built for attackers who had to cut corners. Researching a target, writing convincingly in a second language, impersonating a supplier, and producing enough variants to defeat signatures all took time, so attackers reused templates and infrastructure, and that reuse left patterns. Behavioral detection learned to spot them: new infrastructure, awkward language, odd timing, and requests that did not fit the conversation. Generative AI removes those constraints: Language. Fluent, localized text in any language, with no typos or translation artifacts. Context. Replies that fit the thread, the recipient’s role, and the timing. Persona. Matched writing style, signature blocks, and fully fabricated conversation histories. Variation. A unique message for every recipient, generated in seconds, so there is no template to match. The result, Proofpoint argues, is that behavior has become a weakening signal. When AI lets attackers make every message look normal, the analysis has to change too, from asking whether a message looks unusual to asking what it is trying to do. Thirty Conversations, One Ask The real estate campaign shows what that looks like in practice. Writing 30-plus distinct, plausible property enquiries, each tailored to a different listing and a different agent, is exactly the kind of work generative AI now does in seconds. The opening questions were mundane: whether a property was still open for inspection, what the price guide was, whether a viewing was possible that week. The sender mailboxes were real, and replies landed in threads the agents were already answering. Figure 1. Different properties, senders, and wording, with the same final ask in every thread. In one thread, an inspection enquiry sent at 2:58 a.m. turned into a meeting invitation 13 minutes later, complete with a branded template and a claim that the meeting required the agent’s “immediate attention.” The join link was a genuine google.com redirect, so reputation checks read clean, while a parameter in the URL handed the click to an unrelated site. Because each sender was making first contact, behavioral filters had no history to compare against, and because every message was different, there was no repeated content to match. What the messages shared was not how they looked but what they were trying to get the recipient to do. AI makes it easy to run this pattern against any business that depends on hearing from strangers, including clinics taking new patients, firms signing new clients, banks opening accounts, and insurers quoting policies, Proofpoint said. A variant aimed at insurance agents used quote requests, neighbor referrals, and coverage questions to build trust before sending a spoofed conference invitation that delivered the payload. AI-Powered Disruption AI has also made it easier to run campaigns that aim to disrupt rather than steal. Proofpoint described hostile communications campaigns in which hundreds or thousands of senders write to the same executives, each on a topic tailored to the target’s industry. Some messages carry derogatory language; others carry AI-generated or manipulated images that mock the recipient. Figure 2. Hostile communications campaigns carry no payload. The signal is the pattern. These messages have no link to detonate and no credential to harvest, and any one of them could pass for a single angry correspondent. Scoring messages one at a time will not catch them. The analysis has to recognize disruptive intent across the whole set, and read text and imagery together, since the hostility may sit in an AI-generated picture. Legitimacy on Demand The same shift applies to phishing infrastructure. One phishing-as-a-service kit Proofpoint highlighted presents a single flow behind four different disguises: a court access portal, a document-signing request, an identity check, and a finance report library. Each page displays a verification code and directs the victim to a legitimate sign-in page to paste it. Because the attacker generated the code, entering it authorizes the attacker’s session, a technique known as device-code phishing. Figure 3. Four pretexts in front of one device-code flow. Swapping the disguise is trivial for the operator, so the visual and linguistic fingerprints defenders might match change from one campaign to the next while the objective stays fixed. BEC shows AI’s effect on context most clearly. In another example, a single email contains a quoted thread in which an impersonated audit vendor and an executive at the target appear to agree on an invoice, a 50 percent loyalty rebate, and a payment date. The attached invoice itemizes audit phases, hours, and rates, and the closing line asks for payment that day to a remittance address that differs from the actual sending address. Figure 4. A single BEC message with a fabricated thread and invoice. Names and domains are anonymized.Writing both sides of that exchange and building a believable invoice once took research and hours of work. A language model drafts all of it in seconds, which removes the effort that used to limit how many targets received this kind of attention. Changing the Analysis: From Behavior to Intent If AI lets attackers control how a message looks, the signal that remains is what the message is trying to accomplish. Proofpoint’s approach evaluates that objective, whether it is plausible given the relationship and conversation, and what technique is being used to pursue it. The company announced its Nexus Intent-Based Detection Model in September as part of what it calls the Agentic Collaboration Security system. A bank-detail change request illustrates the approach. The message comes from a known supplier’s real mailbox, inside a real thread, with a clean reputation, and its language is exactly what AI makes easy to produce. Read for intent, however, five details line up: It is the supplier’s first banking change in years. The request does not match the invoice-confirmation thread it replies to. The deadline is tied to a specific payment run. The sender asks to keep the exchange off the thread and deal with one person. Verification is closed off in advance with a claim that the finance mailbox is “mid-migration.” Figure 5. A bank-detail change request read for intent. AI can polish the wording of a request like this. But the intent must match the attacker’s path to success, whether that’s the user clicking a link, entering credentials or joining a meeting. That’s why intent holds up where behavior is a less reliable indicator. Proofpoint positions intent analysis as a third layer rather than a replacement. Traditional detection, built on rules, signatures, infrastructure reputation, and indicators of compromise, still clears known threats quickly and at scale. Modern detection, built on threat actor intelligence and behavioral baselines, still catches known actors and senders that deviate. Intent reasoning targets the AI-crafted messages that pass both. Figure 6. Three layers of detection, each answering a different question. Defenders are using AI here too. Because running deep language-model analysis on every message would be too slow for mail flow, the model is split into three tiers that match depth to ambiguity: Tier one (flash models) evaluates all mail in under 500 milliseconds using machine learning, threat intelligence, computer vision, and language models. Tier two (extended thinking) handles fewer than 1 percent of messages in seconds to minutes, adding sandboxing, topic and tone analysis, and an organizational graph. Tier three (deep thinking) handles fewer than 0.01 percent in minutes, adding multi-stage language model analysis, voice and video, and profiles of privileged individuals. Figure 7. Multi-tier reasoning: most mail is resolved in milliseconds, and only the most ambiguous reaches deep analysis. A message one tier cannot resolve moves to the next, and a malicious verdict can come at any tier. The organizational graph is designed to surface campaigns like the real estate example, where AI-varied requests land across one company but no single mailbox sees more than one. Investigating at Machine Speed AI has also compressed attacker timelines. Automated campaigns can generate and adapt hundreds of messages in the time an analyst triages one, so a missed detection is rarely a single email; it is often a campaign that already includes replies, sign-ins, and mailbox changes. Proofpoint argues that investigation has to change as well, from analyst-driven, ticket-by-ticket review to agentic investigation that keeps pace with the attacker. Its Threat Investigation Agent is designed to run one investigation across email, identity, messaging, browser, and supplier activity, map the blast radius, and feed findings back into detection. Use cases include account takeover, abuse mailbox triage, advanced campaigns, false positive and false negative feedback, and third-party investigative requests. Figure 8. A sample account takeover case in the Threat Investigation Agent, with automatic actions, pending approvals, and an event timeline. In an example case, an RFP-themed credential-phishing lure led to the takeover of a finance user’s account. The attacker signed in from New York and then Dallas, added a mailbox rule to hide replies, and sent about 100 phishing messages to 42 internal recipients. The agent contained the incident four minutes after the trigger, retrieving 92 outbound messages, deleting the rule, blocking the URL, and restoring the user’s settings. Four higher-consequence actions, including a credential reset and 14 days of outbound inspection, were held for human approval. The case also lists what the agent could not determine, such as who clicked a link that sat inside a PDF and was never rewritten, and records failed actions, such as quarantine attempts that did not complete. Defending Against What Attackers Want, Not How They Look The examples Proofpoint shared point to the same conclusion: generative AI has changed the threat landscape faster than behavior-based analysis can keep up. Attackers can now make every message fluent, plausible, and unique, run campaigns that look like ordinary business, and adapt them at machine speed. The behavioral tells that filters once depended on are disappearing. A changed threat calls for changed analysis: keeping traditional and modern detection for what they still catch well, adding intent-based reasoning that asks what a message is trying to achieve, scaling that reasoning across tiers so it keeps pace with mail flow, and investigating incidents at the same speed attackers now operate. Learn more about Proofpoint’s approach to AI, and see a demo, at Proofpoint Nexus.

127hgdq.text: You cannot fully block the two critical PHP flaws called PHP2Shell before today's fix, and the one setting being passed around as a workaround is not enough on its own, the security firm that suggested it now says. PHP will release the fix at 14:00 UTC on October 21 for two flaws it rates 9.2 out of 10, and has given no workaround of its own. Until you can install it, what lowers your risk is taking exposed PHP off the internet or behind access controls, cutting what a compromised server can reach, and having the update ready to apply the moment it lands. Cloudflare says it is seeing early attempts to exploit the flaws, and has pushed emergency rules for sites behind it that it calls a stopgap until you patch. No compromise has been confirmed, the public exploit code going around has not been shown to work, and neither flaw is in CISA's catalog of known exploited flaws.PHP has not said which versions are affected, which part of PHP is involved, or whether any setting changes the risk; it says the full details and the fixed versions come with the release. At the time of writing, that release was not yet out. So nobody outside the group that found the flaws can test whether a given defense works, which is why the advice below is about lowering risk, not promising safety. The setting you were told to change is not protection The workaround spreading on social media and security blogs is one line in a PHP configuration file: session.upload_progress.enabled=0. It turns off Session Upload Progress, a PHP feature that's enabled by default, which records how far a file upload has progressed so another request can check on it. GMO Flatt Security, a Tokyo security firm, suggested setting it early on October 21, saying it could not be sure the change fully addresses the flaws but thought it would help with some probability. Later the same day, the firm walked that back. In an update timestamped 14:00 Japan time (05:00 UTC), it said the setting alone is not a complete fix and that attacks getting around it are expected. It told administrators to prepare their update, watch for attack traffic before the release, and apply the fix as soon as it is out. Two people from the PHP project said the same thing more bluntly. Replying to someone who suggested the upload-progress setting might patch the flaw, Gina Peter Banyard, a PHP core developer and documentation writer funded by the PHP Foundation, wrote: "The only thing I can say is that the only mitigation is patching / upgrading PHP. I sadly know too much." Joe Ferguson, the release manager for the coming PHP 8.6, put it shorter: "ini settings won't save you." The setting cannot be relied on for two reasons. GMO Flatt expects a way around it but has not said what that is. And the whole idea that the flaw lives in Session Upload Progress is a guess: PHP has not confirmed it, the firm itself said it holds only so far as its own research matches PHP2Shell, and an independent code audit argues the specific bug others describe in that feature does not exist in released PHP. That audit is from an anonymous account and PHP's own code will settle it, but it is one more reason not to treat the setting as a shield. Not everyone agrees. One vendor, Upwind, still lists the setting as an immediate mitigation, passing along another researcher's analysis rather than its own tests. watchTowr, which reproduced one of the flaws, says there is "no confirmed patch or workaround at this time." If you already set it No one is telling you to undo the change. The instruction is only not to count it as protection. PHP's own manual already advises turning the feature off where an application does not use upload progress bars, because the stored file names and field names "are not validated and may contain PHP code." If you turned it on by mistake somewhere that needs it, the only cost is that upload progress bars stop working. Check that the change is actually in effect on the process that serves web traffic, not on the command line. The setting is INI_PERDIR, so it can be set in php.ini, .htaccess, or .user.ini. A .user.ini file is read only by the CGI and FastCGI versions of PHP, not by the Apache module, and PHP re-reads it only every 300 seconds by default, so a change there can take five minutes to apply. Under the Apache module, use .htaccess or the server config. Confirm the value on PHP-FPM or mod_php, whichever serves your site, not on php -i at the shell. If you can patch at 14:00 UTC Get ready now. GMO Flatt's advice is to confirm your update steps and the checks you run afterward, rehearse any config change, and line up the people and approvals for a possible emergency restart. When the fix lands, update the runtime that serves web requests, which is PHP-FPM, mod_php, or CGI, not the application on top of it. PHP issues fixes only for its four supported branches, 8.2 through 8.5. Which exact versions carry the fix and how far back the flaws extend will be announced with the release. The Hacker News reported the branch support and the wider background in its earlier coverage of the disclosure. If you cannot patch at once, or run an unsupported version Where an immediate update is not possible, CERT-EU advises organizations to "consider isolating internet-facing applications from public networks until a fix can be applied." Banyard put the same point from inside the project: turning a server off for a day "might be the most sensible thing to do. But that is far from a reasonable thing to demand for most people." Short of shutting down, restrict reach: put the site behind a VPN, allowlisted clients, or authenticated access at the edge, and check that traffic cannot reach the origin directly around those controls. Shrink what an attacker gets if the server is taken over. GMO Flatt's other steps are to reduce the data stored on the server, reduce its privileges, remove stored credentials, including cloud roles, and ensure logging is enabled and kept in a secure location so you can investigate later. Branches older than 8.2, including 8.1, 7.x, and 5.x, are end-of-life and receive no PHP fixes. For those, upgrade, take the system offline, or isolate it; a Linux distribution or hosting provider may backport a fix on its own schedule. Some researchers point to a stronger stopgap than the session setting: blocking requests that carry a multipart/form-data body at the web server, before they reach PHP, because the suspected flaw is in how PHP reads that body. If you try this, block it for more than POST. PHP 8.4 added a function, request_parse_body(), that reads multipart bodies on other methods too, so a POST-only rule can be stepped around.The cost is real: file uploads, and some forms that send multipart without a file, stop working until you remove the block. And like the session setting, this targets a suspected entry path, not a confirmed one, so it reduces exposure rather than guaranteeing safety. A web application firewall is a stopgap here, not a fix, and Cloudflare says so itself. It has pushed emergency rules for the known exploit paths, free tier included, which its CTO calls "a STOPGAP only" ahead of patching. Such rules only see traffic that passes through Cloudflare, and they can miss new attack paths as they appear. If someone else runs your PHP Updating WordPress, Laravel, or another application does not update the PHP runtime underneath it; that comes from your server package, host, or container image. On managed or shared hosting, ask your provider when a fixed PHP build will land and have them stand by. Hosting providers build their packages only after PHP ships the fix: CloudLinux, for one, says its updated packages depend on the upstream release and will be posted when ready. One trap if you run PHP from a Linux distribution's packages: Debian, Ubuntu and similar backport security fixes into the version you already run instead of moving you to a new one, so a patched package can keep an old-looking version number. Do not judge whether you are fixed by the version string alone; check the package changelog for the CVE, or compare the exact package version against your distribution's advisory. What to check when the release lands Exploitation is early and unconfirmed. Cloudflare reports emerging attempts; watchTowr says it reproduced one flaw but has not reported attacks; the public exploit code going around has not been shown to work; and neither flaw was in CISA's catalog of known exploited flaws when it was last checked on October 21. A researcher has posted a video said to demonstrate the exploit chain, and the audit above states that the circulating proof-of-concept code does not fire against released PHP. Treat all of this as a snapshot that can change by the hour. When the fix ships, check the fixed version for your branch, which versions PHP lists as affected, whether PHP confirms or rejects any setting as a mitigation, and whether the session code changed, which also answers the dispute over where the flaw lives. The fixed versions and the advisory will appear on php.net and through PHP's GitHub security advisories, where the project assigns its own identifiers. After updating, review your logs for anything that happened before you patched.

tigvpl.text: The Hacker NewsOct 21, 2026AI Penetration Testing / Web Security An AppSec team can point an AI agent running on a general-purpose model at its own web apps with little setup. Sure, the model writes the attacks. But everything that makes those attacks safe to run against production and worth acting on afterward lives in the harness around the model. The harness is where the engineering in AI pentesting sits. The Hugging Face intrusion OpenAI disclosed in July showed what happens when that harness gives way, even inside an OpenAI evaluation built to contain the agents. Why Each Control Takes Rigorous Engineering Let’s take a closer look at the attack different stages and the role AI agents can take there Scope A pentesting agent makes thousands of decisions about where to send its next request, and the model judges each one against a rule written in plain language. A web app’s real boundary often extends past one domain through redirects and calls to outside services. Enforcing scope means code that inspects every request before it leaves, and OWASP’s 2026 guidance routes privileged actions through a deterministic policy engine that checks them at execution time, outside the model. Credentials Finding exposed credentials is part of what a pentest does, so the agent regularly comes across working keys outside its assignment. Which of those it may use, for what, and when a person gets involved are policy decisions that the code around the model applies on every attempt. Prompt Injection Every page and API response the agent reads, including hidden fields, metadata and comments a user never sees, can carry content written by anyone who can post to the app. A single product review is enough to plant malicious instructions. OWASP ranks prompt injection the top risk for LLM applications and notes that no reliable prevention exists today. The design question is not whether the model gets fooled, but how much damage it can do if and when it does. That comes down to two things: how tightly each action is constrained and which actions require further inspection and human sign-off. Neither is simple. OWASP warns that approval fatigue degrades reviewer judgement at scale, so routing everything to a human simply shifts the failure point down the line. Proof In October 2026, Google stopped accepting product vulnerability reports to its open-source bug bounty program after a surge in automated submissions, the majority of which it said were not valid. A finding a developer can’t reproduce is just another ticket to close. Producing one worth acting on means running the exploit, capturing what it reached, and packaging the result so anyone can replay it, all within the limits of the other controls set. None of this is built once. Every model upgrade can change how the agent behaves, and every release changes the app whose security it tests. And around the controls sit the systems a production agent depends on, including change-triggered testing, routing findings to the developers who own the code, strictly controlling what customer data reaches a model provider, and connecting what the agent finds in the app to the rest of the environment. Across all of it, the pattern is the same. The model reasons about what to try, and deterministic code decides what runs, records it, and stops it when needed. How Pentera Apps Implements the Harness This separation of reasoning and execution is how we approach building Pentera Apps. Instead of letting an AI model send requests directly into an application, Pentera Apps pairs an AI that decides what to test with a deterministic harness that controls what runs. Every action is logged and any test can be paused or stopped at any time. It's the same safety discipline Pentera has applied to production testing for nearly a decade, across thousands of global customers. The harness also produces the proof. Every finding ships with a replayable exploit script, a CVSS 3.1 score and CWE mapping, so developers can reproduce the attack themselves instead of taking it on trust. Once the fix lands, the exact same attack can be re-run to confirm the path is closed. Tests run on demand or on a schedule, with change-triggered testing in CI/CD coming next, so validation stays inline with development. The surrounding systems follow the same discipline. Only minimal, redacted data reaches the LLM, with zero retention and no training on customer data, and data stays in the customer’s region. Every test starts with context from reconnaissance across the customer’s attack surfaces, findings from their security stack, and live threat intelligence signals. That context lets Pentera trace an exploit in a web app be traced into network, cloud, and identity on one platform. In agentic pentesting, the harness determines the results. Pentera Apps builds it in, so security teams get validated findings without building one themselves. Note: This article has been expertly written and contributed by Assaf Regev, AVP Product Marketing at Pentera. Security teams can sign up for early access to Pentera Apps, Agentic Web App Pentesting.

esygxk.text: Attackers took control of more than 300 Tor exit relays in early October and used them to redirect SSH connections to servers that stole login passwords, a researcher found. Exit relays are the last hop in a Tor circuit, where traffic leaves the network for its destination. Only a password login to an SSH server made through Tor between October 1 and 5, after accepting the interception server's host key, could have been captured. The Tor Project began flagging relays on October 4, and by October 5, none remained in the consensus, the list of relays that Tor clients use. At the peak on October 4, the relays carrying the attacker's exit policy made up 7.46% of Tor's exit capacity, measured by consensus weight, according to an analysis of public Tor directory data posted to the tor-relays mailing list. The researcher, who publishes as kaba, scanned all of Tor's roughly 3,000 exits on October 2 and found 333 redirecting SSH to the same 12 interception servers. The directory-data analysis counts 377 relays run by 59 operators that switched to the attacker's exit policy between October 1 and 4, which it calls "a policy match, not proof of compromise." How the Hijacked Exits Intercepted SSH An exit relay only carries traffic to the ports its exit policy allows. The attackers rewrote that policy in the relays' torrc configuration files to allow port 22 (the SSH port), enabling SSH on 342 relays that had blocked it. Another 24 relays that had not been exits at all became exits. "It seems the attacker is gaining access to Linux based hosts and when these machines are running non-exits they are editing the torrc file and turning them into exits to be able to carry out the SSH attack," the Tor Project's network health team wrote in its October 5 notice to relay operators. Most of the affected relays were already exits, the directory data shows. The same change closed the encrypted mail ports, IMAPS and POP3S, and on most relays opened the plaintext-capable ones, POP3 and IMAP. A Tor client only picks an exit that allows the destination port, so these relays stopped carrying encrypted mail and started carrying SSH, Telnet, and, on most of them, plaintext mail. Why the encrypted mail ports were closed is not visible in the data, the analysis says. With port 22 open, an SSH connection through one of these exits went to one of 12 interception servers instead of its destination, kaba found. When a server intercepted the connection, it presented its own host key. A user who already knew the real server's key saw OpenSSH's warning that the remote host identification had changed, and a user connecting for the first time saw the usual prompt to accept a new key. In the October 2 scan, about a dozen exits were serving a fake host key, and the other 300 or so redirected through the same servers without altering the key. A user who accepted the key and typed a password handed it to the interceptor. The interceptor connected to the real server, so the session worked, and every command could be watched and separately logged in with the stolen password to check for sudo and run a base64-encoded Perl installer. In kaba's honeypot, the installer took the same form as the command that put Ebury, a backdoor that hides inside OpenSSH, on one of a relay operator's servers, as described below. A key-based SSH login could not be relayed this way. Under the SSH authentication protocol, , the client's signature includes an identifier unique to each session, so a signature made for the interceptor's session is useless against the real server. The interceptor could still accept a key login itself and show a fake shell, but it could not reach the real server with it. A password, by contrast, travels inside the encrypted session and can be read by the server at the other end, which here was the interceptor. Who Was Exposed, and What to Do If You Were To be exposed, someone had to connect to an SSH server over Tor between October 1 and the afternoon of October 5, land on one of the hijacked exits, have the connection intercepted rather than passed through, accept the interceptor's host key, and log in with a password. No count of victims exists. If you accepted an unfamiliar or changed host key over Tor in that window, treat the password you typed as stolen, change it, and check that server for the Ebury signs listed below. An OpenSSH client that accepted the key saved it in known_hosts. The server that intercepted kaba's connection used an ED25519 key with the fingerprint SHA256:6baCZCPsl+AfQuujUS81fMEE/C7UeJ+AwjrImqmDB3E, though the other interception servers may have used different keys. How It Was Found and Stopped Kaba encountered the attack on the morning of October 2, when an SSH connection over Tor returned a changed-key warning. He then used exitmap, a scanning tool that the Tor Project's network health team also uses, to open an SSH connection from one of his servers to another via each exit in turn. One end checked whether the host key was correct, and the other whether the connection originated at the exit or from an interception server. He reported the results to the health team that evening. The health team also spotted the policy change through its own monitoring. On October 4, it contacted Zimmer, who ran the Quetzalcoatl relay family, the largest group of affected relays, and Zimmer confirmed the change was not his, asked for the relays to be marked bad, and stopped Tor on the server running them. Directory authorities began voting the BadExit and MiddleOnly flags on affected relays at 18:00 UTC that day, and the flags were in the consensus by 21:00. BadExit tells Tor clients never to use a relay as an exit. On the morning of October 5,, a scripted restart swept through 55 of Quetzalcoatl's hosts, with the policy still in place. Who ran it is not known. The directory authorities were by then rejecting affected relays from the network, the Tor Project said in its notice, and the two relays Zimmer had stopped were refused when they tried to rejoin, he wrote. By 17:00 UTC on October 5, no relay with the attacker's policy was in the consensus, and none had returned as of October 9, the directory-data analysis found. Forty-one relays, nine of them Quetzalcoatl's, were still publishing the policy at that point but were not listed. Tor Metrics' count of relays carrying the Exit flag fell by about 370 between October 3 and October 5, matching the number of affected relays, and had not recovered by October 18. Ebury, and How the Attackers Got In Zimmer described his side in a post-mortem on the list on October 7. Two of his servers were running Ebury version 1.8.3: a management server at Contabo that served as the family's VPN gateway and SSH jump host, and a FranTech VPS he calls Switzerland2 that ran two of the exits. Ebury is a backdoor and credential stealer for OpenSSH that has been active since 2009, according to ESET, which estimated in 2024 that it had infected 400,000 servers, with more than 100,000 still infected in late 2023. The attacker logged in to the management server on August 28 with the operator account's password on the first try, gained root within five minutes, installed Ebury, then reached Switzerland2 a little over an hour later and installed it there too. "The root cause was ours: one password reused for SSH login, sudo and the backup passphrase, stored in plaintext on both servers, plus SSH password authentication left enabled on the internet-facing management server," Zimmer wrote. Where the attacker got that password is unknown. Ebury's backdoor logins leave no record. On October 2, the exits' configuration files were rewritten with no login, sudo command, or cron job in the logs, and the two relays published the attacker's policy at 09:34 UTC. It stayed live for about 52 hours on two relays moving roughly 3.4 TiB a day. A routine reboot on October 4 killed the attacker's hidden tools, but Ebury came straight back. The family's "offline" master keys "were not offline: copies sat in the workstation backup on the management server, encrypted with the password the attacker already had," Zimmer wrote. He retired every relay and the bridge in the family and deleted both servers. This Ebury is a single setuid library file, /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libkeyutils.so.1.10.2, with the libkeyutils.so.1 symlink pointed at it. The packaged library is untouched, so dpkg -V and debsums do not catch it, and sshd, sudo, and PAM pass their package checks. Version 1.8.3 is newer than ESET's public indicators, which stop at 1.8.2, and ESET's published detection script, read on October 21, lists no socket name for it. Marc-Etienne M. Léveillé, who co-wrote ESET's 2014 Ebury paper, wrote its 2024 report and has since left the company, replied that version 1.8.3 has been around since at least June 2026 and posted an updated copy of the script that covers it. "Given how many servers had Ebury between 2009 and 2023 (400 000!), there are most likely other compromised Tor relays out there," he wrote. How the other 58 operators' hosts were entered is the main open question. Among their relays listed on October 1, 71 of the 101 hosted on FranTech Solutions, the network behind the BuyVM hosting brand, switched to the attacker's policy, against 13 of 9,054 hosted elsewhere, the directory-data analysis found. Forty relays of 21 operators changed within five and a half minutes on October 1, most by a configuration reload, which the analysis reads as one actor already holding access to all 40. Léveillé's best guess for the password was a login from a host already running Ebury, with a compromised hosting provider as another possibility. ESET has seen providers whose management servers ran Ebury and whose customers' virtual servers ended up infected, he wrote. Kaba counted 26 of the 27 compromised servers outside the Quetzalcoatl family at FranTech/BuyVM and asked on the list: "Could they have compromised those servers at the hoster level?" Quetzalcoatl's own compromise ran through its Contabo management server, and 225 of its 273 affected relays sat on other networks. Who is behind the campaign is unknown, and so is how many of the affected hosts ran Ebury: Zimmer examined two of his, and the directory data shows only the policy. A fake uppercase CRON daemon and NAT rules redirecting port 22 were among the signs other operators reported to the Tor Project. Zimmer's servers had neither, and whether the cases share one actor is open. On Zimmer's relays, the port changes meant any mail retrieval could only happen in plaintext, he wrote, and a hidden process named snf ran on Switzerland2 for most of the window. What it did is unknown. What Relay Operators Should Check The Tor Project's notice asks Linux relay operators to check Relay Search for an Exit flag or exit policy they did not set, and to look through torrc and any included files for changed ExitRelay, ExitPolicy, ContactInfo, MyFamily or Nickname lines. It also lists NAT rules on port 22, unknown listening processes or outbound connections, new users, authorized_keys entries, cron jobs and systemd units, and a tor binary that fails its package check. Zimmer's servers showed none of the host-level signs on that list, only the changed exit policy, so a clean host check does not rule out this Ebury. The signs of the implant, from Zimmer's post, are: File: /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libkeyutils.so.1.10.2, setuid and owned by no package (63,368 bytes on his servers, with a hash that differs on every server) Symlink: libkeyutils.so.1 pointing at that file Socket: abstract UNIX socket @event-0YsOG9WSOE Process: a fake /sbin/rsyslogd (earlier systemd-udevd or arpd) running inside the ssh.service cgroup IP: 185.225.226[.]62, the source of the August 28 login SSH key: RSA SHA256:dvACokMYcXJ2om4wuS+TvdtjrAgPK7rC7ZQHDgvBHzk, used to log in to Switzerland2 SSH keys embedded in the implant: RSA SHA256:KlICz/B59619CpuQdGzgmmvzWBfTMUJ77EwihTYobuo and ED25519 SHA256:OfLY0uF9SwOW9xVjiMXZGDfk6Atmz6CbHy4epknLm8Y Interceptor host key: ED25519 SHA256:6baCZCPsl+AfQuujUS81fMEE/C7UeJ+AwjrImqmDB3E, seen on kaba's connection Check from a rescue system or an offline disk image if you can. On a live server, log in with a key. "Never type a password into a server you suspect, because Ebury will capture it," Zimmer wrote. Start a shell with H=1 I=1 LD_PRELOAD=":" LD_DEBUG=":" bash to get past the userland rootkit before running Léveillé's updated script or the commands in Zimmer's post. If you find it, the Tor Project's steps are: take the relay offline preserve the disk and logs before wiping reinstall rather than clean up generate a new relay identity and treat the old keys as stolen rotate every credential that was on the host Reinstalling matters because the implant survived a reboot on Zimmer's server. Report to bad-relays@lists.torproject.org, and if your IP address was blocked during the incident, write to the same address once your host is clean to have the block lifted, Georg Koppen of the Tor Project said in a follow-up.

rh8ku1.text: Microsoft says it mistakenly flagged a bug causing Always On VPN connection issues as fixed in the October 2026 Windows 11 cumulative updates. Always On VPN replaced the legacy DirectAccess technology and supports domain-joined, non-domain-joined, and Microsoft Entra ID–joined devices running Windows 10, Windows 11, and Windows Server. It runs in the background and establishes secure tunnels back to the user's corporate network whenever their device connects to the internet. Microsoft first acknowledged the issue in a service alert sent to IT administrators in late September, saying it was triggered on systems running Windows 11 24H2 and later after installing the September 2026 security updates when the initial Always On VPN connection failed (e.g., when using automatic protocol selection with IKEv2 and SSTP). "When automatic protocol selection or protocol fallback was configured, affected VPN connections could remain stuck in a Connecting state or fail to connect after an initial connection attempt failed," it said. "In some cases, subsequent connection attempts could display the error, 'The specified port is already in use.'" Mistakenly marked as resolved After releasing the October 2026 Patch Tuesday Windows 11 cumulative updates, Microsoft marked the bug as resolved, but in a Tuesday update it said the issues weren't actually addressed and that a fix would ship later. "This disclosure was mistakenly updated to Resolved status on October 13, 2026. We have returned its status to Mitigated," it said in a service alert sent to IT admins. "A resolution for this issue is planned to be included in an update to be released in the coming weeks. We apologize for any inconvenience or confusion." While Microsoft continues working on a permanent solution, it shared a temporary fix that requires affected customers to choose one of two VPN tunneling protocols to work around the issue. "IT administrators can mitigate this issue by changing the Always On VPN profile from automatic protocol selection to a single protocol, either SSTP only or IKEv2 only, depending on their environment and configuration," it said. "Organizations should select the protocol based on their environment, security, and deployment requirements." The September cumulative updates have been linked to multiple other problems affecting both home and enterprise Windows users. Days after last month's Patch Tuesday, Microsoft released emergency out-of-band updates to fix Hyper-V issues, Remote Desktop Services failures, and USB audio problems. It also shared a temporary workaround for an issue that blocked some Windows 11 users from logging in with valid domain credentials and announced that it is working to address another bug that broke the Windows built-in File History backup feature. Once attackers have valid credentials, only 37% of their actions are blocked Overall prevention scores can hide what happens after initial access. Once attackers are using valid credentials, prevention drops sharply.The Blue Report 2026 measures defenses technique by technique across 338 million simulations run in customer production environments. Get the report

8we56b.text: This story is developing and was written before PHP's scheduled 14:00 UTC release on October 21. Once the release is out, the affected and fixed versions below are confirmed by the official advisory. PHP will ship an out-of-cycle security release at 14:00 UTC today, October 21, for two critical vulnerabilities that its security team has rated 9.2 on the CVSS v4.0 scale but has not described. Security researchers at watchTowr say the two flaws allow remote code execution. Only the four supported PHP branches, 8.2 through 8.5, can receive the fix, and no exploitation has been reported so far. The advance notice followed a leak. On October 20, a post on HN said two PHP remote code execution flaws, rated CVSS 10.0 and affecting versions from PHP 5 onward, would be disclosed on Thursday, October 22. The poster said they had "no evidence beyond 'source: trust me, bro'". watchTowr then posted on X that the leaked information was real, that the two flaws were under embargo, that everyone had been supposed to wait until Thursday, and that it could not share more for now. PHP published its notice that evening, at 19:33 UTC, with the release set for Wednesday, a day before the date watchTowr gave. The notice says PHP may release earlier "should details of either vulnerability become public, or should evidence of active exploitation appear in the wild." The leak carried the flaws' existence, a score, a date, and two CVE identifiers, not how the flaws work. The CVSS 10.0 figure is the leak's. PHP's rating is 9.2 on version 4.0 of the scale. The identifiers researchers are using, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, were also listed in the leaked post. PHP's notice names neither. The claim that every version since PHP 5 is affected is unconfirmed too: watchTowr's own FAQ on the flaws says that scope "has not been confirmed by an official vendor advisory" and that no configuration or feature requirement has been described. PHP says "Full details, affected versions, and the fixed versions will be published with the release." Researchers have started calling the pair php2shell. The name is theirs, not PHP's. Whatever the affected range turns out to be, PHP issues fixes only for its four supported branches, and records each branch's changes in its changelog. Versions 8.2 and 8.3 receive only security fixes, and 8.4 and 8.5 are in active support. Ahead of the release, several trackers, including Alpine Linux's and security researcher Kevin Beaumont, expect the fixes to ship as PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35, the next point release of each branch, though PHP has not confirmed the numbers. Anything older, including 8.1, 8.0, 7.x, and 5.x, is end of life and gets no PHP fix. If the flaws reach those branches, installations on them will have no vendor patch. PHP branches that can receive today's fix Branch Current release (September 24) PHP support status 8.5 8.5.11 Active support until December 31, 2027 8.4 8.4.26 Active support until December 31, 2026 8.3 8.3.35 Security fixes only until December 31, 2027 8.2 8.2.34 Security fixes only until December 31, 2026 Security company Mallory counted about 884,000 internet-facing hosts whose HTTP banner reported a PHP version of 8.1 or older to the Shodan search engine on October 20, 59% of the roughly 1.5 million hosts that reported any version. The count covers banners, not confirmed affected systems, and a further 740,000 hosts reported PHP without a version. PHP has published no workaround. Until the release lands, the preparation comes down to six steps, most of them drawn from a rapid-response post from Huntress, with CERT-EU's isolation advice added. Inventory every PHP install, including PHP bundled in vendor appliances, Windows software, and control panels such as cPanel and Plesk. Be ready to upgrade at 14:00 UTC. Patch internet-facing systems first, and check your Linux distribution and hosting provider for backported packages. On an end-of-life branch, upgrade, take the system off the internet, or put it behind a VPN or a web application firewall until you can. Where patching cannot be done at once, CERT-EU advises that you "consider isolating internet-facing applications from public networks until a fix is available." Watch what PHP starts. Alert on php-fpm, php-cgi, httpd, or apache2 launching shells, interpreters, or download tools. On Linux servers without endpoint detection, Florian Roth's process-watcher logs every program a PHP process starts, with its command line. It sees a program only after it has started and, in Roth's words, "prevents nothing." If you find something, isolate the server, preserve the web server and PHP logs, and look for web shells, new files in the web root, new cron jobs, scheduled tasks, and accounts. Huntress said it had not seen exploitation of the flaws in its partner environments as of October 20, had not built or reproduced a proof of concept, and was not aware of public exploit code. watchTowr's FAQ lists exploitation as none reported as of October 21 and the flaws as not in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. For comparison, when CVE-2024-4577, a PHP flaw in CGI mode on Windows, became public in June 2024, Akamai saw exploit attempts against its honeypot servers within 24 hours. The release should clarify what the notice withheld: which versions are affected, which part of PHP is involved, whether an attack requires a particular way of running PHP, a configuration, or a login, and how PHP itself describes the flaws. At the time of writing, PHP had not released the fixes.

e4cdag.text: Unknown threat actors breached TeamUpdraft's website and potentially gained unauthorized access to customers' connection keys for UpdraftCentral, UpdraftVault, and UpdraftClone, using them to backdoor WordPress sites. TeamUpdraft is the developer behind UpdraftPlus, a popular WordPress backup plugin with over four million active installations. The vendor also offers UpdraftCentral, a remote management service that's used for managing multiple sites remotely. A client component of UpdraftCentral is shipped within every copy of UpdraftPlus. "Over the weekend of 17-18 October we identified unauthorized access to the teamupdraft.com website," TeamUpdraft said in a statement. "Our team responded straight away and worked through the night to contain it – we closed the access route, signed out every account and replaced the keys and credentials that could have been affected." As a result of the incident, threat actors are believed to have accessed its customer database, which holds the following information - Names, email addresses, billing addresses and order history Account passwords, stored only in hashed (scrambled) form and never in plain text Two-factor authentication (2FA) settings Connection keys for UpdraftCentral, UpdraftVault and UpdraftClone TeamUpdraft said the database does not hold any financial information, and that they are handled by Stripe and PayPal. It also emphasized that the UpdraftPlus plugin, along with self-hosted versions of UpdraftCentral and backups sent to customers' own remote storage, are not impacted. "However, if your site was accessed through UpdraftCentral, please also re-authorise your remote storage and change any storage access keys, as a precaution," it said. In addition, TeamUpdraft said it deployed a fix to address the underlying issue, signed out every teamupdraft.com account and reset login security across the site, and released UpdraftPlus 1.26.13 (free) and 2.26.13 (Premium) to automatically disconnect every UpdraftCentral connection made before 10 p.m. BST on October 18, 2026, to prevent the old keys from working. Other steps taken by the developer are listed below - Disconnected every site from UpdraftVault and issued new credentials Replaced every UpdraftClone client key Rotated its keys with payment providers and other connected services Implemented additional monitoring in place Reported the incident to the U.K. Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) and other relevant authorities Users who have a teamupdraft.com account are advised to change their password with immediate effect (and elsewhere, if the same password has been reused), reset 2FA settings, and exercise caution when receiving unexpected emails claiming to be from TeamUpdraft. TeamUpdraft is also recommending that cloud customers of UpdraftCentral follow the steps below as soon as possible, since the connection keys can send commands to the connected sites - Log in to the site's own WordPress dashboard, not through UpdraftCentral. Update UpdraftPlus to version 1.26.12 (free) or 2.26.12 (Premium) or later. Disconnect it from UpdraftCentral: go to Settings > UpdraftPlus > Advanced Tools > UpdraftCentral and delete the connection key. Go to Users and check for any administrator accounts you don’t recognise. Remove them. Go to Plugins, including the Must-Use tab if you can see it, and check for anything you don’t recognise. Remove it. Change the passwords for all administrator accounts on the site. If you find anything suspicious, consider restoring the site from a backup taken before 17 October. Reconnect the site to UpdraftCentral. UpdraftVault users are being urged to reconnect their sites to the backup service, and UpdraftClone users who have created a client key are required to copy the new keys from My Account > UpdraftClone > UpdraftClone Key Management and share them with their clients. The development comes as WordPress security company Patchstack said it observed an attacker holding valid UpdraftCentral dashboard keys issuing commands to install backdoor plugins on connected WordPress sites. The campaign is said to have run continuously through an 18-hour window on October 18 and 19, 2026. "The attacker sends a signed plugin.upload_plugin command over the plugin's remote procedure call channel, which listens on ordinary POST requests to the site root. WordPress installs and activates the supplied plugin through its standard installer," Patchstack security researcher Dave Jong said. Slovakia-based penetration testing company Nethemba, which first detected the attack in the wild, has described the rogue plugin as a backdoor that hooks into every request to the site to check if the URL contains the parameter "?_9f5696=" and compares it with a 32-character token. If a matching token is detected, it creates a user "data-ops43" with the display name "Site Tools," assigns it the Editor role, and grants the account "manage_options" and "install_plugins" permissions, allowing the operator to upload arbitrary PHP plugins and open site settings. "Enabling registration and setting the default role to administrator is enough for the attacker to create a full administrator," Nethemba said. "On a standard WordPress site, an Editor also has unfiltered_html, so the account can put JavaScript into posts that runs in the browser of every administrator." "The backdoor has a second layer as well. The account it creates, with a known password, stays in WordPress even after the plugin is removed, and the attacker can log in with it through the normal login form unless two-factor authentication is enabled for that account." Although an early version of the plugin suffered from a coding error that causes impacted sites to fail with error 500, Nethemba said the threat actor deleted the broken backdoor by sending a "plugin.delete_plugin" command and then uploaded a working version that creates a full administrator account or logs in as an existing administrator. WordPress site owners are advised to check for the following indicators of compromise - Plugin names: Site Health Cache or Site Health 364F, Asset Forge 2, Content Helper, Wp Forge, Query Shelf, Style Bridge 8F5, Media Kit 183, Query Shelf, Post Dock 776, Nav Hub, Speed Desk, Speed Kit 300, Link Latch, Script Shelf, or Feed Case Account names: system_team850, web.tech988, cmseditor170, cms.tech644 or web_mgr684, with an email at @example.com and a display name such as System Team, Web Tech, System Staff, System Ops, or Cms Tech IP addresses: 43.250.53.42 and 2a09:bac5:4e21:2e3c::49b:9 In all, Patchstack said it observed 99 distinct backdoor plugin names, with each sample carrying the line "Small maintenance toolkit: keeps option storage tidy." Wordfence, which published its own analysis of the incident, said a WordPress site may be affected if the below criteria are satisfied - The site had UpdraftPlus Free or UpdraftPlus Premium installed and active while the affected UpdraftCentral connection key was present. The site has, or had during the incident, an active connection key for TeamUpdraft’s cloud-hosted UpdraftCentral service. "This is the second incident in this channel in five months," Patchstack warned. "In June 2026 the vendor fixed CVE-2026-10795 (CVSS 8.1), where an obsolete unsigned message format let an attacker forge UpdraftCentral commands with no keys at all. That was fixed in 1.26.5 and 2.26.5, but exploitation attempts continue, so sites below those versions face both problems at once." The development comes days after the website of the Rank Math PRO WordPress plugin was hit by a software supply chain attack, causing users who downloaded version 3.0.123 between October 15 at 8:02 p.m. UTC and October 16 at 7:12 a.m. UTC to receive compromised versions that planted hidden backdoors. The incident has been assigned the CVE identifier CVE-2026-111862 (CVSS score: 9.8). The issue was fixed in Rank Math PRO version 3.0.124. "The malware may establish persistent access, communicate with rank1cdn[.]com, recreate hidden backdoors on page visits, and expose WordPress credentials, database credentials, API keys, and other secrets accessible to the web server," Wordefence said. The findings also coincide with an advisory from PHP, which said it intends to ship a security release that fixes two critical vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, CVSS scores: 9.2), as information about the flaws leaked ahead of their scheduled disclosure. The flaws have been codenamed PHP2Shell. According to watchTowr CEO Benjamin Harris, the vulnerabilities affect PHP versions 5, 6, 7, and 8, and were originally due for release on October 22 at 11 a.m. ET. "PHP is everywhere. It quietly powers WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento sites, shared hosting platforms, control panels, and an awful lot of software that doesn't even advertise that it runs PHP under the hood," Huntress said. "When a critical bug lands in PHP itself, rather than in one app built on top of it, the number of places you have to go looking to identify vulnerable PHP versions gets very big, very fast."

1d5d77c.text: The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) says the SafePay ransomware gang has breached over 600 critical infrastructure organizations worldwide since 2024. In a joint report with the FBI, the U.S. Secret Service (USSS), Germany's Landeskriminalamt Rheinland-Pfalz, and the UK's National Crime Agency and North West Regional Organised Crime Unit, the federal agency added that paying ransoms does not guarantee recovery of files encrypted in ransomware attacks and urged victims to report incidents to law enforcement. "SafePay is one of the most active ransomware groups and have affected businesses and critical infrastructure in North America, South America, Europe, and Australia—including at least 600 organizations from multiple critical infrastructure sectors since August 2024," CISA said. "SafePay threat actors gain initial access through a variety of means, including credential exposure, brute force password attacks, and exploiting virtual private network (VPN) access—particularly the IP addresses of VPN provider 'Mullvad'." The co-authoring agencies advised network defenders to secure their networks against the ransomware group's attacks by restricting administrative tools and privileges to block lateral movement after compromise and implementing multifactor authentication (MFA) and identity, credential, and access management (ICAM) policies for better account security. Security teams should also keep systems updated, focusing on flaws affecting VPNs, firewalls, and other edge devices added to CISA's catalog of actively exploited vulnerabilities because they're often targeted in SafePay attacks for initial access to victims' networks. "They also use phished account profiles to infiltrate networks and exploit common vulnerabilities and exposures (CVEs) for edge devices and other internet-exposed systems through automated scripts," CISA added. "SafePay actors may disrupt recovery operations by deleting shadow copies and resetting network-attached storage devices containing backups." The advisory also includes indicators of compromise (IOCs) and tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) to previous SafePay ransomware activity observed between November 2024 and August 2026 during FBI, USSS, and Landeskriminalamt Rheinland-Pfalz investigations. Unlike similar operations, ​SafePay emerged in August 2024 as a private ransomware group that doesn't work with affiliates. It has since added hundreds of victims from North America, South America, Europe, and Australia to its dark web leak site, but the actual number of victims it has breached and attempted to extort is higher, since it lists only those who don't pay on its leak platform. This ransomware group is also known for double-extortion tactics, stealing sensitive documents before encrypting the victims' systems and threatening to leak all the stolen data online if a ransom isn't paid. Since the start of 2025, SafePay has slowly filled the gap left by BlackCat (ALPHV) and LockBit ransomware, becoming one of the most active ransomware operations.
