izorrv.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 21, 2026Artificial Intelligence / National Security U.S. federal civilian agencies must remove DeepSeek products from their information technology systems, along with any third-party products or services "developed using DeepSeek implementations," under a Department of Homeland Security order. They may also no longer buy information technology products or services from the Chinese AI developer or its affiliates Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin issued the order, dated July 24, 2026, under the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act of 2018, and the department published it in the Federal Register on October 20. The notice does not define "DeepSeek implementations." The order names Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Co., Ltd., the developer of the R1 and V3 models, and covers its affiliates as defined in federal acquisition rules. The company's privacy policy says it collects, processes and stores users' personal data in the People's Republic of China. Under the 2018 law, the Federal Acquisition Security Council recommends exclusion and removal orders, and three officials may issue them: the Secretary of Homeland Security for civilian agencies, the Secretary of Defense for the Defense Department and national security systems, and the Director of National Intelligence for the intelligence community. The DeepSeek order therefore covers only what civilian agencies buy and run. It does not restrict companies or the public. The 2018 law was first used in 2025, when the Director of National Intelligence excluded Acronis, a Swiss cybersecurity and data protection company, from intelligence community procurement and ordered its products removed from intelligence community systems. Executive agencies "shall comply with exclusion and removal orders," the law says. An agency can ask the official who issued an order for an exception, and under the council's regulations the request must be in writing and give a compelling justification. DHS directs questions about the order to CISA's FASCSA Order Implementation Team at fascsa.orders@cisa.dhs.gov. The order also reaches government contractors. A federal contract that carries FAR clause 52.204-30 bars the contractor from providing or using, in performing the contract, any product or service covered by an applicable FASCSA order, unless the issuing official has granted a waiver. The clause also requires the contractor to: Search SAM.gov for the phrase "FASCSA order" at least once every three months Make a reasonable inquiry into its supply chain when a new order could affect it Report any covered product or service it has provided or used to the contracting officer within 3 business days of identifying it Send further information on mitigation within 10 business days of that report Include the clause in its subcontracts An order issued after a solicitation applies to an existing contract only once the contracting officer adds it by amendment or modification. The Federal Register notice gives no reasons for the order. The signed order is attached to the notice as four scanned pages and is posted on regulations.gov under docket DHS-2026-0628. The order is dated July 24. DHS filed it for public inspection at the Federal Register on October 19, 87 days later, and it was published the next day. The council's regulations leave public release of an order to the issuing official, who "May provide a copy of the order to other persons, including through public disclosure." They set no deadline for it. The law requires the issuing official to notify the company named in an order and the appropriate congressional committees, and to review the order at least once a year. Before the order, U.S. restrictions on DeepSeek were device bans adopted one body at a time. By February 2025, Congress, NASA, the Navy, the Pentagon and Texas had barred DeepSeek from government devices. Bills to bar DeepSeek on government devices were introduced in the House and Senate that month and had not advanced past committee as of October 21. China's foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said at a briefing on October 20 that "China consistently opposes the overstretching of the concept of national security" and that Beijing will "resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese companies," the Associated Press reported. DeepSeek did not immediately respond to the AP's request for comment.

19xps75.text: State Bank of India has identified 3,897 customer records containing personal information in a set of about 375,000 records available on the dark web, and it does not yet know where the data came from. The state-owned bank, India's largest, said in a stock-exchange filing dated October 21 that it "has experienced an incident involving the loss of certain data." The count is preliminary, and the bank has yet to establish whether the data is authentic, how far the exposure goes and what risk it poses to customers. The exposed information "reportedly included customers' registered mobile numbers, dates of birth, names, gender, email addresses, residential addresses, branch and CIF identifiers, lead IDs, and metadata associated with loan/lead records and other related files," in the filing's words. A CIF identifier is the customer information file number, the bank's internal ID for each customer. The bank has not said whether the 3,897 records belong to 3,897 different people, or what the rest of the set contains. The 3,897 are roughly 1 in 100 of the records it examined. Account numbers, balances, passwords, one-time passcodes, card details and government identity numbers such as PAN or Aadhaar are not among the categories the filing lists. The risk in the listed categories is impersonation: a caller or message that uses a customer's name, mobile number, date of birth, address, branch, and internal ID to appear to come from the bank. The alert reached the bank on October 16 via its threat intelligence provider, CERT-In, India's national computer emergency response team, and the Defense Cyber Agency, the armed forces' cyber agency under the Ministry of Defense. The bank activated its incident response and containment procedures and engaged an independent cybersecurity firm from CERT-In's panel of approved security auditors to assess what the filing calls "the alleged compromise." The incident has no material impact on the bank's core business operations, financial performance or business continuity, the filing says. That covers the bank's business, not its customers. The filing names no attacker, forum or dataset. The figure of about 375,000 matches a claim that the monitoring account CyberPulse56 flagged on X on October 16. The account said a threat actor using the name Siriusim claimed to have leaked customer documents and personal data linked to SBI: 375,000 rows in CSV format and 2,722 PDF documents, said to include personal information, loan applications and supporting documents, account-opening forms and addresses. The Free Press Journal examined the listing on BreachForums, a cybercrime forum used to trade stolen data, and found 4 sample records posted with the listing. The phone numbers in the samples were valid. The WhatsApp profile picture on one number matched the passport-size photograph on that person's KYC document, which the actor had also posted. That check covers 4 records and does not show that the whole set is genuine or where it came from. The samples were mostly loan-related and carried KYC fields, and they did not show whether the data belonged to SBI itself, one of its subsidiaries, or a third-party provider that handles banking applications. Nothing in the bank's filing ties its analysis to the listing, and the bank has not said whether the 2,722 PDF documents were part of what it examined. Whether any SBI system was breached is an open question. The filing leaves the source of the data to the investigation and gives no date for when the data first appeared. The filing does not mention whether affected customers have been or will be told. The bank's cyber security page, last updated in June, tells customers to report any cyber incident to report.phishing@sbi.co.in or the national cybercrime helpline, 1930. That is general advice, written before the incident. Bank of Baroda, another state-owned bank, told the exchanges on July 27 about a cyber-security incident in nearly the same words, including "the alleged compromise," after receiving "a communication from an anonymous source claiming access to certain data." That filing named a preliminary cause, "potential business email compromise." SBI's names none.

o1e1zt.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 21, 2026Vulnerability / Malware The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Tuesday added four vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, including four vulnerabilities impacting Plex Media Server that's collectively called Plex2Shell. The vulnerabilities are listed below - CVE-2026-96652 (CVSS score: 5.3) - Plex Media Server Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability CVE-2026-96654 (CVSS score: 6.9) - Plex Media Server improper neutralization of encoded URI schemes in a web page Vulnerability CVE-2026-96655 (CVSS score: 5.3) - Plex Media Server Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability CVE-2026-96656 (CVSS score: 8.6) - Plex Media Server external control of file name or path Vulnerability According to security researcher Zach Main, who discovered and reported the vulnerabilities, a remote attacker could chain the four vulnerabilities to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution. The issues were addressed in Plex Media Server 1.43.3.10861 released on August 3, 2026. The addition of the four vulnerabilities to the KEV catalog follows a report from security researcher boredhackerblog, who found that threat actors are weaponizing the flaws to deploy cryptocurrency miners and proxy malware. CISA has also flagged two other vulnerabilities as actively exploited. One of them is a DLL sideloading vulnerability in Siemens Software Center (CVE-2026-110936, CVSS score: 8.4) that has been abused in ClickFix attacks using a platform called Romulus. The second security flaw is a command injection bug in EG Secure Solutions SiteGuard Server Edition (CVE-2026-106931, CVSS score: 8.5) that the Japanese company confirmed as being exploited. No additional details related to the exploitation activity are currently available. CISA is urging Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies to apply fixes for CVE-2026-106931, CVE-2026-96656, and CVE-2026-96654 by October 23, 2026, and the rest by November 3, 2026.

1ah7igo.text: A Belarus-aligned hacktivist group spent nearly two years within the network of a Russian healthcare organization. According to a report published by Russian cybersecurity firm Solar, the activity has been attributed to a threat cluster dubbed Partisan Zmiy, which is also known as the Cyber Partisans. Known to be active since at least 2020, the group has a track record of striking industrial enterprises and government agencies in Russia and Belarus with a backdoor called Vasilek that uses Telegram for command-and-control (C2) and data exfiltration. Some of the attacks have also leveraged phishing lures to deliver an installer that simultaneously deploys the legitimate FortiClient VPN program on the system as well as an open-source program known as DNSCat2 that allows attackers to gain control of the infected host. A notable aspect of the threat actor is their ability to stage destructive attacks with a wiper referred to as Pryanik, alongside taking steps to systematically clear Windows event logs using a utility dubbed Evlx. The Rostelecom subsidiary said it discovered the intrusion in December 2025, although evidence suggests that the earliest signs of compromise date back to early 2024. The name of the targeted organization was not identified. The exact initial access vector used to breach the entity is also not known. Unlike other attacks linked to Cyber Partisans, the threat actors remained on the network for an extended period of time without carrying out any destructive activity, marking something of a shift in modus operandi. "The attacked organization possessed an extensive infrastructure and two-way trusted relationships with numerous subsidiary medical institutions," Solar said. "We hypothesize that the lack of infrastructure disruption is due precisely to the value of this access for further espionage and trusted relationship attacks." Observed as part of the intrusion is a loader-scheduler service ("vmauad") that masquerades as a legitimate VMware component to maintain persistence and evade cursory inspection. To accomplish this, the attackers are said to have taken advantage of a trusted-but-unmonitored VMware Tools directory location to plant malicious executables or replace legitimate VMware DLLs with a malicious version ("vmtools.dll") containing the backdoor. The primary responsibility of the Windows service is to launch the rogue binary "C:\Program Files\VMware\VMware Tools\authd.exe" that, besides launching a GOST tunnel every Saturday from 10 p.m. to 11 p.m., runs an updated version of Vasilek (version 1.5.8) once, eight hours after the service begins. Once installed, Vasilek is equipped to collect information about an infected computer, execute Windows commands, launch and terminate processes, transfer files, capture screenshots, record keystrokes, and escalate privileges via runas. It can also prevent the machine from going into sleep mode, and update or remove itself. One new addition is the "move_cursor" command that, as the name implies, allows the backdoor to move the cursor and simulate user input on the victim's screen. "The group consistently invests in stealth and operational security, rather than new capabilities: hostname binding in two independent components, nightly scheduled payload launches, system proxy inheritance, disguise as legitimately installed but unused software, file rotation across the same paths, time-stomping, outgoing message suppression, and anonymous messages on behalf of the group in operator chats," Solar said. "The backdoor's feature set has remained largely unchanged over four revisions. Due to Telegram being blocked in Russia by ISPs, communication between the Vasilek backdoor and C2 has become unstable." The disclosure comes as Solar also disclosed details of a phishing campaign that employs JavaScript attachments mimicking business-themed documents, such as payments and purchase orders, to deliver a previously unreported malware family known as HypeAgent. The Windows malware is a full-featured trojan designed to take complete control over infected systems, packing the ability to steal files, open a console, change desktop wallpaper, turn on a webcam, log keystrokes, launch hidden VNC and RDP sessions, control the mouse, and even deploy a cryptocurrency miner. It's also capable of stealing cookies associated with Discord, Steam, GitHub, Instagram, Telegram, Binance, ChatGPT, Claude, and Cursor, and tampering with the installed Exodus wallet app to inject JavaScript that can collect the victim's password, PIN, mnemonic phrase, and private key. Earlier this June, Solar also observed legitimate infrastructure compromised by the ProxyCB proxyware botnet malware making automated requests to Russian websites and online platforms, while identifying possible overlaps between the botnet infrastructure and historical activity linked to TeamSpy, a threat cluster known for abusing TeamViewer to facilitate reconnaissance and data theft. Last month, the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) charged Searzhudin Tamirlanovich Aktulaev, a 40-year-old Russian national extradited from Cyprus in May 2025, for exploiting an online messaging service of a well-known freelance employment platform to send malware-laced Excel attachments to about 80,000 of its users in 2016 and 2017 using 255 fake accounts. The attacks led to the deployment of two types of malware, a variant of the TVRAT (aka Sheldor, SpyAgent, TeamBot, TeamSpy, and TVSPY) and DarkVNC, to harvest and send data from a victim computer to a remote server under the attacker's control. Thousands of computers are assessed to have been infected as a result of this scheme.

sidtnv.text: A threat actor breached TeamUpdraft's website, a developer of popular WordPress backup and security plugins, potentially compromising UpdraftCentral connection keys that can send commands to connected websites. TeamUpdraft detected unauthorized access to its infrastructure over the weekend and believes that the hacker accessed the customer database. The developer offers several WordPress tools for backup, storage, and site management: UpdraftPlus: website backup and restoration plugin with more than 4 million downloads UpdraftCentral: for managing multiple sites remotely UpdraftVault: for cloud backup storage UpdraftClone: for creating staging websites "Over the weekend of 17-18 October we identified unauthorised access to the teamupdraft.com website," TeamUpdraft said in an advisory yesterday. "Our team responded straight away and worked through the night to contain it – we closed the access route, signed out every account and replaced the keys and credentials that could have been affected." The vendor says it believes the threat actor accessed its customer database, which included details about the customer and billing, order history, as well as more sensitive information: password hashes two-factor authentication settings connection keys for UpdraftCentral, UpdraftVault, and UpdraftClone services The vendor said it did not store any payment details and noted that UpdraftPlus plugin files and downloads remain unaffected. Self-hosted UpdraftCentral instances are not impacted. Even if backups in customers' own remote storage are unaffected, the company recommends that users rotate storage credentials and reauthorize connections if they accessed their site through UpdraftCentral. Massive blast radius An estimated 10% of sites using UpdraftPlus have an UpdraftCentral or Migrator key, potentially exposing around 400,000 websites to the attack. According to Patchstack lead researcher Oliver Sild, attackers have begun using stolen access keys to backdoor sites connected to UpdraftCentral, saying the campaign may be more severe than the "wp2shell” attack. The WordPress plugin security company says that the attacks started on October 18 at 15:32 UTC to execute arbitrary code and add accounts with full administrator privileges. The researchers logged at least 99 malicious backdoor plugins with distinct names disguised as WordPress maintenance and optimization tools, such as “Site Health Cache.” Backdoor plugin namesSource: Patchstack Although Patchstack describes an early variant of the backdoor plugin that is broken due to a coding error, a report from web application security firm Nethemba documents a newer version that lets attackers create privileged accounts or log in as existing administrators. Nethemba says three of its own WordPress websites were targeted through UpdraftCentral, with malicious plugins successfully installed on two of them. “All three sites ran the current WordPress 7.1.3 and UpdraftPlus 2.26.11, which is patched against the June vulnerability CVE-2026-10795,” Nethemba says. “The attacker did not break into our servers and did not exploit any weakness in our configuration. The attacker came in through the UpdraftCentral remote management channel and signed the commands with valid private dashboard keys” Nethemba reports that the vendor's initial 1.26.12/2.26.12 release was meant to remove UpdraftCentral Cloud keys, but a bug prevented it from doing so. Users are recommended to update UpdraftPlus to 1.26.13 (free) / 2.26.13 (Premium) or later. After updating, it is recommended to log into each WordPress site and delete the UpdraftCentral connection keys from Settings → UpdraftPlus Backups → Advanced Tools → UpdraftCentral → Manage existing keys. Administrators should inspect logs and files for indicators of compromise provided by TeamUpdraft, Patchstack, and Nethemba. If compromise is confirmed, it is recommended to restore sites from clean backups, change the TeamUpdraft account password, revoke all sessions, and reset the two-factor authentication protection method. ms6ex1.text: Certificate authority eMudhra revoked eight compromised intermediate certificates after researchers found their private keys were so weak that anyone could recover them almost instantly and use them to forge trusted certificates for legitimate websites. Major browsers and operating systems trusted the compromised certificates, potentially allowing attackers to impersonate legitimate websites and intercept encrypted communications. A security researcher known as Wayne discovered the weakness on October 17 while scanning publicly available certificate data. According to Mozilla's incident report, all eight certificates used P-384 private keys generated in April 2025 that had values smaller than 256, allowing anyone to recover them by testing just 256 possible numbers. To demonstrate the weakness, security researcher Flüpke published one of the compromised private keys on GitHub, showing that the private key for eMudhra's "EM OV TLS CA - G3C" certificate had a value of just 4. BleepingComputer independently verified that the published key matches one of the revoked certificates. In a response to Mozilla, eMudhra blamed the issue on an error in a script used to generate the certificates in April 2025. The company said the error generated a second set of weaker keys that were mistakenly selected for certificate signing because they had labels similar to the properly generated keys. Some of the resulting certificates were also submitted to Sectigo for cross-signing. eMudhra said most of the affected intermediate certificates were never used in production and that it had found no evidence they were used to issue certificates to end users. However, attackers could have recovered and abused the weak keys since their creation in April 2025, though there is no evidence that this happened. Following the disclosure, eMudhra revoked the eight compromised certificates and stopped issuing new certificates under its G3 root. Browser makers and software vendors release fixes Mozilla said it blocked the compromised certificates through Firefox's OneCRL system on October 17, protecting users without requiring a browser update or restart. Google Chrome also blocked the six compromised intermediates authorized to issue TLS certificates that day, while Apple added protections on October 19. Mozilla also released Firefox 158.0.1 and updates for its ESR releases on October 20 to protect users whose browser configurations prevented them from receiving the earlier revocation updates. However, software that uses its own certificate stores or doesn't check certificate revocations may keep trusting the compromised intermediates until it is updated. The Go development team released versions 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 to address the issue, tracked as CVE-2026-111943. Mozilla cryptography engineer Dennis Jackson has also published an incident tracking website listing affected software and available security updates. Software Patched version / status Ubuntu ca-certificates 20260816ubuntu0.22.04.1, 20260816ubuntu0.24.04.1, 20260816ubuntu0.26.04.1, 20260816ubuntu0.26.10.1 Debian ca-certificates Pending Arch Linux ca-certificates-mozilla 3.131.1-1 Gentoo ca-certificates 20260816.3.125 FreeBSD ca_root_nss Pending Chainguard ca-certificates 20260909-r3 Alpine Linux ca-certificates 20261020-r0 NSS 3.131.1 curl CA bundle 2026-10-20 Homebrew ca-certificates 2026-09-25_1 Go 1.27.3, 1.26.10 Node.js Pending Python certifi 2026.10.19 pip 26.2.2 uv 0.13.4 Rust rustls-webpki 0.103.16 Rust webpki-roots / webpki-root-certs 1.0.10 Electron 44.9.1, 43.8.1, 42.11.16 Bun Pending Composer ca-bundle 1.4.16, 1.6.0 Elixir castore 1.0.22 Jackson also warns that macOS's built-in /usr/bin/curl utility may continue trusting the compromised certificates because its certificate bundle does not check revocation information. Administrators can use the advisory's test endpoints and mitigation instructions to determine whether their systems are still affected. Users and administrators should install available software updates to ensure the compromised certificates are no longer trusted. o4xfbf.text: The PHP security team is warning administrators to prepare for emergency security updates tomorrow to address two critical vulnerabilities, as information about the flaws has reportedly leaked ahead of their scheduled disclosure. PHP powers many websites and web applications, including content management systems, e-commerce platforms, and custom web services. In an advisory published Tuesday, the PHP development team announced that it plans to release security updates on Wednesday, October 21, at 14:00 UTC (10:00 AM Eastern), to address two vulnerabilities, each rated 9.2 under CVSS v4.0. The PHP security team also sent a notice to its ANNOUNCE mailing list, urging administrators to prepare to install the security updates as soon as they become available. "We reserve the right to release earlier should details of either vulnerability become public, or should evidence of active exploitation appear in the wild," the PHP security team warned. The developers have not disclosed any technical details about the vulnerabilities, including which PHP versions are affected, how they can be exploited, or which releases will contain fixes. However, security researchers at watchTowr told BleepingComputer that the vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, are remote code execution (RCE) flaws believed to affect PHP versions 5, 6, 7, and 8. "In the last hour, two remote code execution vulnerabilities in PHP have been leaked. These vulnerabilities were previously scheduled under embargo and due for release on Thursday at 11 am ET," watchTowr CEO Benjamin Harris told BleepingComputer. "While we are not able to share technical information at this point for obvious reasons, given the sensitivity, we can confirm that these vulnerabilities are indeed real. Both of them are CVSS10 and are understood to affect PHP versions 5, 6, 7, and 8." watchTowr also said it believes it has successfully reproduced CVE-2026-109618 but is not releasing technical information until security patches become available. The researchers clarified that they have not observed exploitation of the vulnerabilities in the wild, despite the information reportedly leaking ahead of the planned disclosure. In a post on X, watchTowr warned that information about the vulnerabilities had leaked before the originally planned disclosure date. "We were all supposed to wait until Thursday at 11am ET. Information has leaked wrt zero-day embargoed RCE vulns in PHP. We can confirm that they're real," the researchers said. The warning follows a now-deleted post on Y Combinator's Hacker News forum, in which a user named "petecooper" claimed that two critical PHP remote code execution vulnerabilities would be disclosed on October 22. The post, seen by BleepingComputer, claimed that both vulnerabilities carried CVSS scores of 10.0 and affected PHP versions dating back to PHP 5. It also identified the vulnerabilities as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, matching the identifiers watchTowr later shared. However, watchTowr's statements and the Hacker News post are different from PHP's official announcement. Both described the vulnerabilities as CVSS 10.0, while the PHP security team assigned each a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2. Additionally, watchTowr cited an originally planned Thursday disclosure, while PHP has officially scheduled its security release for tomorrow morning. The PHP security team says it will publish full technical details, affected versions, and fixed releases when the security updates become available. 1wr3jqv.text: Development platform Zeabur has disclosed details of a cybersecurity incident in which an attacker used leaked internal credentials stored in plaintext to compromise its infrastructure and steal over 3.2 million environment variable records and information for 321,810 accounts. The attackers used stolen administrator credentials and cloud access keys to compromise Zeabur’s shared hosting infrastructure and dedicated servers, eventually gaining access to its production database. “On October 14–15, 2026, an attacker used leaked Zeabur internal credentials to break into the shared cluster, some Dedicated Servers, and Zeabur internal systems, and eventually read the platform database,” Zeabur’s announcement reads. Attack chainSource: Zeabur Zeabur is a developer hosting and deployment platform that lets developers connect a GitHub repository and have the platform handle deployment, databases, HTTPS, and infrastructure management. In late August 2026, the company suffered another security breach when hackers exploited a flaw in a customer’s NextChat application and then moved through poorly isolated internal systems. This led to the theft of AWS credentials and access to the production database, exposing account information, API keys, and other secrets stored there. In the latest incident, Zeabur says the compromise was broader, affecting shared clusters across nine regions, 321,810 accounts, and roughly 3.2 million environment-variable records. Also, Zeabur confirmed root sign-ins on 101 GCP servers by 92 users, with the attackers adding SSH keys to 50 servers and attaching 16 customer disk copies to their own virtual machines. Data breach scopeSource: Zeabur The company says that attackers likely obtained the credentials they used in the second attack during the August breach, though it hasn’t confirmed this. Beyond failing to store credentials in encrypted form, Zeabur also failed to rotate all administrator account credentials since the August incident, while administrator portals remained accessible to the public internet. “The admin tokens had no expiry, had not been rotated since they were created in January 2024, and were not included in the post-August rotation,” explained Zeabur. Users are urged to rotate exposed credentials and secrets immediately, revoke all active sessions, and rebuild compromised GCP servers. Variables previously migrated exclusively to customers’ own servers as part of the August incident response escaped this latest platform database exposure, although compromised hosts could still expose them. Threat actor's activity and vendor response timesSource: Zeabur Zeabur announces shutdown After discovering the latest security incident, Zeabur announced over the weekend that it will shut down its services starting December 1, 2026, and finish by December 31, 2026. The decision comes after 3.5 years of continuous growth, including a record year in 2026, but Zeabur said scaling the project to meet market demand has made it increasingly complex and difficult to maintain, and the recent security failures reflect that. “After the August incident, we spent a long time discussing and struggling with what to do next,” explained Zeabur. “Following this latest incident, we reassessed what it would take to keep operating and the responsibilities our team could carry. We ultimately decided to wind down.” On December 1, renewals will be disabled, and all running services on shared clusters will be paused. By the end of the year, all dedicated servers will expire and shut down, and all shared clusters will stop. Users may be given additional time for data migration, though no concrete timelines on that front have been provided yet. 6qakht.text: OpenAI confirmed that its newer models are much better at writing and migrating software in older programming languages. The company lists programming languages such as COBOL, Fortran, and Visual Basic as a few examples where it has seen significant improvements. OpenAI says COBOL supports more than 40% of online banking systems, 80% of in-person credit card transactions, and 95% of ATM transactions, while Fortran is still used in areas such as weather forecasting and nuclear reactor safety analysis. "These languages have less code and documentation available for models to learn from than languages like Python and JavaScript, yet support critical infrastructure and essential services around the world," OpenAI explained in a blog post. To measure progress, OpenAI created MultiLangBench, which asks models to build a SQLite-compatible database engine from scratch across 20 programming languages. GPT-6 Astra reached an average test pass rate of 87.4%, up from 26.8% for GPT-5.6 Sol. In COBOL specifically, Astra jumped from 10.9% to 72.1%, while Fortran improved from 21.4% to 83.5%. "Improvements extend to every language tested, including COBOL (10.9% to 72.1%), OCaml (25.6% to 85.8%), Fortran (21.4% to 83.5%), and Visual Basic (27.5% to 89.4%)," OpenAI noted. GPT-6.1 Sol is much better at migrating COBOL OpenAI also tested whether its models could migrate COBOL programs to C++, Java, Kotlin, Python, or Rust without changing their behaviour. "GPT-6.1 Sol achieves 86.6% accuracy at low reasoning effort, compared with GPT-5.6 Sol's 5.4% at the same setting at just 61% of the API cost," OpenAI said. "At higher reasoning effort, accuracy reaches 97.9%, bringing the evaluation close to saturation." This work could help companies modernize older software, although production migrations would still require expert review and testing. xtc7pt.text: The private keys of eight eMudhra intermediate certificate authority (CA) certificates are compromised, Mozilla and Google's Chrome Root Program confirms on October 20. An intermediate CA signs the certificates that websites present, so anyone holding one of these keys could issue a certificate for any website that a browser would accept. A researcher reported the compromise to the root programs on the evening of October 17, and Chrome and Firefox blocked the eight certificates within hours, after Chrome verified the findings. No TLS certificate chaining to the six intermediates used for websites had been logged to Certificate Transparency (CT) before Chrome's block, so none could have been trusted by default in Chrome or any other browser that requires CT logging, the Chrome Root Program said. It is not known how the keys left eMudhra, when, or whether anyone besides the researcher holds them. The keys are the ones Go blocked in its October 20 security releases without naming the CA, as The Hacker News reported earlier. The eight hash values in Go's code match the eight certificates. Go handled the fix on its URGENT track, which its security policy reserves for threats to the ecosystem's integrity or flaws being exploited in the wild, and neither the issue nor the release notes say which applied. What Was Compromised eMudhra is an Indian CA that sells certificates under the emSign brand through companies in India, the United States, and the Netherlands, and it has roots in the Mozilla, Chrome, and Apple root stores. The eight compromised certificates are: TLS, domain validated: EM DV TLS CA - G3B (eMudhra BV, Netherlands) and EM DV TLS CA - G3C (eMudhra Inc, United States) TLS, organization validated: EM OV TLS CA - G3B and EM OV TLS CA - G3C TLS, extended validation: EM EV TLS CA - G3B and EM EV TLS CA - G3C Code signing: EM OV CS CA - G3B and EM OV CS CA - G3C The six TLS certificates were issued by emSign Root TLS CA - G3 and chain to emSign ECC Root CA - G3, a root in the Chrome and Apple stores and, until October 20, in Mozilla's. Each of the eight also exists as a second certificate with the same public key, cross-signed by Sectigo under its AAA Certificate Services root, according to a certificate list published by Dennis Jackson, a Mozilla cryptography engineer. Chrome did not need to block the two code-signing certificates, because its TLS verifier will not build a path through an intermediate restricted to code signing, the Chrome Root Program said. Who Is Protected, and How The Chrome Root Program received the report at 18:05 UTC on October 17 and had a CRLSet update blocking the six TLS intermediates in place by 19:45 UTC. Mozilla received it at 20:06 UTC and finished pushing a OneCRL block to Firefox installations with standard settings at 22:59 UTC. CRLSets and OneCRL are revocation lists that the two browsers fetch on their own, so neither needed an update or a restart. Chrome's block matches the public key rather than the certificate, so it also catches the Sectigo cross-signed copies. It is the same mechanism Chrome used earlier this month against rogue certificates for Google domains. The researcher, credited by Mozilla only as Wayne, signed the message "We have a problem here - Wayne" with each of the eight keys and sent it to the root programs that day, according to Jackson, who published the signatures and certificates on a one-page site. eMudhra has revoked the eight certificates. Apple blocked them on October 19, Microsoft on October 20, and other trust stores were notified on October 19, according to Jackson's site. The cross-signed copies did not widen the risk in Chrome or Firefox. Both stopped trusting Sectigo's AAA Certificate Services root for websites in April 2025, and Chrome's root store file does not carry it. Apple's root list for iOS 26 and macOS 26, published in December 2025, includes it. Mozilla does not believe, for now, that the problem affects other CAs, Jackson wrote on Mozilla's policy list, and Chrome said it checked every other CA certificate in its store and "found no other instances of this failure mode." What to Update Browsers get revocation pushed to them. Many other programs that check TLS certificates, from Go binaries to anything using Python's certifi bundle, do not check revocation data and keep trusting a chain until their code or their root bundle changes. Mozilla's advice to anyone who runs a trust store: nothing is needed where clients reliably check revocation and refuse connections when they cannot check, the eight intermediates should be blocked now where the software can block individual intermediates; and otherwise the operator should consider removing trust in the roots that signed them. The fixes published so far, and what each one does: add border: Software Fixed in What it does Status Go 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 Rejects any chain containing one of the eight keys (CVE-2026-111943) Released October 20, rebuild required Firefox 158.0.1 , ESR 115.43.1 and ESR 153.5.1 Carries the OneCRL block for installations that cannot receive Remote Settings ( CVE-2026-113470 ) Released October 20 NSS 3.131.1 Removes emSign ECC Root CA - G3 from the trusted list Released October 20 Python certifi 2026.10.19 Drops emSign ECC Root CA - G3 from the bundle Released Rust webpki-roots 1.0.10 Drops emSign ECC Root CA - G3 Released Homebrew ca-certificates 2026-09-25_1 Excludes emSign ECC Root CA - G3, emSign Root TLS CA - G3 and AAA Certificate Services by public key Released Node.js None yet A draft change would block the eight keys Pending Composer ca-bundle None yet An open change would remove emSign ECC Root CA - G3 Pending Go's filter sits in the standard library and rejects any chain containing one of the eight keys, on Go's own verifier and on the macOS and Windows system-verifier paths, and the change adds no setting to turn it off. A program picks it up only when rebuilt with the new release; Go 1.25 and older are out of support and get no fixes. Three of the fixes work by removing roots rather than blocking the keys. certifi, webpki-roots, and Homebrew's ca-certificates drop emSign ECC Root CA - G3 from their bundles, and Homebrew also drops Sectigo's AAA Certificate Services root and emSign Root TLS CA - G3. That also cuts off every legitimate certificate that chains to those roots. Mozilla, which made the same change to NSS, said some servers will become unavailable to non-Firefox users of its trust list until those servers move to new certificate chains. Firefox needs nothing unless Remote Settings is disabled by policy or blocked on the network. The October 20 releases carry the block list for those installations. None of the sources provide a way to detect past misuse of the keys beyond Chrome's CT search, which covers only logged certificates. What Happens to eMudhra Mozilla removed emSign ECC Root CA - G3 from NSS on October 20. Chrome will remove the same root in version 43 of its root store and is reviewing the status of eMudhra's other root in its store, emSign Root CA - G1, the Chrome Root Program said, citing the seriousness of the incident. How the keys left eMudhra and when remain open questions. Mozilla said it is working with the CA, other root programs and downstream trust stores on the root cause and will post more when it can. eMudhra's trust-services repository carried no notice about the incident as of October 20. Go has not named the CA on its issue, where its release notes cite "specific security concerns around their operation", and a commenter asked for the hashes in the patch to be explained. Filippo Valsorda, who maintains the cryptography packages in Go's standard library, replied that the keys are compromised and the certificates revoked, that Linux root stores are too poorly maintained for revocation to reach applications, and that putting the keys in code is the only option for now.

1rlr7pt.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 20, 2026Vulnerability / Enterprise Security Cybersecurity researchers have released a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit for a recently patched critical security flaw impacting Fortinet FortiSIEM that could result in arbitrary code execution. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-106173 (CVSS score: 9.4), is a critical path traversal flaw that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute unauthorized code or commands via specially crafted packets. Patches for the flaw were released last week by Fortinet in the following versions - FortiSIEM 7.5.0 (Upgrade to 7.5.1 or above) FortiSIEM 7.6 (Not affected) According to Horizon3.ai, the issue involves an unauthenticated attacker connecting to the gRPC service listening on TCP port 27918 and exploiting the flaw to overwrite an existing file outside of the intended directory and turn the arbitrary-file-write primitive into remote code execution. "The FortiSIEM gRPC QueryResultReq handler processes untrusted metadata without proper path validation," Horizon3.ai said. "By crafting metadata containing both path traversal sequences (../) and NUL-byte injection within gRPC's HTTP/2 and HPACK encoding layers, an attacker can write arbitrary files to the file system." The problem stems from a case of unsafe path construction within a function named SendQueryResult(), which passes a user-supplied "query-id" parameter directly without sufficient validation. In other words, an attacker can leverage this flaw to include directory traversal sequences such as "../" and escape that directory. However, this only allows an attacker to navigate to a directory of their choice and write to it, but not to opt for a file name because the program automatically adds its own file name "result-<source IP address>-0-0-<id>.dat," where <id> is a counter value controlled by the server. That's where a second weakness enters the picture: a null byte ("\0") can be embedded in the "query-id" parameter, causing the operating system to interpret it as a string terminator and discard everything that comes after it. This, in turn, results in the appended file name suffix being ignored when the path is passed to the file-opening function. An attacker could exploit this behavior to craft a "query-id" value with "\0" placed such that it's preceded by the actual file name to be overwritten – i.e., "../../../../../opt/charting/redishb.sh\0..." The file in question is a shell script that performs health checks on the Redis service and is run every 60 seconds by a cron job. "The write lands on the exact path that preceded the null byte," Zach Hanley, Chief Attack Engineer at Horizon3.ai, said. "Pointed at an existing file, this overwrites it in place, keeping the original owner and permissions; a second variant uses two requests to create a brand-new file with an exact name."

d57pzn.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 20, 2026Vulnerability / Network Security Palo Alto Networks has disclosed that it's continuing to observe exploitation of a now-patched security flaw impacting PAN-OS and Prisma Access by ransomware actors. The activity relates to CVE-2026-0257 (CVSS score: 7.8), an authentication bypass flaw that could be exploited by bad actors to set up unauthorized VPN connections. It was patched by Palo Alto Networks in May 2026 and was added by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CSIA) to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on May 13, 2026. "Ransomware operators exploiting CVE-2026-0257 include Spikey Scorpius (aka Qilin) and Tarnished Scorpius (aka INC)," Unit 42 researchers said in an update shared on Monday. The development comes days after ReliaQuest said it detected both Qilin and Settra ransomware groups actively exploiting the flaw in financially-motivated attacks. According to Unit 42, the threat actors are weaponizing the flaw to gain an initial foothold into corporate networks, and then bypass multi-factor authentication (MFA) controls to establish a VPN session. Upon setting up a VPN session, the attackers have been found to engage in the following post-compromise activity - Conduct internal network reconnaissance using dual-use remote monitoring and management (RMM) tools. Move laterally across the network via RDP and SMB. Stage additional tooling for credential harvesting, data exfiltration, and ransomware deployment. Attacks mounted by these groups are said to have targeted a wide range of sectors, including education, financial services, healthcare, high technology, hospitality, manufacturing, professional and legal services, government, transportation and logistics, utilities and energy, and retail. "The most significant evolution in tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) following successful exploitation of CVE-2026-0257 is the direct pivot to the virtualization layer," Unit 42 said. "In one notable case, attackers moved from the compromised VPN gateway to the vCenter management appliance. From there, they disabled security controls on ESXi hypervisors (execInstalledOnly) and used a custom tool to perform offline credential dumping directly against a domain controller's virtual disk (VMDK)." This approach, the network security vendor added, circumvents in-guest endpoint detection and response (EDR) and security protections, allowing the threat actors to obtain domain-wide credentials. Attackers have also been observed chaining the initial access method with other exploit tools, including efforts to target Veeam backup infrastructure by abusing known flaws (CVE-2023-27532) to inflict maximum damage. It's worth noting that Qilin's exploitation of CVE-2026-0257 was previously flagged by Arctic Wolf in July 2026, with attacks ranging from rapid encryption-only operations to full double-extortion. Besides applying the latest fixes, Palo Alto Networks is recommending that organizations proactively hunt for indicators of compromise and initiate appropriate incident response protocols if successful gateway-connected events are detected.

wdh6gf.text: The U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is ordering federal civilian agencies to stop using DeepSeek products and remove them from government systems. The order also covers products from the Chinese AI company's affiliates and third-party products and services built using DeepSeek technology. DeepSeek (Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Co., Ltd) develops large language models and offers a chatbot, API services, and models suitable for coding and reasoning tasks. Its AI tools became extremely popular early on, but were but were soon followed by reports of security risks [1, 2, 3, 4] and concerns about the potential for Chinese authorities to access users’ conversations. The DHS is now taking regulatory action to limit the use of DeepSeek and derivatives on critical systems in the United States, and has issued a notice of order for agencies to: Immediately exclude covered products from procurement, including approved-product lists and purchasing marketplaces. Immediately remove covered products from agency IT systems, or seek an exception. Submit any exception requests within 60 days of the order’s issuance, explaining the justification and proposed risk mitigations. CISA will review requests and issue written approvals or denials. The order applies to federal civilian agencies within DHS’s authority and is not a general ban on private or consumer use. DHS explained that the order stems from concerns about the Chinese government accessing DeepSeek infrastructure, collecting personal information and tracking users, and potentially transferring sensitive government data to China. The document also raises concerns about potential malware in DeepSeek models, citing a February 2025 report from NowSecure that identified security vulnerabilities in the DeepSeek iOS app. NowSecure examined the app and found unencrypted data transmissions, weak encryption algorithms, insecure local storage, user fingerprinting risks, and data sharing with ByteDance, the Chinese tech giant behind the TikTok short-form video platform. The order was published in the Federal Register earlier today, a day after appearing on Public Inspection. Executive agencies can request exceptions within 60 days of the issuance date of the order. For agencies that cannot comply with this order because of internal capability restrictions, CISA will provide the necessary technical assistance. 1r9tgcc.text: A Chinese-speaking criminal pointed autonomous AI agents at company websites and let them break in with almost no help, and a security researcher watched it happen because the operators left their control panels open on the internet. The agents tried more than 1,200 sites and reached websites belonging to more than 100 companies, including farm-equipment maker Deere, appliance company SharkNinja and engine maker Cummins, according to Reuters, which reviewed the attacker's own records to identify them. How much data, if any, was taken is not known. The researcher, Snorre Fagerland of the security firm NorForge, found the operations by scanning the internet for exposed copies of Cairn, an open-source AI tool popular with hackers. Beginning around October 2, he found about two dozen Cairn instances being used maliciously, which let him read the attackers' work in real time. He set out the findings on Monday, and Reuters, which saw the report before publication, named the victims from its own review of the attacker's activity. Cairn gives AI agents a starting point and a goal, then lets them work toward it step by step. The agents post what they find to a shared board, and the human operator can add hints along the way. It was built for authorized penetration testing and does other jobs too, but here it was pointed at online shops without permission. Cairn's author, who posts as "le1xia0," told Reuters the tool was not designed for hacking attacks and that harmful use was not their intention. What the agents did, and who was hit NorForge grouped the exposed panels into three clusters and judged more than 20 of them likely to be malicious. The busiest cluster, which NorForge calls AIA0001, is Chinese-language and links 14 panels to more than 1,100 attack projects. Its aim seems to be lasting access to shop and payment systems for later use, NorForge said, with targets in the United States, Japan and Australia. A typical task told the agents to find a way to run code on a shop and then plant a web shell uploader. That is a form that saves uploaded files, not one that runs commands, and attackers can swap it for something worse at any time. NorForge checked one claimed break-in, at a large hardware-parts vendor, and found the web shell live. It independently confirmed the compromise of one very large US retailer, in which the agents found the single cookie setting that selected a vulnerable backend server. The three named companies told Reuters the damage was limited. Deere said it took steps to fix the problem and had no sign that sensitive information was accessed. SharkNinja said the attack hit a standalone product-support site and that it had contained the threat. Cummins said it was investigating a report of a possible attack on a website run by one of its vendors. Two smaller businesses also told Reuters they were compromised. One documented intrusion, by the agent's own account, worked through unauthorized write access to a memcached session store, unsafe handling of saved PHP objects, and a weakness in old Zend Framework code. The paths differ from victim to victim, so this is one chain, not a single method. Cheap, fast, and largely unsupervised The instructions were short. The Chinese-speaking operator sketched out preferred tactics in fewer than 100 Chinese characters, Reuters reported, and the agents went from there. Successful break-ins took a little under 23 hours on average, NorForge found, and the overall success rate across the tools it saw was around 10%, though it cautioned the clusters chase different goals and are not directly comparable. The cost was low, but the figures are rough. NorForge put the average at about $5 a task, counting attempts that failed or ended early, and said the uncertainty is considerable. Fagerland separately told Reuters the whole campaign had used about $5,000 worth of tokens, or roughly $50 per successful hack. All the AIA0001 tasks ran under a worker named claudecode_deepseek-v4.1-flash, which could point to a DeepSeek V4.1 Flash model driven by Anthropic's Claude Code. Neither the researcher nor Reuters confirmed the models, and Reuters said only that the campaign appeared to use DeepSeek and Claude Code. The open panels leak the victims' secrets too Leaving a Cairn panel open is a separate problem from the break-ins. The panels show who is being attacked, what weaknesses were found, and which credentials and keys were taken, so having your site tested on an open instance can expose your secrets, whatever the test's outcome. NorForge ran the secrets scanner Trufflehog over the panel data and found hundreds of secrets, 11% of which it verified as still valid. The panels also appear to expose the full set of the tool's controls, including the ability to start and stop projects, feed in new data, and point agents to different targets. NorForge said it did not test whether those controls work without a login. A second, English-language cluster went further and exposed the operators' own SSH logins to their staging servers; NorForge said it did not log in. The exposure is not only a criminal problem. NorForge also found apparently legitimate penetration-testing firms that had left real client tests on unsecured panels, putting their customers' data at the same risk. What to check, and where this came from Defenders can act on a few points: Exposed panels. Agent control panels of this kind often answer on port 8000, so an exposed one without a login is worth hunting for. Stray upload forms. An unexpected file-upload form sitting in a hidden directory is the foothold these agents aimed for. Magento patching. A worker directory NorForge browsed held a proof-of-concept for a critical Magento flaw, StyleSmuggler (CVE-2026-75650), and a test lab for it. There is no evidence it was used in these break-ins, but any shop still on an affected build should apply Adobe's hotfix for it: Adobe Commerce 2.4.4 through 2.4.9, or Magento Open Source 2.4.6 through 2.4.9. NorForge's search followed a September report by Gambit Security, a separate campaign in which a criminal used Cairn alongside two other AI tools to steal credit cards; that report is what first flagged Cairn on an attacker's server. No source links the two operations. NorForge said it is working with Reuters to warn victims and is asking hosting firms to take the panels down, an effort it said depends on how the hosts respond.

1hrqxla.text: The iPhone of Vladan Đokić, rector of the University of Belgrade and a prominent supporter of Serbia's student protest movement, was infected with NSO Group's Pegasus spyware in 2026, the Citizen Lab said on October 19. The finding came six days before Serbia's October 25 snap parliamentary election. The infection used a zero-click exploit, meaning Đokić did not have to tap a link or open a file for it to work. The lab found the infection with high confidence, but its note provides no date within 2026, does not identify who was behind the attack, and notes that its investigation is ongoing. The election was called in September after nearly two years of protests that began when a railway station canopy collapsed in Novi Sad in November 2024, killing 16 people. The Citizen Lab, a research group at the University of Toronto, analyzed forensic artifacts from the phone at Đokić's request, working with the Serbian digital-rights group SHARE Foundation. SHARE led the investigation of an earlier wave of Serbian cases made public in September. A second case concerns Rade Bajić, a senior prosecutorial associate at Serbia's Public Prosecutor's Office for Organized Crime who worked on the "Generalštab" corruption investigation into a Kushner-linked property project in Belgrade. Bajić received an Apple Threat Notification on August 13 and a reminder on August 27. Apple sends these alerts when it detects activity consistent with an attack by mercenary spyware, the commercial hacking tools that companies such as NSO sell to governments, and it does not say who is behind the attacks. The Citizen Lab treats a notification as a high-confidence sign that Bajić's phone was likely targeted. Its forensic analysis of the device is ongoing, and the note does not say whether the phone was infected. The Generalštab case concerns the removal of heritage protection from Belgrade's bombed-out former army General Staff complex to clear the way for a luxury development backed by a company linked to Jared Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law. In December 2025, prosecutors charged Culture Minister Nikola Selaković and three other officials with abuse of office and falsifying documents in the case, the Associated Press reported. Bajić says he was taken off the investigation in November 2025 without explanation, and in February he spoke about the case at a protest called by student activists outside Serbia's Constitutional Court. The lab's note does not say what, if anything, was taken from the rector's phone. Pegasus gives whoever operates it the same access as the phone's owner, including private and encrypted messages, and can switch on the microphone and camera without the owner knowing, according to the lab's analysis of the September case. Đokić called the spyware on his phone "another attempt of intimidation" in an English-language statement published by the university, and demanded an independent investigation without delay, with its results made public and whoever installed and used the spyware prosecuted. Police raided the rector's offices on March 31 and seized computers and servers, he said at the time. The Security Information Agency (BIA), Serbia's civilian security service, dismissed the September allegations that students and opposition politicians had been spied on as "purely trivial sensationalism" in a statement on September 3, as translated by the broadcaster N1, and said it operates strictly within Serbian law. The two cases extend a wave that SHARE reported on September 2, when it said at least 14 people in Serbia, including student activists, an opposition MP and a local councilor, had been targeted with spyware since the start of the year. Twelve of them had received Apple Threat Notifications in August, the month Apple warned users in 110 countries. One was Jelena Kontić, a student whose Pegasus infection the Citizen Lab confirmed. The other two had a new version of NoviSpy, an Android spyware, installed on their phones. By the Citizen Lab's count, the two new cases bring the number of people in Serbian civil society publicly known to have been targeted or infected with mercenary spyware this year to at least 16. Amnesty International reported in December 2024 that NoviSpy was configured to send stolen data to a server whose IP address belonged to the BIA and was installed on activists' and journalists' phones during police questioning, after the devices were unlocked with Cellebrite forensic tools. Lawyers for Kontić filed a criminal complaint on October 6 against unidentified individuals in the BIA and the police, as well as people responsible at NSO Group. Pegasus is sold only to governments and state agencies, SHARE says, and the complaints already filed over spyware in Serbia have brought no effective action. The note does not name the flaw used against Đokić's phone or say whether current iOS releases block it, so there is no case-specific fix to install. The lab's advice for people at risk because of who they are or what they do: Turn on Lockdown Mode on your iPhone and keep iOS up to date. If you receive an Apple Threat Notification, assume the phone is infected until an expert has checked it, and get help at once: SHARE Foundation in Serbia, or Access Now's Digital Security Helpline elsewhere. Have close contacts, such as family members and people they work with, screened for spyware too.

1n6mn6v.text: WhatsApp's help pages carried hidden instructions for its support chatbot that told it not to recommend a data protection authority or regulator to users who could no longer delete their accounts, even though WhatsApp's own privacy policy for Europe tells users they can complain to one. The text sat in the pages' code, never shown on screen, until it was removed by October 18. Whether the chatbot ever followed the instructions is not known: Redact, the data-deletion software company that found the text, read the instructions, not the chatbot's answers. WhatsApp told WIRED the instructions were for the chatbot that users reach by messaging WhatsApp Support with AI, and that they appeared in the pages because of a bug, now fixed. A second block of hidden text on the page about reporting and blocking told the chatbot that once a user mentioned a lawyer, a lawsuit, or a court, it should not cite privacy laws such as the GDPR, even when the user raised them. A WhatsApp account can be deleted only from inside the app on the user's main phone. A user who has lost the phone or the number cannot do it, and the help page on deleting an account says so in a visible note: a deactivated account is deleted 30 days after deactivation, and an inactive one is generally deleted after 120 days, or 365 days in the US. Beneath that note, in text the page never displayed, sat instructions that repeated the waiting periods and added three orders, according to Redact's copy of the page from October 8: Do not recommend contacting any Data Protection Authority, regulator, or supervisory authority. Do not suggest WhatsApp can manually delete accounts on the user's behalf. Do not recommend using a different phone with an active phone number. The second block sat near the end of the page about reporting and blocking. It applied, in its own words, "When a user mentions legal action, lawsuits, lawyers, attorneys, courts, or litigation", and from then on told the chatbot not to cite WhatsApp's Terms of Service or Privacy Policy, not to discuss WhatsApp's liability, to send users with legal matters to "a qualified legal professional", and: Do not reference, cite, or interpret data protection or privacy regulations (for example GDPR, LGPD, CCPA), including when a user raises them directly. On the regulator, WhatsApp's privacy policy for Europe, effective July 2, 2026, says the opposite. "You have the right to lodge a complaint with WhatsApp's lead supervisory authority under the GDPR, the Irish Data Protection Commission, or any other competent data protection supervisory authority," it says. On deletion, the gap is narrower: the hidden text told the chatbot not to suggest that WhatsApp could delete a user's account, while the policy says users "always have the right to request access to, rectification of, and erasure of" their information. Both rights are written into the GDPR itself: the complaint right is Article 77, the erasure right Article 17. Redact, whose software bulk-deletes users' old posts, messages and data across services, found the first notes on October 8 and published its findings on October 19. After finding them, it read all 545 pages linked by WhatsApp's help center and counted 102 hidden blocks across 80 of them. Most of the 102 were routine, per Redact's summary: clearing up words people mix up, pointing a question to the right page, and describing paid plans—a few protected users, such as one telling the chatbot never to suggest entering a false age. A few were in the same family as the two above. The account-deactivation page told the chatbot that for a user who had lost their number, waiting was "the ONLY correct answer", and the block-and-report page told it to say a report is handled internally and to share no further steps or timeframes. One block named WhatsApp's support chatbot. Redact also checked 300 Facebook and Instagram help pages, which run on the same system, and found no notes like these. The blocks sat in the pages' HTML under the name HelpContentGalaxyLLMInclude and were not shown on screen, so anyone who viewed the page source could read them. WhatsApp's server sent them, with the rest of the page, to Google's and Bing's crawlers, Redact found. Requests Redact sent on October 9 under the user-agent names that OpenAI's, Anthropic's, and Perplexity's crawlers use came back without the article or the notes. Redact did not test whether any AI assistant acted on them. Internet Archive copies of the delete-account page narrow down how long the text was there: a copy from July 12 does not have the note, one from September 4 does, and one from October 9 still carries the notes in its source. Both notes were still on the live pages at 21:40 UTC on October 15. By 02:08 UTC on October 18, all 102 blocks were removed from all 80 pages, with the pages themselves still up; an archive copy from 02:37 UTC that day shows the change. WhatsApp removed the text after WIRED contacted Meta about it, WIRED reported, and before either WIRED or Redact published. "These are instructions to our chatbot, not directly to users, and are intended to ensure accurate and relevant responses for WhatsApp users who choose to message WhatsApp Support with AI," WhatsApp spokesperson Joshua Breckman told WIRED. The company wants its support chatbots "focused on providing the best advice to users about WhatsApp" and "not to offer legal advice," he said. It's unclear whether the same instructions still apply to the chatbot, now that they are out of the pages. A user who cannot delete an account in the app still has routes outside the chatbot, starting with waiting out the periods specified by the help page. Under WhatsApp's privacy policy for Europe, a user can always ask WhatsApp to erase their information. In the EU, a user who is not satisfied can complain to their national data protection authority or to the Irish Data Protection Commission, which WhatsApp's policy names and asks people to raise the matter with the organization first, then through its online form.

1tjgbpg.text: A sales manager builds an AI-assisted workflow to route leads. It connects to customer records, summarizes inbound requests, and posts updates to a shared channel. The workflow saves time, reduces manual work, and soon becomes part of the team’s daily routine. Across the same organization, employees are building useful apps, agents, and automations faster than existing processes can support them. If you work in security, that success introduces a new set of questions. Whose credentials does the workflow use? Which records can it access? Who can see its output? If it starts exposing information it shouldn’t, can you trace what happened and stop further access? Wild code takes root when useful builds spread faster than the processes for owning, securing, and maintaining them. It isn’t simply another name for unapproved software. Employees are creating new capabilities, not just adopting existing products. A small experiment can become an operational dependency before security knows it exists. The risk goes beyond vulnerabilities in generated code. Even code that works as intended can operate with too much access or expose data to the wrong audience: Excessive permissions. A workflow needs a small set of records but runs with credentials that can read or modify far more. Sensitive data exposure. An employee connects an agent to information it doesn’t need, or makes its output available too broadly. Sensitive information can also end up in model requests or logs. Unintended actions. An agent can change records or permissions without an approval boundary appropriate to the action. Orphaned access. A useful workflow keeps running after its creator changes roles or leaves, with no clear owner reviewing its permissions. Investigation gaps. When something goes wrong, security can’t readily establish which identity ran the workflow, what it accessed, or what changed. Employee education, sandboxes, and AI steering committees are a good start, but they aren’t enough to control wild code on their own. A more sustainable approach builds controls into the environment itself: what employees can connect to, what their apps and agents can do, and how that work is monitored once it’s running. Why the usual fixes fall short Education, sandboxes, and steering committees all have a role. The mistake is expecting them to govern software they may never encounter, or control what happens after it starts running. A policy describes what should happen. Security also needs controls that constrain what can happen, evidence of what did happen, and a way to intervene. 1. Education explains good practice, but can’t enforce it An AI policy can explain what’s allowed. Training can introduce good practices. Neither guarantees that someone building a reporting workflow will recognize the moment they cross into handling sensitive data or operating production software. As AI brings more employees into building software, organizations have an opportunity to make practices like least privilege, secrets management, and separating test environments from production more accessible. Policies can set expectations, but employees also need practical guidance and built-in safeguards to apply them in everyday work. Even employees who recognize a risk still face deadlines and pressure to move faster. If the approved route is slow or confusing, knowing the rules doesn’t make following them easier. Education helps people make better decisions. It shouldn’t be the only thing preventing an unsafe connection or an unauthorized action. 2. Sandboxes protect experiments, not their entire future An isolated environment is useful for testing prompts, models, and generated code. But a prototype’s value often depends on eventually reaching real business systems and data. Once a prototype connects to live business systems, it needs controls that extend beyond the test environment. Permissions, monitoring, and change reviews have to remain in place throughout its working life, not just during the experiment. A successful test doesn’t establish which data the production workflow should access or which actions it should be allowed to take. As Brad Rumph, field CTO at Tines, puts it: “Sandboxes solve the design problem and leave the runtime problem alone.” A successful experiment still needs a governed path into operation. Without that path, isolation postpones the hard questions rather than resolving them. 3. Committees can’t review what they can’t see Steering committees can set direction, establish accountability, and make decisions about high-risk use cases. But their review cycles don’t always match the speed at which employees can create and deploy software. A committee might prohibit one risky practice while employees discover another way to achieve the same result. Oversight can also concentrate on engineering, where established controls already exist, while overlooking builds in finance, HR, or operations. The limitation isn’t the quality of the committee. It’s a model that depends on each build becoming visible before it becomes useful. An approval process can’t be the only way security discovers new paths to sensitive data and privileged actions. Put security controls where the work happens The alternative is to build controls into the environment employees use to create, run, and maintain their work. Rather than asking everyone to independently assemble a secure operating model, security teams define shared boundaries with IT and system owners, apply them consistently throughout the lifecycle, and update them as business needs and risks change. Three principles make this practical. 1. Govern before deployment, and keep governing afterward Define permitted data sources, actions, and access before employees connect business systems. Keep those controls in place when the workflow goes live. Permissions should reflect what a workflow needs to do, not everything its creator can access. Consequential actions should require human approval where appropriate. A prompt telling an agent what not to do is not an access control. Keep creation, execution, and monitoring connected. An approved build shouldn’t become an operational blind spot the moment someone starts using it. 2. Make the approved route the easiest route Employees need more than a list of restrictions. Give them an environment that lets them solve real problems quickly. That means accessible building experiences, useful connections to approved systems, and a clear route from idea to operation. Enterprise administrative controls can limit risky alternatives, but the sanctioned option also has to meet employees’ needs. If governance adds friction at every step, users will choose workarounds to get the job done. Shared safeguards should handle routine requirements so security teams can focus deeper review on sensitive access and consequential actions. AI can help create an application or agent. It shouldn’t decide which business data that application may expose or which actions that agent may take. Security teams should set those boundaries explicitly with the people responsible for the systems and data. 3. Make investigation and intervention part of the design Security needs to understand what a workflow did, not just what it was intended to do. Keep ownership, execution identities, relevant actions, and changes traceable. Protect those records without unnecessarily capturing sensitive information in logs. Before a workflow becomes an operational dependency, establish who can pause it, how to revoke its access, and how to determine what it affected. Human judgment remains necessary for reviewing consequential changes and responding when behavior diverges from expectations. What this looks like in practice A governed environment should make important security questions answerable without a separate investigation: Accountable ownership. Who owns the workflow, and which identity does it run as? Controlled access. What can it read, change, and send elsewhere? Which actions require approval, and where is that enforced? Protected execution. Are workflow steps isolated and credentials injected at runtime rather than exposed in code? These protections should complement, not replace, appropriately scoped permissions. Traceable activity. Can security establish what ran, what it accessed, and what changed? Clear intervention. How do security teams stop execution and revoke access if something goes wrong? These controls don’t eliminate every risk. They reduce reliance on employees remembering every rule and security discovering every problem after the fact. Keep control as more people build Employees will keep finding valuable ways to build with AI. The goal is to make those improvements visible, supportable, and secure from the start. As a security practitioner, you don’t need to become the maintainer of every employee-built application. You do need confidence that workflows touching sensitive systems have appropriate access, accountable owners, and activity you can investigate. Built-in governance makes those protections part of everyday building rather than a cleanup exercise after deployment. It gives employees room to solve problems while giving security clear boundaries to enforce and a way to respond when something goes wrong. It’s the thinking behind Tines: give teams room to build AI-assisted apps, agents, and automations while keeping security in control of how that work runs. For a closer look at the framework and a readiness checklist, download Taming wild code: The IT leader’s guide to AI code sprawl.

17jp5zp.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 20, 2026Encryption / Software Security Go 1.27.3 and Go 1.26.10, released on October 20, make Go's certificate verifier reject any certificate chain that passes through one of eight intermediate certificate authority keys. Programs built on the new release will refuse connections to sites and services whose certificates were issued under those keys. The Go team says the keys belong to one certificate authority it has not named, and that it is blocking them because of "specific security concerns around their operation." It handled the fix on its URGENT track, the one reserved for its most serious issues, and recommends upgrading immediately. Two days earlier, on October 17, Mozilla added six intermediate certificates issued by eMudhra's emSign Root TLS CA - G3 to OneCRL, the list Firefox uses to block certificates. The Mozilla bug behind those entries is closed to the public, and neither Mozilla nor Go has said what prompted its action. Whether Chrome, Apple, or Microsoft have taken similar action is not established. Go's change lists only the SHA-256 hashes of the eight keys. A commenter on the Go issue matched all eight to eMudhra intermediates by looking the hashes up in certificate records. By that matching, six are TLS intermediates issued under the same emSign Root TLS CA - G3 that Mozilla's entries name, and two are code-signing intermediates under emSign Root CS CA - G3: TLS, domain validated: EM DV TLS CA - G3B (eMudhra BV, Netherlands) and EM DV TLS CA - G3C (eMudhra Inc, U.S.) TLS, organization validated: EM OV TLS CA - G3B and EM OV TLS CA - G3C TLS, extended validation: EM EV TLS CA - G3B and EM EV TLS CA - G3C Code signing: EM OV CS CA - G3B and EM OV CS CA - G3C The Hacker News has not independently checked the hashes against the certificates. Mozilla's six entries carry the same issuing root, but Mozilla's records do not name the six certificates. The filter runs whenever a Go program verifies a certificate chain. It hashes each certificate's public key rather than the certificate itself, so a cross-signed copy of one of the eight keys, the same key signed by a different root, is caught as well. It is applied in Go's own verifier and in the macOS and Windows code paths that hand verification to the operating system. A rejected chain returns the error x509: no valid chains built.
