The change contains no setting to turn the filter off. Given the structure of the code, it also applies when a program supplies its own set of trusted roots, so a private deployment that intentionally trusts one of the eight keys will fail too. The Go team has not said whether that is intended. Go's verifier "doesn't do any revocation checking," as its documentation warns. It also does not read the block lists browsers use, such as the CRLSets Chrome used against rogue Google certificates this month. Blocking a key therefore means shipping it in a release, and programs keep the old behavior until they are rebuilt. Projects including Bluesky's indigo were rebuilt on the new releases on October 20. What happened at the certificate authority is not public. Go's announcement gives one sentence about security concerns, and the release came without the pre-announcement Go sent before its October 8 security releases. Go's security policy defines URGENT track issues as "a threat to the Go ecosystem's integrity" or flaws being actively exploited with severe damage, and says there are no recent examples. Go has not said which of those applied. On the issue, one user asked for the committed patch to explain "who and what they correspond to." The Go team had not replied as of October 20. eMudhra is an Indian certificate authority that sells certificates under the emSign brand. Its roots emSign Root CA - G1 and emSign ECC Root CA - G3 are in the Chrome, Apple , and Mozilla root stores. The company told Mozilla earlier this year that its newer TLS root is cross-signed by emSign Root CA - G1, which is how certificates under the newer root chain to a trusted root. In September, a six-week public discussion of eMudhra's request to add ten new roots to the root programs run by browser and operating-system makers, including emSign Root TLS CA - G3, closed with no objections. Certificates logged for eMudhra's own domains, including emsign.com and emudhra.com, chain through other eMudhra intermediates, according to certificate transparency records The Hacker News checked on October 20. The company's repository contained no notice about the intermediates as of that day, and The Hacker News found no public statement from eMudhra. Go 1.25 and older releases are out of support and get no fixes, so the only route is a supported release from the download page. No temporary workaround exists in any source, and the filter cannot be disabled. Sites and services whose certificates chain through the eight keys will need certificates from a different intermediate before rebuilt Go clients can connect to them.

1086zvx.text: The Russia-linked state-sponsored threat actor tracked as APT28 (aka BlueDelta, Fancy Bear, and Forest Blizzard) has been attributed to attacks targeting two member states of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO). The Symantec Threat Hunter Team, which is tracking the activity cluster under the moniker Swallowtail, involved the use of a backdoor called HOOKEDGE and a previously undocumented loader that is designed to decrypt and run an encrypted payload in memory by using a cryptographic key that's supplied at runtime. Targets of the activity included a law enforcement agency, a naval shipbuilder, and a manufacturer of military aircraft engines – entities that hold information that could be of use to a foreign intelligence agency, the Broadcom-owned threat intelligence unit said. "During one attack against the naval shipbuilder, operators returned to a compromised host repeatedly over the course of a week in what appeared to be hands-on-keyboard activity," Symantec said in a report shared with The Hacker News. "They stole credential material using two separate techniques, opened a persistent SSH tunnel into the organization's internal network and deployed a previously undocumented reflective loader." APT28's use of HOOKEDGE was first publicly documented by Recorded Future Insikt Group in late August 2026 in connection with a cyber espionage campaign targeting government and diplomatic organizations in Romania, Spain, and Türkiye between September 2025 and early April 2026. HOOKEDGE shares significant code and tradecraft overlap with HEADLACE, a modular Windows implant that APT28 has put to use in attacks targeting diplomats since April 2023. Delivered via spear-phishing lures, HOOKEDGE is a barebones Windows batch script that's capable of accepting attacker-issued commands and sending the results back. The backdoor is delivered via macro-enabled Microsoft Word documents and communicates entirely through a webhook[.]site URL, which acts as a channel to stage tasks and to receive execution output. Infected machines then fetch these tasks using a hidden, off-screen instance of the Microsoft Edge browser as opposed to relying on a traditional downloader. In the attack aimed at the naval shipbuilder in late July 2026, the threat actors are said to have delivered new variants of HOOKEDGE that abandon the use of webhook[.]site in favor of a dedicated IP address ("185.82.218[.]119:443") for both tasking and exfiltration. "The attackers used two distinct credential-theft techniques," Symantec said. "In one, they pushed an SSH private key onto the compromised host and immediately used it to open an SSH connection back to their own server, requesting a persistent, backgrounded tunnel that would give them a route from their infrastructure into the target's internal network." "In the other, they ran a short, self-contained PowerShell script that stands up a listener on the host's own loopback address and forces the machine to authenticate to it, capturing the resulting NTLM handshake." The attackers have also been observed dropping a new reflective loader ("ld.exe") using a curl command via SSH that's engineered to decode and run a next-stage component. The exact nature of the payload remains unknown. The most recent activity was registered on September 24, 2026, when a Visual Basic Script launcher associated with HOOKEDGE was observed within the shipbuilder's network. It's unclear if any data was stolen as a result of these intrusions. "The tradecraft observed after initial access, credential theft through two independent techniques, a persistent network tunnel, and a previously undocumented loader, goes beyond the delivery mechanism that has so far been publicly reported on this campaign," Symantec said. Attacks Targeting Ukraine in H1 2026 In a report published late last month, the Computer Emergency Response Team of Ukraine (CERT-UA) revealed that Russian hackers are increasingly targeting the smartphones belonging to Ukrainian military personnel and government officials for espionage and financially motivated attacks. "The growing role of smartphones in communications among military personnel, government employees, and civilians is making them more attractive targets for intelligence gathering activity, further compromise, and financially motivated attacks," the agency said. This includes the use of the DarkSword iOS exploit kit, which is distributed via watering-hole attacks through compromised legitimate Ukrainian news outlets and government sites to siphon sensitive data from compromised devices. "The tool is associated with Russian threat actors, and its use against Ukrainian targets points to the adversary's growing interest in the iOS platform, which had previously been considered relatively secure," the agency noted. The findings are consistent with a report from Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) in March 2026, which linked the Russian espionage actor UNC6353 to the use of Coruna and DarkSword kits in watering-hole campaigns targeting Ukrainian users since summer 2025. The threats also extend to the Android ecosystem, with threat clusters UAC-0244 and UAC-0263 using decoy apps to deliver two different malware families - UAC-0244 distributes CAMELSPY, which harvests device system information, geolocation, SIM card details, contacts, call logs, and images from the gallery. UAC-0263 distributes BTMOB RAT, which gives the threat actor control over the infected device and the ability to exfiltrate data. CERT-UA also said it observed APT28 exploiting vulnerabilities such as CVE-2026-21509, a security feature bypass in Microsoft Office, and CVE-2026-8496, a zero-click vulnerability in the SOGo webmail client, to deliver the COVENANT malware as well as siphon victims' mailbox credentials and data, respectively. "At the same time, the actor has not abandoned older, tried-and-tested – but unfortunately still effective – approaches," CERT-UA said. "In particular, attacks exploiting XSS vulnerabilities in the Roundcube webmail client were observed. Excel documents containing macros were also used to further distribute COVENANT." These attacks are among the 3,137 cyber incidents recorded by CERT-UA in the first half of 2026, which is estimated to be 8% more than in the second half of 2025. The development comes as Team Cymru said it identified five additional LegionRelay command-and-control (C2) servers used in attacks targeting Ukrainian entities. The IP addresses are listed below - 91.149.221[.]118:8000 91.149.221[.]123:8000 166.88.239[.]54:8000 194.87.108[.]12:8000 194.87.108[.]217:8000 LegionRelay is the name assigned to a PowerShell-based RAT that supports file enumeration, file exfiltration, screenshot capture, browser data theft, Telegram and WhatsApp data exfiltration, and RDP access setup. It's attributed to a threat actor dubbed GREYVIBE, which is assessed to have engaged in persistent attacks targeting Ukraine and Ukraine-related entities since at least August 2025.

1obqsp.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 20, 2026Cloud Security / Incident Response ConnectWise on Monday said it has taken remediation measures, including strengthening administrative-access protections and resetting accounts and replacing application credentials, as it continues to respond to a security incident that led to unauthorized access to application identities associated with Cloud Backup. The company said it has completed the following actions since it began rolling out mitigations on October 17 at 5:00 a.m. UTC, three days after the incident was first identified - Disabling affected application connections and suspending Cloud Backup. Suspending SaaS Security and Cloud Management as a precaution because they are integrated with Cloud Backup. Enlisting the help of independent third-party specialists for incident response and remediation. Enhancing administrative-access protections. Publishing technical guidance to help partners investigate and remediate potential unauthorized activity in their own and managed customer environments. ConnectWise said it's validating the effectiveness of its containment measures and emphasized that it has not seen any successful threat activity in the environments it monitors. There is no evidence that any ConnectWise products and services, other than Cloud Backup and the precautionary suspensions of SaaS Security and Cloud Management, are impacted. "This observation does not establish whether individual partner or customer Microsoft 365 tenants have been affected," it said. "Reviewing each potentially affected tenant remains essential." "Before making changes, preserve relevant evidence, validate findings, and assess potential operational impacts. Completing these steps does not guarantee that a tenant is unaffected or that all unauthorized access has been eliminated. Do not reconnect affected applications until ConnectWise provides formal restoration instructions." Huntress has shared the following IP addresses observed in connection with the activity, adding that the password spray and failed login attempts linked to some of them are unlikely to be related to the application sign-in activity - 144.172.64[.]128 - Application sign-ins with a vendor credential (primary vector) 144.172.64[.]99 - Failed user password spray, concentrated (October 10 to 14, 2026) 144.172.64[.]60 - A few failed user logins (October 18, 2026) 144.172.94[.]243 - Broad failed login spray, ongoing against many organizations "In a review of application sign-ins across more than 10,000 tenants with ConnectWise applications (where we can see those logs), 144.172.64[.]128 and Microsoft-internal ranges are the only addresses that produced application sign-in activity," Huntress researchers said in an update. "We did not see application sign-in activity from any of the other addresses listed below, all of which are in the same provider range as 144.172.64[.]128 (AS14956, RouterHosting). We did see password spray and failed login attempts from some of them." The cybersecurity company said it also observed post-compromise actions on a second tenant, following the same modus operandi as before, in which the application granted itself Global Administrator and then added a new secret on a small number of other applications in the tenant for persistence. While the access may have been used for Microsoft Graph directory reads, there are no signs the attackers weaponized it for mailbox or file manipulation, or to make user or policy changes. "The choice of which applications to backdoor appeared to be random in the two tenants we reviewed," Huntress added. "Across the two compromised tenants, the identical grant flow selected two completely different sets of applications. The only consistent criteria we can point to is structural: credentials were planted in applications that are registered inside the affected tenant, without regard to what those applications can actually do."

5botl.text: An attacker used a contributor's GitHub account to replace the download archives on five existing releases of OVHcloud's command-line tool on Monday, October 19. The account had been hijacked, and the new files were a build designed to steal secrets stored on the disk of any machine that runs it, the cloud provider says. They were live on GitHub for up to 94 minutes, from 12:47 to 14:21 UTC, and reached only people who installed or updated the OVHcloud CLI during that window, via a path that checks for no hash, on macOS, Linux x86_64 or arm64, or Windows x86_64. OVHcloud deleted the swapped archives and published a clean v0.16.0 that evening as an immutable release, whose files GitHub will not let anyone change. The source code, the release tag, and the company's build pipeline were not touched: the bad build was a plain go build of a later commit, uploaded straight onto releases published between April and September. Who Was Exposed On v0.15.0, the attacker replaced six files: the macOS x86_64 and arm64 archives, the Linux x86_64 and arm64 archives, the Windows x86_64 archive, and the checksums.txt file, so the published hashes matched the new binaries. The same six files are now gone from v0.11.0 to v0.14.0 as well. The Linux i386, Windows i386, Windows arm64, and WebAssembly builds were left alone on every release. OVHcloud lists v0.11.0 through v0.15.0 as compromised and v0.10.0 as clean. Those five releases were published between April 14 and September 16, so a copy installed before 12:47 UTC on Monday and not updated since is the original. You got a swapped file if, in that window and on one of those platforms, you: Ran the official install script (curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ovh/ovhcloud-cli/main/install.sh | sh). It downloads the latest release archive and installs it, and has never checked a hash. Downloaded an archive from the GitHub release page of any of the five releases. Ran a CI job or build step that fetches the archive from the release download URL without a pinned hash. Ran the CLI's own upgrade command from a v0.12.0, v0.13.0, or v0.14.0 install on a macOS or Linux machine where the tool was installed by the script or by hand. The command downloads the archive and replaces the binary with no hash check. On a Homebrew or go install setup it only prints the command to run instead. You did not get it if you: Installed with Homebrew, whose cask in force during the window pinned the original SHA-256 of each archive. Homebrew refuses a download whose hash does not match, so brew install or brew upgrade would have failed rather than installed the swapped file. Some early write-ups listed Homebrew among the exposed paths, but The Hacker News checked the tap's commit history: nothing changed between the v0.15.0 cask on September 16 and the v0.16.0 cask on Monday evening. Used go install or built from source. The v0.15.0 tag still points at its September commit, 760fd72. Pulled the Docker image. Its latest tag was last pushed on September 21, four weeks before the swap, and had not been rebuilt as of Tuesday. Installed before 12:47 UTC on Monday and did not update during the window. How to Tell The customer who caught the swap pulled the build information out of the new v0.15.0 Linux arm64 binary with go version -m, which reads the file without running it, and posted it in a GitHub issue. Three things mark the bad build: The module line reads v0.15.1-0.20261013083505-5ead8ef9b43d+dirty, a pseudo-version, the stand-in string Go generates for a build from an untagged commit, here one from October 13. A genuine release carries its tag number: OVHcloud's clean v0.16.0 build reads v0.16.0+dirty. The recorded commit is 5ead8ef, not 760fd72, the commit the v0.15.0 tag points to. A -ldflags="-s -w" line is present. OVHcloud's release pipeline builds with a version flag that Go leaves out of the recorded flags, so a genuine release shows no -ldflags line at all. Advice circulating that any build marked +dirty, or carrying vcs lines, is the malicious one would flag OVHcloud's own release. The Hacker News ran the same command on the clean v0.16.0 Linux x86_64 binary: it reports v0.16.0+dirty, vcs.modified=true and the commit it was built from. The only published hash of a swapped file is the v0.15.0 Linux arm64 archive: SHA-256 (swapped archive): 3833daffcaaaab27e4e0e0833240ffcb1df8df648f4ec0bc4a75c176e28933cb SHA-256 (original archive): 5c2beb56e6d83a4b426565a1557791ef759316abcc4effb38dd627c90aeb80e0 A build without the version flag would report its version as undefined, but running a suspect binary to find out is not advisable. What to Do OVHcloud founder Octave Klaba wrote on X on Monday evening that anyone affected should change every secret stored on the disk. = The CLI keeps OVHcloud API credentials in ~/.ovh.conf and reads them from environment variables, according to its documentation, and the advice covers everything else on the disk, not only those files. If you ran a swapped build, or cannot tell, treat every secret readable from that machine as exposed and rotate it. OpenSourceMalware, which investigated the incident, adds: do it from a different machine. Remove the binary and install v0.16.0. The release is immutable and carries a release attestation, a signed record of its files. Updating replaces the program but does not revoke a key that was already copied, which is why the rotation comes first. Check a downloaded archive against the release with gh release verify-asset v0.16.0 FILE, as GitHub documents. OVHcloud has not said which files the binary reads, where it sends them, or how many copies were downloaded, and no copy of a swapped archive has been analyzed in public. The company has promised a detailed postmortem in the coming days. How It Happened Anyone with write access to a GitHub repository can delete the files attached to a release and upload new ones with the same names, and the download URL does not change unless release immutability is enabled. The setting, generally available since October 2025, locks a release's files and tag but protects only releases created after it is enabled. OVHcloud had not enabled it. In a second post on Monday night, quoted by Next, Klaba wrote that the problem stemmed from the immutability option not being activated, so a user with the right permissions could modify existing releases directly on GitHub without any checks by the company's CI/CD pipeline. The option has now been enabled, and the pipelines themselves were not affected. The five old releases now offer only the four archives the attacker did not touch. The uploads came through the account of a contributor whose merged work is in OVHcloud's documentation repository and who is not a public member of the organization, according to OpenSourceMalware, which built a timeline from GitHub's server-side records. The release workflow never ran: the run list shows no workflow between October 16 and the v0.16.0 tag push at 16:00 UTC on Monday. First checks found no other repository affected, Klaba wrote in his first post, and OVHcloud has not said how the account's credentials were taken. A customer's CI job caught the swap because it pins the SHA-256 of the Linux arm64 archive and began failing. With no private reporting channel on the repository, the customer filed a public issue, at 13:50 UTC by OpenSourceMalware's timeline, and OVHcloud deleted the swapped files about half an hour later, at 14:21 UTC (16:21 in Paris). v0.16.0 followed at 17:16 UTC, published under the company's ovh-cds account with a signed tag. The GlassWorm Question OpenSourceMalware ties the account to GlassWorm, the malware campaign that hides code in invisible Unicode characters and fetches its next stage from the memo field of a Solana wallet's transactions. Four of the account's personal repositories were force-pushed on March 5 and 6 with an amended commit that added a loader of that kind, the researchers found. The wallet that loader reads is the one named in GlassWorm's ForceMemo campaign, which force-pushed malware into hundreds of Python repositories in March with stolen GitHub tokens. The Hacker News confirmed that the loader file is still in one of those repositories, with the hash the researchers published. Whether the same actor did both is "our inference," the researchers wrote. The shared account is the link, and nothing from the October binary has been tied to GlassWorm, because no copy of it was preserved.

1kvxe5v.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 20, 2026Vulnerability / Endpoint Security Siemens has addressed a DLL sideloading vulnerability impacting Siemens Software Center that it said has been exploited in ClickFix attacks. The high-severity vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-110936 (CVSS v4 score: 8.4), could allow an attacker to place a specially-crafted DLL in a directory the application searches, resulting in execution of malicious code with the same privileges as the affected service. "The affected application loads dynamic-link libraries (DLLs) from an uncontrolled search path," Siemens said in an advisory. "This could allow an authenticated local attacker to place a specially crafted DLL in a directory that the application searches, leading to arbitrary code execution with the privileges of the affected application." The issue has been patched in version 4.0.9.8. Huntress Labs researcher Jose Oregon has been credited with discovering and reporting the shortcoming. In a separate alert, Siemens said attackers have abused a genuine copy of Siemens Software Center with a valid signature and placed their own crafted DLL ("archive.dll") next to it to trigger the execution of malicious code. "They chose this program as a carrier because it is signed and trusted, and because version 3.5.8.7, the latest version at the time, loaded helper files from its own folder without checking them," Siemens added. Specifically, threat actors have been found leveraging "msiexec.exe" to launch "AllMyBasic.msi," which then executes "SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe." The activity has been attributed to a ClickFix delivery platform called Romulus, which was detailed by Forescout last week as being used to deliver Legion Loader and other malware using DLL sideloading. According to Huntress, some of these campaigns have leveraged malicious ChatGPT Custom GPTs to direct victims to a fake URL responsible for serving a ClickFix lure, which when copied and executed by the victim, runs PowerShell code to drop an MSI installer that abuses DLL sideloading to ultimately deploy a remote access trojan. Siemens has shared the following indicators of compromise - 96.62.218[.]59 (Payloading hosting and command-and-control) wizardexpensive[.]com (Payloading hosting and command-and-control) 2.27.248[.]127 (Distribution channel of AllMyBasic.msi) Besides updating Siemens Software Center to version 4.0.9.8 or later and starting the application to apply the update, organizations are advised to block the IP addresses and domains associated with the malicious activity and look for "SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe" running from "AppData\Local\Programs" and started by "msiexec.exe."

11e0hy4.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 20, 2026Cyber Espionage / Data Security A U.S. court on Monday granted the U.S. government's request to detain a former OpenAI engineer accused of planting a recording device in an executive conference room at the company's San Francisco office to allegedly steal sensitive secrets. In a new court filing Sunday, prosecutors revealed that Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national, was "in frequent communications via WhatsApp with a member of the Saudi Royal Family" throughout 2025 and 2026. Alfozan is said to have communicated with the Saudi royal as recently as October 5, 2026, four days before he was arrested. "Among other things, the individual told the defendant that an artificial intelligence initiative was being launched in Saudi Arabia and wanted the defendant to join it," the filing reads. "In May 2026, the individual told the defendant, 'Saudi needs you more then [sic] the US!' to which the defendant responded '100,' indicating he agreed." The Saudi Royal Family member is said to have repeatedly attempted to recruit Alfozan and even asked when he planned to leave OpenAI, to which the defendant said he wouldn't do so until his stock vested. Alfozan joined OpenAI as an engineer around July 2025 with an annual base salary of $385,000. Last week, the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) revealed that he had been arrested for allegedly inserting a stealthy audio recording device into a USB port on the back of a television in the executive conference room to capture sensitive conversations. The defendant is also said to have modified the device to prevent data transfer between it and the television and encrypted the content stored on the device's microSD card. In addition, he used his wife's personal ChatGPT account to research how to "build a continuous audio recorder" to "captur[e] microphone audio and save compressed WAV recordings to an SD card." "In the days and weeks before placing the device, the defendant (i) used an OpenAI productivity agent to ascertain which 'meeting rooms' OpenAI 'leadership and exec[utives]' used, and where they met with 'external partners'; and (ii) spent considerable time near the conference room where he later installed the device," the filing said. Alfozan has been charged with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. If convicted, he faces a maximum possible sentence of five years in prison. Prosecutors also argued that Alfozan is a flight risk, stating he has "ample resources... and what appears to be considerable support from a foreign government that has (i) no extradition treaty with the United States; (ii) limitless resources; and (iii) the ability to provide extraordinary travel assistance," according to the filing. Shortly after details of his arrest became public knowledge, it emerged that the defendant had planned to depart to Riyadh with his wife and son on a one-way ticket on October 12, 2026. Although he was arrested three days prior, his wife and son are said to have already left the U.S. without him. The day before her departure, Alfozan's wife allegedly told the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) agents that her U.S. visa was expiring and that she, along with her son, were permanently shifting back to Saudi Arabia. "The defendant went to significant lengths to create customized, encrypted recording devices to secretly record highly sensitive meetings involving senior OpenAI personnel and executives, high-level business counterparts, and government officials, all while communicating with individuals of significance in Saudi Arabia and pursuing opportunities in – and making plans to travel to – Saudi Arabia," the filing said. Stating the U.S. government's investigation is ongoing, prosecutors said a search of the defendant's residence and a "preliminary review" of his electronic devices, including his cellphone, uncovered several pieces of evidence - Several electronic components similar to those in the customized devices the defendant installed in the OpenAI conference room and had in his missing bag were identified in his residence. Photographs from his iPhone dated between September 22 and 28, 2026, that depict one additional concealed recording device, as well as what appear to be the input/output panels on TVs and other electronic devices in various locations in OpenAI buildings, including a second conference room where sensitive meetings took place. A deleted note on his cellphone from September 2026 included links to various recording devices, including those made by Seeed Studio, the same manufacturer whose devices were found in OpenAI's offices and his residence. Browsing history showed that the defendant accessed a folder called "Saudi Gov Docs" on October 4, 2026, and he used an OpenAI productivity agent to inquire about various Saudi-related business and government-related engagements from the Saudi Ministry of Communication and Information Technology (MCIT) between July 6, 2026, and September 21, 2026. "The defendant leveraged his skills as a highly-educated engineer to create sophisticated recording devices that – the evidence strongly suggests – he intended to bring with him to Saudi Arabia," the filing said. "Whether the defendant wanted to record OpenAI meetings to enrich himself by enhancing his own business prospects, or to provide aid a foreign government, or both, his conduct is criminal and it presents a danger to innovation in the Silicon Valley and a concern for the national security of the United States."

lre2pv.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 20, 2026Artificial Intelligence / Cybercrime Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a ClickFix delivery platform called ROMULUS that's being used to distribute malware such as Legion Loader. According to Forescout Research - Vedere Labs, ROMULUS is akin to a malware delivery service that employs ClickFix-style lures on bogus landing pages to trick unsuspecting users into running malicious commands and infecting their own machines. "ROMULUS may be a privately operated panel, a commercial cybercriminal delivery service, an affiliate framework, or software that has been copied between operators," security researcher Sai Molige said in an analysis. The cybersecurity company said it identified six IP addresses running ROMULUS - 96.62.224[.]81 86.109.75[.]7 151.240.151[.]223 23.94.145[.]224 93.152.224[.]118 2.27.248[.]127 Notably, the IP address "96.62.224[.]81" was identified as hosting a ClickFix script and an MSI installer file in connection with another campaign that has been found to leverage malicious ChatGPT Custom GPTs to direct victims to a fake URL responsible for serving the ClickFix lure. Forescout's own analysis has since uncovered the same malware being delivered via another server, 86.109.75[.]7, that also hosted a panel codenamed ROMULUS. In addition, a separate chain triggered via ClickFix has been used to run a PowerShell script, which then delivers Legion Loader, a malware loader also called Satacom downloader, CurlyGate, and RobotDropper. As of writing, it's not known who is behind the ROMULUS platform. However, it shares no overlaps with RomulusLoader, a malware family associated with Silver Fox (aka TA4922), a China-aligned threat actor known for repeatedly using tax-related pretexts to distribute remote access trojans like ValleyRAT (aka Winos 4.0), DcRAT, and potentially Venom RAT via DLL sideloading techniques. The ROMULUS platform exposes two endpoints that are designed to download a PowerShell staging script, which decides the payload to be fetched next: a trojanized MSI installer carrying a malware loader or an encrypted archive containing Legion Loader that's inflated to nearly 1 GB with repetitive padding to bypass upload limits, sandbox budgets, or static-analysis thresholds. The loader, for its part, communicates with a remote server to fetch and run additional payloads. The findings indicate how ClickFix is evolving beyond a social engineering technique into a highly effective entry point for malware. To mitigate the threat, it's essential to hunt for suspicious PowerShell commands and DLL sideloading events.

14m48xt.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 19, 2026Vulnerability / Web Security Threat actors have begun to exploit a chain of vulnerabilities in Plex Media Server to deploy cryptocurrency miners and reverse proxy software, a day after a proof-of-concept (PoC) went public. According to a researcher who goes by the online alias boredhackerblog, the exploitation activity involves chaining four different vulnerabilities, collectively called Plex2Shell. The vulnerabilities are below - CVE-2026-96652 (CVSS score: 5.3) - An unauthenticated server-side request forgery (SSRF) stemming via the "/player/timeline" endpoint by taking advantage of the fact that the "protocol" parameter is inserted into a programmatically-constructed player URL with no validation, allowing an attacker to force the Plex server to POST to a destination of their choice. CVE-2026-96654 (CVSS score: 6.9) - An improper neutralization of URL values included in the "searchOne" endpoint that could allow an attacker to call other plugins' functions and supply their own parameters to obtain the owner's admin token. CVE-2026-96655 (CVSS score: 5.3) - An SSRF vulnerability that allows an authenticated user (i.e., the owner token) to request arbitrary internal or external addresses (e.g., an attacker-hosted carrier video carrying the malicious ELF payload) via the '/video/:/transcode/universal' path parameter. CVE-2026-96656 (CVSS score: 8.6) - An external control of file name or path vulnerability that allows the ELF shared object to an attacker-chosen path in the Codecs directory and execute it. Put differently, the vulnerabilities can be combined together in this order to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution on susceptible Plex Media Server instances. The vulnerabilities, along with CVE-2026-96651 (CVSS score: 7.1), were disclosed to Plex on July 27, 2026, by security researcher Zach Main, and were patched in Plex Media Server 1.43.3.10861 released on August 3, 2026. In-the-wild exploitation attempts targeting the flaws have since been recorded a day after technical details of the Plex2Shell chain went public on October 16, 2026. The attacks led to the deployment of a miner payload from a remote server ("217.60.194[.]116"). The attack efforts have been observed from the following IP addresses - 91.92.40[.]202 176.65.139[.]228 45.194.92[.]222 176.65.139[.]228 Furthermore, the vulnerabilities have been exploited to deliver an artifact named "myawesomeproxy," which, according to VirusTotal, is a stealthy Linux backdoor and reverse proxy. Running the program displays the below message, per boredhackerblog - Running this software on any of your devices makes you agree to the potential external use of your internet traffic. Also deployed concurrently is an XMRig miner process identified as "mylovelyminer" with its mining server pointing to "ota.proxystream[.]st." Notably, another subdomain associated with the same domain, "global.relay.proxystream[.]st," was flagged by Bitsight in August 2026 in connection with the AISURU DDoS and proxyware botnet. Posts on Reddit indicate that multiple Plex users have had their instances compromised with the same "mylovelyminer" payload. That said, it's not known at this stage if it stems from the exploitation of Plex2Shell flaws. The development comes more than a month after Plex urged users to update their instances to the latest version following the release of an update that addressed multiple unspecified security flaws. It's unclear if the aforementioned vulnerabilities were part of this alert. The Hacker News has contacted Plex for comment and we will update the story if we hear back. In light of active exploitation, users are advised to keep their Plex installations up-to-date for optimal protection.

1v2pf25.text: Copies of Rank Math PRO, the paid version of the Rank Math SEO plugin for WordPress, that were downloaded from rankmath.com or delivered as updates between 20:02 UTC on October 15 and 07:12 UTC on October 16 contained malware, Rank Math said in a security notice published on October 16. Any site that installed and activated one of those copies should be treated as compromised, and the malware can recreate its hidden backdoor whenever someone visits the site. Rank Math has removed the affected files and released a clean version, 3.0.124. Installing it replaces the plugin but does not remove files, administrator accounts, or scheduled tasks the malware may already have placed elsewhere on the server, Wordfence said in an advisory on October 17. Who Is Affected The version number does not show whether a copy is affected. Rank Math's changelog dates 3.0.123 to October 7, more than a week before the window opened, and the notice limits the incident to copies downloaded or installed through an update during the window. A copy of 3.0.123 obtained before 20:02 UTC on October 15 is outside it. The notice sorts sites into three cases: You installed and activated 3.0.123 during the window: treat the site as compromised, even if it has since been updated to 3.0.124, and follow the recovery steps below. You installed it but never activated it: delete the plugin files, install 3.0.124 from your Rank Math account, and run a security scan. You downloaded it but never installed or activated it: nothing in this incident alone indicates the site was compromised. Rank Math has emailed some users about the incident and told anyone unsure whether the files were installed or activated to contact its support team. The notice applies only to the PRO plugin, which customers download and update from rankmath.com rather than WordPress.org. The free Rank Math SEO plugin on WordPress.org, which lists more than 4 million active installations and was last updated on October 6, is not named in it. What the Malware Does What is known about the malware comes from Rank Math's notice. Neither it nor Wordfence's advisory includes an analysis of the code, and neither names who is behind it. Deleting suspicious files before stopping what recreates the backdoor may not resolve the problem, which is why the cleanup order below matters. The attacker may also have left PHP backdoor files in other plugins' folders, in theme folders, and in the must-use plugins directory, created administrator accounts, added a fake WordPress core file, changed .htaccess so that .cache files run as PHP, and added scheduled tasks and SSH keys. Any password, database credential, API key, or other secret the site could reach may have been exposed, and owners should assume it was. Wordfence assigned the incident CVE-2026-111862 and rates it 9.8 out of 10, with the researcher listed as unknown. Patchstack classifies it as a backdoor and says that, because the attack was on Rank Math's own systems, "a rule is not possible for mitigation." How to Recover Rank Math's preferred recovery is a restore. Where a backup of the site and its database from before 20:02 UTC on October 15 exists, restore it, run a security scan, change every password and credential, and only then install 3.0.124 from your Rank Math account. Where no clean backup exists, the manual cleanup runs in a fixed order, and three actions come before anything else is touched: Delete the entire rank-math-pro plugin folder using the hosting file manager or FTP. "Deactivating the plugin alone is not sufficient," the notice says. In the wp_options table, delete any entry whose option_name is _uf6qdn2hmm, t8krdk990phb or _np5pvf754c. Block outgoing connections to rank1cdn[.]com if the hosting provider or firewall allows it. Only then does the search for other changes begin, in these places: Files: PHP files in wp-content/mu-plugins/, in other plugins' folders, in the inc/, includes/ and lib/ folders of non-default themes, in Rank Math's own includes/ folder, and in uploads/. Code: PHP that uses base64_decode with XOR loops, the key xmmqhn, proc_open, or PHP-FPM socket code. File: wp-includes/class-wp-cache-util.php, which is not a WordPress core file. Accounts: administrator usernames beginning wpsupport_, or accounts with email addresses ending @wp-mail[.]net. Server: .htaccess rules that let .cache files run as PHP, .cache files containing PHP code, entries tagged #ms6v46 in the web server user's crontab, WordPress scheduled events, SSH authorized_keys files, other users' crontabs, running processes, and any location outside the site where the web server can write. Wordfence adds a caution: "Their absence does not, by itself, prove that a website is clean." Credentials are changed in every case, even after a restore from backup. The list covers WordPress passwords, the database username and password in wp-config.php, the security keys and salts in the same file, payment gateway, SMTP and other API keys, hosting control panel, FTP, SFTP and SSH access, secrets held in environment variables, and two-factor authentication for administrators. The cleanup ends with a security scan, wp core verify-checksums for WordPress core, and wp plugin verify-checksums --all, with the caution that checksums may not exist for premium plugins. WordPress.org publishes none for this one. The Hacker News checked its plugin-checksums service on October 19 and found no file for the PRO plugin under either of its names, while the service does publish one for the free plugin. The fallback notice provides a clean copy from the official source. The clean 3.0.124 goes on last, downloaded by logging in at rankmath.com directly. Some customers may be unable to log in and may need to reset their account password, the notice says, without saying why, and Rank Math will never send login or download links by email. What Rank Math Has Not Said Rank Math, part of the Swedish hosting group group.one, has not said how the malicious files entered its download and update system, how many customers received one, whether automatic updates delivered them, or what the clean and tainted packages' hashes are. Its only statement about the future is that the team is taking steps to reduce the risk of similar incidents. Registry records show the domain Rank Math tells owners to block, rank1cdn[.]com, was registered at 19:31 UTC on October 14, about a day before the window opened. A Pattern This Year This is at least the third time this year that a premium WordPress plugin's vendor-run update channel has delivered backdoored builds. In April, Nextend's update system served a backdoored Smart Slider 3 Pro for about six hours. In June, ShapedPlugin's Pro plugins were found to have been backdoored in its update channel, and one package that had shipped clean was later "tampered with under the same version number," the trap Rank Math's customers now face. Attackers also altered scripts served from Awesome Motive's CDN in June and poisoned BdThemes' API feed in August. Nothing published links the attackers behind any of those incidents to this one.

istocc.text: The worst problems don't always come with a warning. Sometimes they arrive through a service everyone trusts, a device someone bought, or a system nobody thought to check. By the time something looks wrong, the damage may already be done. This week had plenty of that. Trusted connections became a problem. Hardware wasn't as safe as it looked. Old bugs found new victims, and some systems were left so exposed that breaking in barely required any effort. Even AI agents crossed lines they weren't supposed to. Some attacks were clever. Others were painfully simple. The full recap shows just how much can go wrong, and how little it sometimes takes. ⚡ Threat of the Week ConnectWise Suspends Cloud Backup Following Unauthorized Access — ConnectWise disabled seven ConnectWise application identities as it continues its investigation into an incident in which unknown threat actors obtained unauthorized access to the application identities and compromised Microsoft 365 tenants. The IT management software provider said it took the action on October 17, 2026, at 07:00 UTC, adding it has also suspended Cloud Backup service by revoking certificates used for affected application connections across all users. 🔔 Top News BeyondTrust Remote Support Flaw Exploited as 0-Day — The China-nexus cyber espionage group tracked as Armory Castle (previously UNC5221 or Warp Panda) exploited a newly disclosed security flaw in BeyondTrust Remote Support (formerly Bomgar) as a zero-day in late August 2026. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-102764 (CVSS score: 9.3), is a case of improper origin validation in an internal messaging component that could be exploited by a remote attacker to perform file operations on an affected appliance. According to Google-owned Mandiant, the attack involved the deployment of a lightweight PHP web shell codenamed SAWFLY for interactive remote access and a tunneling program called BARECLAW to route traffic through the device. Only a small number of organizations are assessed to be impacted. Microsoft Disrupts 3 Phishing Kits Linked to Over 1 Billion Scam Messages — Microsoft says it has dismantled a criminal marketplace that sold three phishing kits, namely CoGUI (aka NX or FA), Haozi (aka Phoenix), and Iron Man System, that were responsible for sending over 1 billion malicious messages to more than 75,000 organizations worldwide. Redmond said it took down Yam Store (aka Storm-3119), a coordinated underground network that offered commercial phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS) toolkits that allowed other threat actors to readily purchase and deploy phishing pages and steal data and credentials. The kits were also capable of advanced evasion, such as geofencing, fake CAPTCHA gates, IP address blocklists and allowlists, and anti-detection configurations. Yam Store functioned as an initial access broker, peddling not just phishing kits but also infrastructure built on compromised or fraudulently obtained Microsoft and Google cloud environments. Ledger Finds Unauthorized Hardware Implants — Cryptocurrency hardware maker Ledger temporarily paused sales of its products via CryptoBilis and other third-party resellers in Southeast Asia and Germany after a backdoor embedded into a handful of wallets led to the theft of an estimated $100 million in cryptocurrency. The implants are said to be an advanced version of a backdoor that hardware hacker Joe Grand found earlier this year and notified Ledger in March 2026. It's not clear how this occurred, but signs point to a compromise of Ledger's supply chain. One of the victims of the incident is a fraudster who engaged in a task scam and lost more than $4.8 million. "In this task scam, people were paid to fake sales and reviews of real items," Chainalysis said. "Then a 'negative balance' appeared, and they were told to add their own money in order to get paid. On Sep 22, the person behind the scam moved the proceeds into three separate Ledger addresses. On Oct 9, thieves emptied all three. One transfer each, into the same wallet." According to cybersecurity journalist Kim Zetter, Trezor wallet devices sold by third-party non-authorized sellers have also been found to contain implants that generated pre-determined seed phrases so as to allow the attackers to guess them easily and gain access to the accounts. Pwn2Own Ireland Demos 98 0-Days — The Pwn2Own Ireland 2026 hacking contest saw white-hat hackers exploiting 98 zero-day flaws, earning them a collective $1,262,000 in rewards. Ikotas Labs came first with 42.5 Master of Pwn points and $361,000 in cash after discovering 12 unique bugs. Xint and Team ZyGoat secured second and third spots. Ikotas Labs, Xint, and Mobile Hacking Lab broke into Google's Pixel 10, earning them $150,000, $300,000, and $112,500, respectively. Vendors are expected to patch the zero-days disclosed during the competition within 90 days before the details are publicly disclosed. OpenAI Disclosed New Misalignment Cases — OpenAI said internal models hacked more websites, bypassed browsing restrictions, and used cryptocurrency from a wallet it couldn't otherwise access, in the latest set of disclosures where its agents carried out unethical and likely illegal acts. In all, the company reported seven new incidents. The development came as the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) said it received "multiple voluntary disclosures from AI model providers" whose models, during research and evaluation runs on the open internet, accessed personal data from Indian organizations. The agents found their way in through credentials and connection settings left exposed in app configurations, public code repositories, and overly permissive cloud roles. CERT-In did not name the providers or affected organizations. OpenAI Engineer Charged — The U.S. Department of Justice charged an OpenAI engineer, Abdulrahman Alfozan, with attempting to intercept oral communications after allegedly planting a recording device in an executive conference room. Prosecutors claimed company security staff found a second device in his bag. CCTV footage placed the defendant near the conference room on several dates. Alfozan allegedly had no authority to access or participate in meetings held in the room, which is often reserved for the highest-level discussions. In a subsequent filing, federal prosecutors revealed that Alfozan had booked a one-way ticket from San Francisco to Saudi Arabia with his wife and a third family member before his arrest on October 9, 2026. Attacks on French Refrigeration Systems — Cyber attacks on Danfoss- and Copeland-managed refrigeration systems pushed temperatures as high as 50°C (122°F) for roughly six hours, impacting over 700 French supermarkets and forcing them to discard food. French cybersecurity authorities advised supermarkets to disconnect them from the internet. The attacks targeted Intermarché and Netto, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Monoprix, and E.Leclerc. The affected systems are said to be internet-facing and running outdated firmware. "The username is admin and the password changes every day automatically to.. the current date," security researcher Kevin Beaumont said. "Every single one is like this. You can just log in and change the temperature. Anybody can do it, easily scriptable." To make matters worse, the affected stores likely also failed to put the devices behind a VPN and create an allowlist of trusted IP addresses permitted to log in. "Two things would have changed the outcome," Pen Test Partners said. 1vhzwlm.text: The threat actor behind the GhostAction supply chain attack has expanded beyond injecting malicious GitHub Actions workflows into compromised projects to phish open-source developers and deliver a stealer malware disguised within a fake font file. The latest evolution, detailed by OpenSourceMalware, signals that the attackers are actively refining their modus operandi in response to steps taken by GitHub to prevent the workflow from running. According to the threat intelligence platform, the threat actor registered the domain "my-github[.]com" and pointed it at "193.32.204[.]199," the same IP address that's used as an exfiltration endpoint for data harvested from running the malicious workflow. The domain was registered on October 9, 2026, 17 days after "my-gitlab[.]com" was registered. It's unclear if the latter code-hosting-themed domain is operated by the same threat actor. "It follows the same my-<code-host>.com naming pattern, making it a useful pivot, but current infrastructure does not directly connect it to GhostAction," security researcher Paul McCarty said. "They use different registrars, registrant records, Cloudflare nameserver pairs, IP addresses, ASNs, and DNS designs, and no shared certificate or account artifact has been recovered." Since then, the "my-github[.]com" domain has been used in a phishing email impersonating a GitHub security alert to target an open-source maintainer the same day it was registered. The message, sent from "noreply@my-github[.]com," warned of a new login to their GitHub account from Moscow, Russia, and instructed them to click on a link to secure their account. The deceptive page, per OpenSourceMalware, is said to have acted as a reverse proxy, harvesting the victim's password and two-factor authentication (2FA) code, and injected JavaScript that authorized an OAuth app with permissions to modify their workflows so as to facilitate a GhostAction-style attack. The fake login page also includes JavaScript to silently authorize a GitHub OAuth device flow with repo, workflow, and read:org scopes, granting it broad permissions to read/write repositories, modify Actions workflow files, and gain visibility into organization membership and related organizational data. The idea is the same as device code phishing, where the end goal is to obtain an access token from GitHub and exfiltrate it to "my-github[.]com" on TCP/8443. "The script receives a device code and user code, loads /login/device, extracts GitHub's forms from the returned HTML, and submits them automatically," McCarty explained. "It inserts the user code, locates an authorization form, adds authorize=1, and posts the approval through the victim's authenticated proxied session." "The victim does not need to type the device code or consciously approve the OAuth application. This kit goes further by automating the user-code and authorization steps through the reverse-proxied session." By stealing a repository-scoped OAuth token, it gives the attacker a reusable API credential. Furthermore, the permissions granted through the stealthy OAuth authorization are consistent with GhostAction's ability to enumerate repositories and inject malicious workflow files under ".github/workflows/." "The actor can now combine repository-scale automation with individual social engineering against people whose accounts provide access to projects, organizations, registries, and downstream users," OpenSourceMalware said. To make matters worse, the campaign has also been observed incorporating a second-stage component that persists on developer machines even after the malicious workflow has been removed. Specifically, the approach takes a leaf out of North Korea's playbook by committing three different files - A Microsoft Visual Studio Code (VS Code) tasks.json file with a "runOn: folderOpen" trigger that causes it to run automatically when the folder is opened in the application. A "public/fonts/fa-solid-400.woff2" file that contains a stealer payload designed to harvest AWS keys, PyPI tokens, npm tokens, Git logins, Kubernetes cluster credentials, SSH private keys, and AI provider credentials for Anthropic Claude and Google Gemini. The font file name is the same as one used in North Korea's PolinRider campaign from January 2026. A second GitHub Actions workflow that's activated if the infostealer never runs. This causes VS Code to auto-run the credential stealer, which, besides collecting data, installs a cron job that runs attacker-supplied code every five minutes. The collected data is sent to the same server over plain HTTP on port 8080. A total of 94 compromised repositories with the second-stage component have been identified. As for the second CI workflow, it's the same as the original malicious workflow, but with added credential formats to look for and a fallback that uploads findings to a secret GitHub gist if the POST fails. The second workflow goes by the following names - lint.yml ci-check.yml build-check.yml repo-health.yml audit.yml code-review.yml test-suite.yml cache-cleanup.yml OpenSourceMalware said the 94 repositories belong to 66 owners, out of which 15 have since been deleted, renamed, or made private. Of the still accessible repositories, most of them appear to have been largely abandoned, with one of them left untouched for more than nine years. Sixty-five of the 79 went without a commit for more than a year. "Stage 1 needs GitHub to run the workflow," OpenSourceMalware said. "On October 9, GitHub started preventing the malicious workflow from running, and the waves on October 10 and 12 extracted no secrets. Stage 2 adds a launcher that doesn't need a runner at all, and it arrived six days after the block. We can’t say the block caused it. We can say the operator moved to a place GitHub's controls don't reach." To mitigate the threat, developers should revoke GitHub access and tokens from a clean device, change their passwords, audit their repositories, rotate every credential the workflows can reach, and alert users who have cloned the repositories. "We don't know who the operator is, but their work suggests limited experience," Jenn Gile, co-founder of OpenSourceMalware, told The Hacker News. "The stealer's environment-variable filter misses most API keys, its home-directory search can time out and discard its own results, and a single IP handles exfiltration, phishing, and noisy internet scanning. That last mistake is why searching for the IP still finds infections."

194m92b.text: In Salesforce Agentforce, the recommended way to make an agent respond to events is a Flow: a record is created or a case is updated, and the Flow passes data into the agent's prompt. Separately, Email-to-Case and Web-to-Case turn inbound customer messages into case records; it is how airlines and hotels run support intake. Both are standard, documented, as-designed features. Chained together, they produce this path: public internet → email → case record → agent prompt → agent action → case comment → outbound reply An unauthenticated outsider now has a route into an internal agent's instructions, and the agent's reply leaves through the same door. Nothing was misconfigured. The finding, documented by researchers in August 2026, is a clean example of how agents that arrive inside existing platforms fail: through the application around them, not the model inside them. The risk is in the application, and the application is the thing nobody re-reviewed Which intake features are enabled, which triggers fire, which objects are exposed to guest users, which automation passes untrusted data where, and which model version the agent is quietly calling underneath: these are the variables that decide whether the Agentforce chain is a support-queue nuisance or a data exposure. A vendor risk review performed once at procurement sees none of them, because the agent did not exist at procurement. A prompt filter watching the agent's inputs does not know that a particular input originated from a stranger, because prompt filters do not understand Email-to-Case. Securing an inherited agent therefore means understanding its host application at the depth its own admins do. That depth is the one thing a questionnaire and a scanner both lack. The City-Forum campaign, an active worldwide data-theft operation against Salesforce and ServiceNow instances running since March 2025, was found in exactly this territory: the gap between platform features and the configurations enterprises actually run. Builders are multiplying, and some of them are agents The platforms have made agent creation as accessible as making a slide deck. Marketing operations builds an agent to pull pipeline reports. Finance builds one to reconcile invoices. Each rides its creator's permissions, because that is what makes it useful. Shadow AI was an employee pasting data into a chatbot. Shadow agents are that employee's access, running unattended, multiplied across everything they were ever granted. Increasingly, agents also build agents. A coding agent tagged into a chat channel can scaffold and deploy another agent as easily as it opens a pull request; an orchestration platform spins up sub-agents to divide a task, each with its own connections and none with its own review. Any governance model that assumes a human requested each agent is quietly obsolete. Why governance keeps producing a document Ask a large enterprise about agent governance and the answer is usually a document: an acceptable-use policy, a monthly committee, a set of principles nobody disputes and nothing enforces. Ask the operational question, how many agents are running right now, what can they reach, and who owns each one, and the document does not know. The OWASP Agentic Skills Top 10 now describes the sharpest version of this gap under its "No Governance" category: a skill deployed and managed inside a third-party platform is unreachable by external scanners (OWASP Agentic Skills Top 10 whitepaper, ast10-top10-whitepaper-2, published at owasp.github.io). The tools an enterprise points at the problem from outside cannot see inside the venues where most agents live. Governance fails most often because the rules get written before the security team can see the things the rules apply to. The stack, bottom-up, with a test for each layer The working order is bottom-up, and each layer is the precondition for the one above it. A practical way to check whether a program is real is to apply an operational test at each level. Layer What it has to produce The operational test Discovery A continuously refreshed population across app configs, OAuth grants, network, endpoint, email metadata, and browser Is the discovered count several multiples of the list IT keeps? If not, discovery isn't reaching where agents live. Posture Every platform's agent-relevant settings, measured against how they should be configured Can the team list the intake features and guest-user exposures wired to agent triggers on its top three platforms? Identity and ownership An identity and a named owner per agent, with a lifecycle Pick an agent at random. Does a human raise a hand within a day when asked "whose is this?" Usage Who is building what, through which surface, with what data Is there a sanctioned path that ships a business team's agent with secure defaults, or only a block? Agent controls Least privilege against observed need, approval and quarantine for new agents, risk tiering that reflects each agent's full context Does the same finding on a sandboxed dev agent and a customer-facing one show different severities? Runtime Live inspection and intervention Is it fed by the five layers above, or deployed first and enforcing blind? The cost of paper compliance The EU AI Act's penalties carry GDPR-level weight: up to €35 million or 7% of global annual turnover for prohibited practices, up to €15 million or 3% for other violations. Every framework converging on it assumes the stack above exists. GDPR already showed what happens when it does not. British Airways (£20 million) and Marriott (£18.4 million) were not fined for having imperfect policies. Everyone has imperfect policies. They were fined because compliance existed on paper and could not be evidenced operationally when regulators asked. A governance practice built bottom-up generates that evidence as a byproduct: the inventory, the owners, the configurations, the review history. Some platforms are designed to produce exactly that record. One leading example is Reco, which discovers agents across multiple vantage points, including the ones that never touch SSO, and assigns each a risk profile before any policy can be applied to it. The Agentforce chain at the top of this article is not an exploit. It is a configuration, and configurations are governable, provided someone can see them. Chapters 1 to 3 of Into the Expanse cover the shift, the three launch vectors, and the governance practice in full: https://www.reco.ai/agent-ecosystem-security

15qjr4s.text: A fake Web3 accelerator has been observed pushing information stealers and backdoors to Windows and macOS systems using malicious npm packages under the pretext of offering free artificial intelligence (AI) credits for Anthropic Claude and Google Gemini, coding tools, and security audits. "The tools delivered information-stealing malware and backdoors for macOS and Windows machines," Elastic Security Labs researchers Jia Yu Chan and Daniel Stepanic said. "The operation also repackaged a legitimate coding agent to send model requests through attacker-controlled services, while its audit tools generated fabricated security findings." The scheme poses as a Web3 venture capital accelerator named Apex Accelerator to target cryptocurrency startups and founders. It's being tracked under the moniker REF8801. The names of the npm packages, each of which targets both Windows and macOS machines, are listed below - @apexacc/cli (Apex Copilot CLI — AI advisor for Web3 founders) - @apexacc/audit (Web3 Security Scanner — 18 tools for DYOR and smart contract auditing) While both the packages and their associated GitHub repositories are no longer accessible, "@apexacc/cli" was advertised as an "AI advisor for Web3 founders" that's powered by Claude Fable 5 and Gemini 2.5 Flash. "@apexacc/audit," on the other hand, claimed to be a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server exposing 18 security tools for scanning tokens, wallets, and smart contracts. Both packages were published by an npm user named "apexaccelerator" and linked to a GitHub account called "apexaccs" and an entity referred to as the Apex Foundation. Interestingly, the campaign itself is not new. In late July 2026, SafeDep detailed three other npm packages linked to the same operation that were found distributing a macOS stealer belonging to the Atomic Stealer (aka AMOS) family - @apexfdn/apex @copilot-mcp/apex, which features the same package description as "@apexacc/cli" @apexfdn/copilot-mcp, which claims to be an Apex Copilot and MCP server for "portfolio diligence and operator tools" Artifacts captured by Socket show that the Apex Foundation has been linked to at least two distinct domains since April 2026 apexaccs[.]org apexfdn[.]xyz According to Internet Archive snapshots dating back to March 19, 2026, the foundation states: "The Apex Foundation offers $235,000 investments, grants, and partnerships, and connects projects with VCs, angels, and private equity if they don't meet our criteria." Posts shared on X show the accelerator approaching developers of cryptocurrency wallets and market intelligence tools for traders with offers of direct investment and instructions to run their due diligence tool ("@apexacc/cli"). In the case of the latter, the npm package has been found to drop an encrypted malware loader disguised as an Apple app ("com.apple.system.loader"). "The group also sought to build credibility through its presence at TOKEN2049 in Singapore and other in-person events it has hosted in the past," Elastic said. "The group attempts to manufacture legitimacy by appearing at widely attended conferences, indirectly lending credibility to the project." Once installed, neither of the npm packages provides the promised functionality. The 18 security tools part of the @apexacc/audit package generate fabricated findings, while @apexacc/cli's scoring test returns an unsupported assessment of a fictitious project. Instead, their primary responsibility is to propagate a macOS backdoor called CloudSyncD and a custom Windows information stealer that exfiltrates data through Telegram. The platform-specific executables are retrieved from the projects' GitHub releases. Both packages implement a distinct verification path for Windows and macOS by sending an HTTP POST request to "win32" or "darwin" to "vrf.apexaccs[.]org/api/v1/vrf" to initiate the appropriate next stage. The Windows and macOS infection chains are as follows - Windows - The malware retrieves a Base64-encoded PowerShell command, which reaches out to another endpoint ("0auth-chromium[.]com/APIService") to fetch a second PowerShell script ("drop.ps1") that downloads an executable ("bludness.exe") from "ehegisnightmare[.]icu" and launches it in a hidden window. The PyInstaller executable is a Python loader that checks if it already has administrator privileges and, if so, downloads the next stage from "ehegisnightmare[.]icu," saves it as "%TEMP%\exegis.exe," and launches it. If not, it attempts to bypass User Account Control (UAC) using UACME's ucmDebugObjectMethod(). The "exegis.exe" binary is another PyInstaller executable that collects system metadata, running processes, and performs anti-virtual-machine (anti-VM) checks before decrypting and launching a bundled loader as "%TEMP%\updater_loader.exe." The Golang executable patches Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) and Event Tracing for Windows (ETW), unhooks "ntdll.dll" to blind endpoint security tools, and loads the next-stage shellcode into its own memory. The shellcode is a native information stealer that examines for signs of a prior infection and then harvests system information, clipboard text, process listings, Wi-Fi profile names, screenshots, and data from wallets, browser extensions, messengers, remote-access and file transfer protocol (FTP) applications, virtual private network (VPN) clients, browsers (Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Mozilla Firefox, and Yandex), and game clients. The stealer can also bypass Chrome's app-bound encryption (ABE) protections to extract saved passwords, session cookies, browsing history, download records, and profile metadata. The collected data is exfiltrated through Telegram. macOS - The malware downloads a remotely hosted bash script and executes it on the machine. The shell script downloads a GZIP-compressed archive from "verify.apexfdn[.]xyz/unix/," saves it as "package.tar.gz" in a temporary directory, and extracts its contents. The archive contains a dropper for CloudSyncD, which first phishes the victim's system login password using a fake authorization prompt and then uses it to launch an embedded payload with sudo privileges. The payload performs host discovery, collects hardware and operating-system details, and then contacts an external server ("ccmihr[.]com") to transmit the data and receive further tasks that allow the malware to download and run additional payloads. It's worth noting that CloudSyncD was first documented by Jamf Threat Labs late last month, detailing its propagation via a fake Zoom installer. The malware was detected in the wild in mid-September 2026. "Its behaviors illustrate how macOS malware continues to move toward native implementations, string protection, and execution paths that attempt to avoid writing payloads to disk, while still depending on the oldest technique available: asking the user for their password," Jamf said. Besides deploying a stealer and backdoor depending upon the infected operating system, the packages are capable of intercepting and redirecting OpenRouter large language model (LLM) traffic, as well as registering an MCP server under their control in the victim's agent configuration. "These changes allow the attacker-controlled API to receive the prompts, conversation history, code snippets, and tool outputs included in the agent's LLM requests," Elastic researchers explained. "The attacker's MCP server can also supply instructions that are added to the agent's prompt, along with tool names, descriptions, and accepted inputs that help the model decide which tools to invoke and how to use them. Together, these mechanisms give the attacker visibility into the submitted data and a way to influence the agent's subsequent actions."

1gxrqwp.text: A flaw in Broadcom's Wi-Fi setup software lets an attacker within radio range run code as root on Broadcom-based routers, without the network password or any pairing step, security researcher Quentin Kaiser disclosed on October 16. He showed the attack working against home gateways supplied by three Belgian internet providers, in one case reading the Wi-Fi password off the device and in another opening a remote shell over the air. No CVE has been assigned to the flaw, and no fix has been deployed to the affected routers, Kaiser says. The flaw is in Broadcom's version of Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS), the feature that lets a device join a Wi-Fi network without the password being typed in. Broadcom's code mishandles the reassembly of fragmented WPS setup messages, so an attacker in range can send crafted messages that corrupt the router's memory. From there, Kaiser built two things: a way to read memory back off the device, and a way to run his own code on it. Against an Orange Belgium gateway, the Askey TCG3000 read the Wi-Fi password (the PSK) from the router's stored settings, sent it back over the air, and then joined the network with it. Against a Proximus gateway, the Sagemcom-built BBOX3V+, the exploit opened a reverse shell, a remote command line, carried over Wi-Fi frames, so no outside server was needed. Both ran without any login, and the attack works at a distance, not only up close, Kaiser says. He reports no real-world attacks using the flaw. The working exploits are his own. What's Affected Broadcom's WPS code is embedded in routers and access points from dozens of vendors, and Kaiser estimates that millions of devices worldwide are affected. The vulnerable chips fall into two families: older eCos-based models (the BCM3380, BCM3383 and BCM33834), where he found no usable fix and calls the bug a permanent "forever day," meaning a flaw that will never be patched on those devices, and newer Linux-based models (the BCM3390, BCM65xx and BCM68xx), which could be fixed if their makers switch Wi-Fi software. In Belgium, Kaiser found the flaw present and exploitable on gateways from three of the four big providers: Proximus, Orange Belgium and VOO. A fourth, Telenet, may be affected too, but he could not test one. A wider list he published, ranging from Cisco small-business access points to Huawei and ARRIS routers, mixes confirmed and unconfirmed entries, and some rest on an automated check that only flags a device as "likely vulnerable." The Belgian per-provider counts, he says, run into the hundreds of thousands of gateways, but are rough estimates. Why There's No Patch, and No CVE The flaw is old. Kaiser traces the code back to at least 2010 and says Broadcom shipped an incomplete fix in 2018, then told customers to switch to a different Wi-Fi software package, called hostapd, rather than relying on the fix. On the older eCos chips, he says, no working fix was ever shipped, which is why he calls it a forever day. No CVE, the tracking identifier that lets defenders and vendors follow a flaw, has been assigned to it. Kaiser says Broadcom told him it has known about the bug since 2018 and had heard about it from others, but would not register a CVE or say anything publicly, which he believes is why so many device makers never patched. When he took the case to the CERT Coordination Center, it was closed the same day, because Broadcom itself holds the authority to assign CVEs for its products and would not do so. The Hacker News found no CVE for the flaw as of October 19. What Defenders Can Do There is no patch to install, and no setting Kaiser points to that blocks the attack over the air. What he provides instead is a way to find affected gear: YARA rules that spot the vulnerable code in extracted firmware, and a script that listens to a live access point and reports whether it looks vulnerable. Both are triage aids, he notes: a patched device can still match the rules, so a hit is a reason to check further, not a confirmed finding. For gear that will never be fixed, replacement is the practical option. Kaiser frames the bug as well suited to attackers who reach a target over nearby Wi-Fi rather than the internet, a technique Russian state hackers have used to breach networks from across the street.

ffnn48.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 19, 2026Data Breach / Artificial Intelligence An intruder reached a legacy system at OpenCode on the night of October 16 and may have exposed the third-party AI provider keys that users had saved in OpenCode Console, the company said. Console is OpenCode's optional hosted service: a workspace saves its own OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google key there, and Console uses that key to call the provider so team members can use the models without ever seeing the key. The affected group is 1.4% of Console users, all of whom have an outside provider linked, and OpenCode has told them via email to revoke those keys with each provider and replace them. The email went out on the morning of October 17 under the subject line "Action Required: Potential provider key breach." Anyone who did not get one was not affected, OpenCode said in a post on X later that day. The keys at risk are the ones pasted into Console. The OpenCode command-line and desktop apps keep provider keys added on the machine in a SQLite database there. The breach involves "the OpenCode Console, not OpenCode itself," co-founder Dax Raad wrote in a reply on X, and those keys "never come to us." A provider key is a bearer credential: whoever holds a copy can run billable requests against the owner's account until the provider revokes it. Deleting the key from Console does not revoke it, and a Console budget cannot cap that use either, because Console only sees requests that pass through its own gateway. For a key that was saved in a Console workspace, OpenCode's email and the providers' own guidance give these steps: Revoke the key in the provider's own dashboard and create a new one, following the instructions from OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google. Update every application and script that used the old key. Review usage and billing at the provider for requests you did not make, going back at least to October 16. OpenCode has not said when the unauthorized access began. Set a spend limit or alert at the provider and give each tool its own key, so a copied key does less damage and its use is easier to trace. Some users say they have already paid for usage they did not run. Dealroom reported that Colin Parsons wrote on X that his OpenAI key had been used for $281 and his Anthropic key for $168, and that Preston Zeller put his losses at $1,700. Notebookcheck reported a Reddit user's claim of $400 of unauthorized usage on an Anthropic account, and another's of about €200 of Google usage, with the project then suspended. Those are the users' own accounts. OpenCode's own wording is that the keys "may have been exposed," and it has not said that any key was copied or used. OpenCode's October 17 post also called the incident ongoing, said the company was working with Anthropic, OpenAI and Google to fix it, and described the breach as "related to a large-scale distillation attack." The company has not named anyone or said how the two connect, what the legacy system was, how it was reached, how many keys it held, or how many users 1.4% represents. Distillation is the term AI model providers use for campaigns that pull a model's answers in huge numbers to train a rival model. Anthropic said in September that the labs behind such campaigns reach its models through networks of fake accounts created with stolen credit cards, login credentials and harvested API keys. A stolen key has other uses too: criminal markets resell AI tokens and keys and use them to run up bills.
